scenes.synopsis: Open on the morning after the Last Assembly — victory, and the household already counting its cost.
scenes.prose:
> "You were magnificent last night," Letitia said, not looking up from the household book, "and the laundry bill has tripled."
> Rose stood in the doorway of the morning room in her dressing gown, hair still pinned from the night before, and regarded her aunt with the weary amusement of a general being presented with the quartermaster's reckoning after the battle. The house smelled of cold wax and spent flowers. Somewhere below, a footman was moving chairs, and each scrape across the parquet sounded like a small, reproachful cough.
> "The Assembly was a triumph, Letitia. Must it be annotated?"
> "Triumphs are the most expensive line in this book." Letitia turned a page with the care of a woman defusing something. "Candles, musicians, the second supper — the one we did not order but could not decline — and Mr. Quill's fee for the affidavit service, which I have marked in red because it frightens me."
> Rose crossed to the window. Hartwell House sat quiet in the September light, the street below going about its business as if no one had nearly lost everything the night before. A crossing-sweeper worked the corner with philosophical patience. A carriage she did not know rattled past without stopping. The ordinary world had resumed, punctually, as though ruin had merely been a rumor it had declined to believe.
> "Rackham is destroyed. The estate is saved. That is what the red ink bought."
> "The estate is saved," Letitia agreed, "and everyone in London knows it, which is precisely the problem." She closed the book. "Before the ruin was proved engineered, we were pitied. Pity is private. Now we are watched. Watching is public, and the public expects to be entertained."
> "By what? By me?"
> "By the price of it. People do not trust a ruin reversed without a fee somewhere." Letitia rose and came to stand beside her, and her voice softened by a fraction. "You did not sleep."
> "I slept," Rose lied, and felt the familiar, childish comfort of the untruth.
> "You never lie well before breakfast. Drink your tea before it does something irreversible." Letitia pressed the cup into her hands. "And Rose — whatever the morning costs, it costs less than last night nearly did. Remember that when the bills come dressed as callers."
> Rose drank. The tea was strong, and faintly bitter, and exactly what the morning required.

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the physical aftermath of victory: what winning has done to the house itself.
scenes.prose:
> The Assembly's flowers were still dying in the great hall.
> *(System: Hartwell House shows the morning after — chairs stacked along the walls, candlesticks half-guttered, a single glove dropped beneath a window seat like a casualty.)*
> Rose walked the length of the room she had saved. The floor gleamed where the dancers had been; the air held the stale sweetness of wax and orange water and crushed petals, and a faint, sourceless chill where the doors had stood open too long into the September night. Victory had a smell, she decided, and it was not unlike a church after a wedding nobody was quite sure about.
> She picked up the glove — not hers; some guest's, flung or forgotten in the press of the evening — and turned it over in her hands. Kid, dove-grey, expensively cut, the thumb worn soft by habit. Somebody's evening, abandoned at the height of it. She set it on the mantel beside the Hartwell clock, which had kept ticking through the whole of it — through the toasts, the affidavits, the moment Rackham's ruin had been proved engineered and the room had gone silent in that particular way of a ballroom deciding what to believe.
> Ruin, exposure, rescue, triumph. The clock had not paused for any of them.
> *(System: a texture moment — no choices, no cost.)*
> "You survived us," she told the clock, and wound it, and the key turned with the small, obedient resistance of something that had never once doubted its own continuance. She envied it that. There had been months — she could count them now, and did not wish to — when the house had felt like a place holding its breath, waiting for the ticking to stop. Last night the breath had been let out all at once, in a ballroom, in public. The relief had been magnificent. The aftermath, she was discovering, was housekeeping.
> Behind her, the footmen moved the stacked chairs with elaborate quiet, as though the room itself were sleeping off the evening. Rose let them. She had spent a season learning to command rooms. This morning, the room could command itself.

scenes.synopsis: Letitia names the new danger — not debt, but audience; Drummond's terms are still withheld, and the ton is watching the Hartwells wait.
scenes.prose:
> "Mrs. Nance Bell has already printed," Letitia said at breakfast, folding the Gazette with the deliberation of a woman handling evidence. "Eat your eggs. The news will not improve them, but the eggs will improve the news."
> "The Assembly was yesterday. The paper cannot have—"
> "The paper has. The proprietor misses nothing." Letitia slid the sheet across the cloth, past the marmalade, and tapped the second column with one decisive finger. "Read it. It is not cruel. That is what troubles me."
> Rose read, and read again, and set the paper down with unusual care, as though it were warm. "'Survives.' 'Waits.' It is only a paragraph, Letitia."
> "It is a paragraph that places a price on you in public. The ton does not watch passively, Rose. It prices. And you are, at this moment, the most interesting price in London — the ruin reversed, the engineer of it destroyed by your evidence, the house standing when every bookmaker in the clubs had laid odds against it." Letitia buttered her toast with the briskness of a woman who had decided not to be alarmed before ten. "Do you know what the ton does with an interesting price? It watches it move. And it takes a commission on the movement."
> "Then let them look." Rose reached for the marmalade with more attention than it deserved. "Looking is not billing."
> "No," said Letitia, "but it is the first step toward billing, and you would do well to remember who did the looking before the ruin. Nobody watched us then. Everybody watches us now. The difference is not flattering." She paused. "And there is the matter of Drummond's terms, still unnamed, still outstanding, like a guest who has not yet sent her regrets."
> The toast, Rose thought, tasted of ash and strategy. She ate it anyway, and folded the Gazette herself, and found that her hands were steadier than her appetite.

scenes.synopsis: Texture — Rose alone with the estate papers, feeling the shape of a victory that has not yet been paid for.
scenes.prose:
> The estate papers were stacked on the escritoire in order of dread.
> *(System: the morning's quiet — Quill's affidavit copy, the banker's letter confirming the debts struck, the solicitor's draft of the Hartwell settlements.)*
> Rose ran a finger down the spine of the bundle. Every page was a door that had closed behind her, and every closed door had a cost written on the inside in someone else's hand. The ruin had been engineered — proved, printed, believed — and the engineer destroyed at her own choosing. That was the part the ton applauded: the girl who had faced down Rackham in a ballroom and lived to dance the last set.
> The part the ton did not applaud was Drummond's withheld terms. Lady Agatha Drummond had lent the Hartwells the rope of public credit when the ruin was at its worst — her name spoken in the right rooms, her carriage seen at the right door — and Drummond did not lend rope for sport. Somewhere, in some drawer of that formidable lady's, there was a ledger with Rose's name in it, and the entry was not yet written. Rose could feel it, the unwritten entry, the way one feels a draught from a door one cannot see.
> She lifted the banker's letter and read the confirmation again — the debts struck, the settlements drafted — and tried to feel the relief the words were supposed to confer. It came, but thinly, like tea poured through too much water. Victory, she was learning, was not a state. It was a receipt. And receipts, presented at the wrong counter, could be refused.
> "Win first," Rose told the papers. "Pay after." The papers declined to comment, and she stacked them again in their order of dread, and went down to breakfast feeling precisely as wealthy as a woman who has won everything and owns nothing she has not already promised away — to Drummond, to the ton, to the watching street.

scenes.synopsis: The household staff's loyalty frayed — Rose overhears what survival costs below stairs.
scenes.prose:
> "They say she sold the silver to do it," came the whisper from the passage, and Rose stopped with her hand on the door of the stillroom, arrested mid-step like a woman caught eavesdropping in her own house — which, she reflected, was exactly what she was.
> "She did not sell the silver," said the second voice — old Marlow, the housekeeper, sharp as a carving knife and twice as certain. "The silver is where it has always been. But something was sold, and don't you ask me what, because the knowing of it is above your station and mine, and the asking of it is above your wages."
> "They say the jewels went first. The Hartwell diamonds—"
> "The Hartwell diamonds are in the strongbox, and you will mind the stillroom shelves and not the strongbox, or I shall mind your notice for you."
> Rose stepped back from the door rather than forward. Below stairs, the victory was already being priced in rumor: the silver sold, the jewels pawned, the house mortgaged twice over, Miss Hartwell's dresses let out by a dressmaker working on credit and hope. The truth — that Rackham's engineered ruin had collapsed under its own evidence — was less interesting than the fiction, and fiction, as Marlow would have been the first to say, traveled faster than the post.
> She found Letitia in the morning room and reported the exchange without comment, and Letitia listened with her mending held perfectly still.
> "The staff will talk," Letitia said at last. "Staff always talk. The question is what they talk to, and to whom."
> "They talk to each other."
> "For now." Letitia resumed her stitching. "Houses leak, Rose. It is their nature — the walls are thin and the wages are thinner, and a good story is the only currency below stairs that never devalues. Mind what you say inside yours."
> "I said nothing."
> "Then mind what others hear you almost say." Letitia bit off her thread. "It amounts to the same, once it reaches the passage."

scenes.synopsis: Texture — Élise at the fitting table, already reading the season's new brief in Rose's posture.
scenes.prose:
> Élise arrived before noon with a basket of muslins and the expression of a general surveying a battlefield.
> "The Assembly gown survived," she announced, circling Rose with a critical eye that missed nothing and forgave less. "You did not. Look at you — shoulders like a woman carrying a piano, and a jaw set for a week of disagreeable callers. Sit. No, stand. Stand is better for the carrying of pianos."
> "I am carrying a piano. It is called the Hartwell name."
> "Then we shall dress the pianist." Élise pinned a length of pearl-grey muslin to Rose's shoulder and stepped back, head tilted. "The season has turned, chérie. Last spring you dressed to be believed — every seam a plea, every collar a character reference. This autumn you dress to be paid — or rather, to be seen paying. There is a difference, and the difference is in the collar."
> "What does the collar say?"
> "That you owe nothing and know it." Élise's smile was all professional confidence. "A collar to the jaw says: I have read the ledger and I am not afraid of the total. A collar at the throat says: let us discuss terms like civilized women. An open collar says — " she paused — "things we do not say before noon, and not to creditors."
> Rose studied herself in the glass, the muslin falling in its provisional folds. "And if the ton does not believe the collar?"
> "The ton believes what it is told by cloth, my love. It has no other education." Élise pinned a second length, burgundy this time, and the two fabrics lay side by side like two different arguments. "We shall see whether London believes the collar or the rumor. My money — " she tapped the pearl-grey — "is on the collar. The collar does not gossip. The collar does not leak. The collar merely stands, and lets everyone else do the talking."

scenes.synopsis: Letitia presses the question of Drummond's withheld terms — the one unpaid debt that matters.
scenes.prose:
> "She has said nothing," Letitia said, when the tea had gone cold between them and the afternoon had settled into the particular stillness of a house waiting for the post. "One day since the Assembly, and Lady Agatha Drummond has not called, not written, not so much as nodded at you across a room. That silence is not absence, Rose. It is a bill being drafted."
> "She held our credit when no one else would. I am grateful."
> "Gratitude is a currency she accepts, but she sets the exchange rate, and she does not publish it in advance." Letitia set down her cup with a small, definite sound. "You chose to withhold her terms when the ruin fell — your call, your right, and I backed you in it. But a withheld term is not a forgiven term. It is a term accumulating interest in the dark, and the dark is where Drummond does her best arithmetic."
> Rose looked out at the square, where a carriage she did not recognize had stopped at the corner and stood there a moment too long before moving on. "Do you think she will be cruel?"
> "I think," said Letitia, "that she will be exact. Cruelty would be a kindness — it would give you something to fight, something to resent, something to tell Augusta about over tea. Exactness gives you only something to pay." She followed Rose's gaze to the window. "Was that carriage known to you?"
> "No." Rose watched it turn the corner with the particular attention of a woman learning to watch carriages. "It is the third today I have not known."
> "Then London has begun its audit." Letitia rose and rang for fresh tea, briskly, as though bustle could answer uncertainty. "Drink something warm. Whatever Drummond is drafting, it will be presented in daylight, on heavy paper, and you will meet it the way you met the Assembly — standing, and in the right collar."

scenes.synopsis: Rose's private resolve — she will follow the money up the chain, not merely survive the social price.
scenes.prose:
> Alone in the library, Rose opened Quill's memorandum on Rackham's affairs and read it a third time.
> The ruin had been engineered — but engineering has engineers, and engineers have creditors. Rackham's debts had not evaporated with his disgrace; they had scattered, like shot from a fired gun, lodging in émigré notes, in foreign paper, in obligations that predated the Hartwell ruin by decades and would outlast it by longer. Somewhere up that chain was the money's true shape — not the ruin, which had been the symptom, but the system that had made the ruin profitable — and the shape had a name she did not yet know.
> She took up a pen and wrote, in the margin, a single line: *Follow it up.*
> It was not a plan. It was barely a sentence. But it was the first thing since the Assembly that had felt like her own choice rather than the consequence of someone else's — not a reaction to Rackham, not a debt to Drummond, not a performance for the ton. Hers. The pen scratched against the paper with a sound like a small door unlocking.
> The library door clicked — a footman with the afternoon post, letters fanned on the salver like a losing hand. Rose set the memorandum aside, but the line stayed in her head, ticking like the Hartwell clock.
> *Follow it up.*
> Up past Rackham, past the scattered debts, past the émigré notes with their faded continental hands, to whoever had understood, before she was born, that a Hartwell could be ruined at a profit. She folded the memorandum and slipped it into the escritoire's locked drawer — not hidden, exactly, but no longer lying about in the open like an invitation. Letitia was right about houses leaking. The library had ears, the passages had memories, and a single line in a margin was the kind of thing that traveled.
> But it was hers, and she would keep it.

scenes.synopsis: Drummond's summons — a card, a time, no subject; the bill is being presented.
scenes.prose:
> The card arrived with the afternoon post, on paper so heavy it could have served as a weapon.
> *(System: the footman presents it on a salver, as if it might detonate. Rose takes it up.)*
> It bore no crest, no seal — only engraved text in a hand of absolute authority:
>
> *Lady Agatha Drummond*
> *At home tomorrow, eleven o'clock.*
> *Miss Hartwell is expected.*
>
> No subject. No please. No reason given, because none was owed. A time, a place, and the full weight of a name that had held the Hartwells' credit through the worst of the ruin — presented on paper that had clearly cost more than the words it carried.
> "Expected," Rose read aloud. "Not invited. Expected."
> Letitia, who had gone very still, set down her embroidery and came to look over Rose's shoulder. "She does not summon people she means to ruin. She ruins them without the courtesy of a warning — a word dropped at the right dinner, a carriage seen turning away from the wrong door. A summons is — if not kind — at least procedural."
> "Procedure for what?"
> "For the naming of the price." Letitia took the card and studied it as one might study a writ, turning it to the light. "Eleven o'clock. A morning call, formal, witnessed by daylight. She means the ton to know you went to her — the hour guarantees the street will be full of callers' carriages. She means you to know that she means it. There is no softness in this card, Rose. There is not even the pretense of softness."
> Rose turned the card over. The back was blank — no hint, no softening, nothing carried over from the engraver's hand. Just the weight of the paper, and the weight of the name, and the small, cold certainty settling in her chest that the three days of silence had been the drafting, and this was the presentation.
> "Then I shall go," she said, "and I shall be dressed for it."
> "You shall," said Letitia, already reaching for the bell to summon Élise. "And the collar, my love, will be to the jaw."

scenes.synopsis: ★ DRESSING RITUAL — preparation for the formal morning call on Drummond. Twenty decomposed micro-decisions at 5 coins each (≈100 coins; S2 ritual pricing — S1's tutorial-free ritual does not apply). Jewels from owned pieces only; the jewel shelf is always open but never a ritual step.
scenes.prose:
> *(System: the occasion brief is published.)*
>
> **Occasion brief — A Creditor's Morning Call**
> *Lady Agatha Drummond, eleven o'clock. The brief is the armor of respectability: morning dress for a woman who owes nothing and must be seen to know it. Editorial criterion — every choice is judged on whether it says* paid in full *without saying a word about money. Dull is death; defiant is suicide; exact is everything.*
>
> Élise reads the brief twice, nods once, and clears the fitting table like a woman preparing a surgical tray.
>
> Élise lays out three directions on the fitting table:
>
> **A. The Pearl-Grey Citadel** — pearl-grey lutestring, high collar, silver-grey pelisse; severe, untouchable, a fortress in muslin.
> **B. The Burgundy Statement** — deep burgundy merino, velvet-trimmed spencer, jet buttons; power worn openly, a woman who has already won.
> **C. The Ivory Diplomat** — ivory jaconet with a dove-grey shawl, cameo at the throat; softness as strategy, the negotiator's dress.
>
> *(System: the player commits to a direction — remembered for the Drummond interview. Then the pins begin. Each pin costs 5 coins from play earnings; no Crown SKUs touch the ritual. Jewels come from owned pieces only — the jewel shelf is always open but never a ritual step.)*
>
> **Pin 1 — The gown's ground:** lutestring, merino, or jaconet — the fabric that carries the whole argument. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 2 — The collar's height:** to the jaw (fortress), to the throat (parley), or open (dare). *5 coins.*
> **Pin 3 — The sleeve's fullness:** leg-of-mutton restraint or plain bishop's simplicity. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 4 — The bodice's line:** seamed severity or draped ease. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 5 — The waist's emphasis:** sash, belt, or the gown's own cut speaking alone. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 6 — The skirt's sweep:** trained formality or walking-length business. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 7 — The pelisse or spencer:** silver-grey wool, velvet-trimmed merino, or dove-grey shawl. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 8 — The button's statement:** jet (mourning for the ruin), pearl (peace declared), or covered silk (discretion). *5 coins.*
> **Pin 9 — The glove's fit:** kid so close it reads as a second skin. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 10 — The glove's color:** grey, black, or ivory — each a different sentence. *5 coins.*
>
> *(Story morsel: Élise pins the collar to Rose's jaw and steps back. "Drummond will look first at your throat," she says. "Creditors always do. They are checking for the pulse of panic. Give her bone, not blood.")*
>
> **Pin 11 — The bonnet's brim:** wide (shade, distance) or close (candor, nerve). *5 coins.*
> **Pin 12 — The bonnet's trim:** ribbon, feather, or bare straw speaking for itself. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 13 — The hair beneath:** coiled severe, or softened at the temple by exactly one curl. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 14 — The shoe's heel:** low and certain. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 15 — The stocking's shade:** silk, clocked or plain. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 16 — The reticule:** small enough to prove you carry nothing to hide. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 17 — The handkerchief's edge:** lace or hemstitched plain — a creditor notices. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 18 — The scent:** orange water (innocence) or nothing at all (the boldest choice). *5 coins.*
> **Pin 19 — The posture rehearsal:** Élise walks Rose the length of the room — chin, shoulders, the door-handling of a woman expected, not invited. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 20 — The final mirror:** the whole armor, head to heel, judged against the brief's single question — *does it say paid in full?* *5 coins.*
>
> *(Story morsel: at Pin 20, Élise adjusts one jet button by a quarter inch and nods. "There," she says. "That is a woman who could look at a ledger without flinching. Drummond will hate it. Which means it is perfect.")*
>
> *(System: 20 pins × 5 coins = 100 coins drawn from play earnings. The completed direction is remembered — Drummond will react to it. Owned jewels may be added freely from the open shelf at any point, never as a step.)*

scenes.synopsis: The night before the call — Letitia's last counsel, and the household's held breath.
scenes.prose:
> "You will not sleep," Letitia said, setting a cup of chocolate by Rose's bed with the air of a woman administering medicine. "So I shall not pretend to expect it. But you will lie down, and you will be still, because Drummond can smell a sleepless night the way a hound smells fear, and you will not give her the satisfaction of the scent."
> Rose sat on the edge of the bed in her nightdress, the chosen direction hanging on the wardrobe door like a second self — the pearl-grey, or the burgundy, or the ivory, complete to the last pin, the collar at its exact height. It looked, in the candlelight, like armor waiting for its knight: patient, exact, faintly reproachful.
> "What if the price is something I cannot pay?"
> "Then you will negotiate the terms of the impossible, as women have done since Eve." Letitia drew the counterpane up with the brisk tenderness she reserved for crises. "She held our credit when the ruin was at its worst. Whatever she asks, it will be something she believes you have. Drummond does not ask for what does not exist. That is her particular cruelty and her particular mercy — she never demands the impossible, only the expensive."
> "Comforting."
> "It is meant to be exact." Letitia kissed her forehead, a thing she had not done since Rose was twelve, and the suddenness of it — the unguarded affection, unpermitted by daylight — loosened something in Rose's chest that the whole day's exactness had held shut. "Paid in full, remember. The collar says so. You have only to stand inside it and let it speak."
> "And if she asks for something the collar cannot cover?"
> "Then," said Letitia, turning down the lamp, "you will do what Hartwells have always done when the cloth runs short. You will improvise, and you will make it look like the plan."
> The house settled around them into its held-breath quiet. Rose lay down, and was still, and did not sleep.

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the walk to Drummond's house; London watching the Hartwell carriage go.
scenes.prose:
> The carriage turned into the square at ten minutes to eleven, and Rose felt the street notice.
> *(System: the morning call as procession — curtains twitching, a footman pausing mid-errand, the particular silence of a fashionable street observing a fashionable errand.)*
> She sat very straight in the chosen armor, gloves exact, bonnet brim at the rehearsed angle, and watched London watch her go to her creditor. There was no hiding this call; Drummond had seen to that with the word *expected*, engraved on heavy paper and delivered by the afternoon post like a writ. The ton would know by noon that Miss Hartwell had presented herself at Lady Agatha Drummond's door, and by dinner they would know — or invent — what it had cost. The invention, Rose suspected, would be the more expensive of the two.
> A maidservant stopped sweeping a doorstep to stare. A gentleman on horseback slowed, openly, and was rewarded with nothing — Rose kept her gaze level, her chin at Élise's rehearsed height, the very picture of a woman going about an errand of no particular consequence. *Let them look,* she thought, and was surprised to find she meant it. *The truth will be exact. The truth is always exact. It is only the price that is negotiable — and the negotiation, like the call, will be conducted in daylight.*
> The carriage stopped. The door opened. The house of Lady Agatha Drummond regarded her with all its windows like eyes — tall, grey, unblinking, the facade of a woman who had never once in her life been surprised by a caller, and did not intend to begin now.
> Rose descended, adjusted one glove by a quarter inch — Élise's quarter inch — and walked up the steps like a woman expected, not invited. The door opened before she knocked. Of course it did. Drummond's household, like Drummond, did not waste gestures on uncertainty.

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — DRUMMOND'S PRICE. The interview: Drummond names her terms — sponsor Miss Honoria Drummond, the dull but deserving niece. Reputation, not money.
scenes.prose:
> Lady Agatha Drummond received her in a morning room the color of old money, seated behind a desk that had clearly witnessed the ruin of greater houses than the Hartwells'.
> *(System: Drummond looks first at the throat — bone, not blood — and something in her expression adjusts by a fraction.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." No offer of tea. "I shall be brief, because brevity is the courtesy I extend to debtors I respect. When your house was falling, I held its credit — without security and without sentiment. The account is now due."
> "Name it," said Rose. The collar held.
> "My niece." Drummond folded her hands. "Miss Honoria Drummond. Twenty years old, respectable, accomplished in the manner of a metronome, and — I shall not insult us both — dull. Dull as ditchwater and deserving as a sermon. She requires a sponsor for the season. Not a chaperone — a *sponsor*. Your name on her invitations. Your carriage beside hers. Your introduction at the dances that matter, your afternoons given over to her calls, your visible, repeated, unmistakable endorsement."
> Rose said nothing. The afternoons — the at-homes, the musicale — all now to be shared with a girl she had never met. She understood, with a clarity like cold water, that the price had been set long before she walked up the steps.
> "It is reputation I am spending, Miss Hartwell, not money. Yours." Drummond's smile was a thin, exact thing. "You have a great deal of it at the moment, and reputation, unlike money, increases when it is visibly spent on the deserving. Refuse, and the ton will hear — from no one in particular, as these things travel — that the Hartwells are finished after all. That the victory was hollow. That the house cannot pay its debts of honor."
> *(System: the price is named. The choice is Rose's.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — Drummond's price:*
- **Accept outright** — *Standing+, Drummond pleased.* Rose accepts without qualification; Honoria becomes her shadow for the season, and Drummond's favor is banked — but the ton will say Miss Hartwell was bought cheap.
- **Accept with conditions** — *Standing+, Drummond wary.* Rose accepts but names terms of her own — limited afternoons, her choice of dances — and Drummond respects the nerve while noting the defiance; Honoria's sponsorship begins on a shorter leash.
- **Ask for time** — *Standing−, Drummond displeased.* Rose asks a week to consider; Drummond grants it with glacial courtesy, and the ton spends the week pricing her hesitation.

scenes.synopsis: Honoria herself — dull, deserving, and unexpectedly human; the price acquires a face.
scenes.prose:
> Miss Honoria Drummond was waiting in the anteroom when Rose emerged, and rose with the nervous grace of a girl who has been told to stand and cannot remember why.
> She was not beautiful. She was not plain. She was — Rose searched for the word and found only Drummond's own — *deserving*, in the way of a well-kept ledger: fair hair neatly dressed, a grey morning gown of perfect propriety, hands folded exactly so, everything in its place and nothing in it surprising. Dull as ditchwater, her aunt had said, and Rose saw at once that it was both true and unkind — true in the way of a room with no windows, unkind in the way of an aunt who had decided, twenty years ago, what the room would contain.
> "Miss Hartwell." Honoria curtsied, a fraction too deep, and recovered with a small, mortified smile. "My aunt said — that is, I am to thank you. For whatever you have — I mean —" She stopped, pink to the ears, and began again with visible effort. "I know I am not interesting. Aunt Agatha says interesting is a luxury and I must not expect to afford it. But I am grateful. Truly. And I know — " her voice dropped — "I know what I cost you. Aunt Agatha does not think I know, but I do."
> And Rose, who had prepared herself to resent the girl — to file her under *price paid* and endure her with exact, chilly courtesy — felt the resentment falter. Dull the girl might be; but there was something in the directness of the gratitude — no art, no maneuver, no pretty pretense that the arrangement was anything but what it was — that disarmed like a hand extended without a glove.
> "We shall do very well, Miss Drummond," Rose heard herself say, and was not entirely sure it was a lie. The girl's relief was so plain, so unguarded, that Rose felt something shift in her own chest — not forgiveness of the price, exactly, but a first, reluctant curiosity about the person the price had purchased.

scenes.synopsis: The reveal coda — home from Drummond's, Rose sees the armor in the mirror and understands what it bought.
scenes.prose:
> *(System: reveal coda — the ritual's payoff. Rose stands before the glass in the full chosen direction, the morning's armor complete.)*
> Home again, Rose stood before the cheval glass and looked at what Élise had built: the collar at its exact height, the jet button — or pearl, or silk — at its exact quarter inch, the bonnet brim at the rehearsed angle, the glove fitting like a second skin. The armor of respectability, worn into a creditor's house and worn out again, not a pin displaced.
> "Well?" Letitia asked from the doorway, where she had been hovering since the carriage turned into the street.
> "She looked at my throat," Rose said. "Exactly as Élise said she would. First — before the greeting, before I had quite crossed the room. And she adjusted — I saw it, Letitia, a fraction, the way one adjusts a sum that has come out unexpectedly in one's favor — as if the collar had answered a question she had not asked aloud."
> "And the price?"
> Rose told her. Honoria. The season. The name, the invitations, the dances, the afternoons. Reputation, not money — the one currency in which the Hartwells were suddenly, inconveniently rich. She watched her aunt's face as the terms landed, one by one, like stones dropped into still water.
> Letitia was silent a long moment. "It could have been worse."
> "Could it?"
> "She could have asked for money. Money you could have counted, borrowed, repaid on a schedule." Letitia came to stand beside her at the glass, and the two of them looked at the armor together. "This — this she will count in public, all season, and you will never know the total until it is over. Every ballroom is a ledger now, Rose. Every introduction a line item."
> In the glass, the armor looked back at Rose: paid in full, the brief had demanded. The collar stood at the jaw. The throat showed bone, not blood.
> The glass, Rose thought, was the only witness that knew the price of the paint — and the paint, for all its exactness, was already beginning to feel like a second skin she would wear until Christmas.

scenes.synopsis: Augusta's counsel — the dragon's price is real because it spends what Rose has.
scenes.prose:
> Augusta received her in the small salon at Ravencroft House, where the light fell like a judgment and the tea was strong enough to stand a spoon in, and where the Dowager had been holding court over London's debts of honor since before Rose was born.
> "So," said the Dowager Marchioness, without preamble, setting down her cup with the finality of a gavel, "Agatha Drummond has named her price, and you have come to me to be told whether it is fair."
> "I have come," Rose said carefully, "to be told whether it can be borne."
> "Borne? My dear, it can be borne the way a saddle can be borne — it will chafe, it will shape you, and by Christmas you will have forgotten what it was to ride without it." Augusta poured with the precision of a woman who had poured through three reigns and outlasted two of them. "The girl is dull. I have seen her at the opera — she applauds in the right places and has never once had an original thought about the music. But dull is not a flaw in a débutante; it is a feature. Dull girls do not elope, do not gamble, do not write poetry about footmen. Dull girls marry well and gratefully, and their sponsors are remembered fondly at christenings twenty years hence."
> "You think I should pay it."
> "I think," said Augusta, setting down the pot, "that the dragon's price is real because it spends what you have. She did not ask for money — you have little enough of that to spare, whatever the ton believes about reversed ruins and surviving Assemblies. She asked for the one currency in which you are suddenly, inconveniently rich, and she asked it in daylight, on heavy paper, where refusal would have been its own announcement." The old eyes were shrewd and not unkind. "Spend it, Rose. Spend it visibly, spend it well, and let the ton see that Miss Hartwell pays her debts of honor in daylight. There is no better advertisement for solvency than a creditor seen to be satisfied."

scenes.synopsis: Augusta names the deeper game — Drummond's price is also a leash; and the de Valcourt name surfaces, with Augusta's flicker.
scenes.prose:
> "There is more," Augusta said, when the second cup was poured and the footman had withdrawn, "and you know it, which is why you are sitting there looking like a woman at a solicitor's instead of a woman at tea."
> "A sponsor is a sponsor. What more could there be?"
> "A sponsor is never only a sponsor when Agatha Drummond arranges it." Augusta's spoon circled her cup, slowly. "She has attached your name to hers — or rather, to her blood. Every room Honoria enters on your arm is a room where the Hartwell name and the Drummond name are seen to stand together. That is not a price, my dear. That is an alliance, priced as a debt so that you cannot refuse it. Agatha does not collect debts. She collects positions."
> Rose frowned. "You make it sound like a treaty."
> "All debts between great houses are treaties. Yours simply has better stationery." Augusta paused, and the spoon stopped circling. "There was a time — " She stopped, and something crossed her face like a cloud over a familiar field — there and gone, but Rose had spent a season learning to read rooms, and she read it. "The de Valcourts understood this. The old émigré paper — the notes, the obligations — they were never about money either. They were about who stood next to whom, in writing. A signature is a far more durable thing than a sum."
> The name sat between them a moment too long. Augusta smoothed it away with a practiced hand, inquiring after the chocolate, but Rose had seen the flicker — the briefest catch, as of a woman stepping on a stair she had not expected to find there.
> "You knew them," Rose said quietly. "The de Valcourts."
> "Everyone knew everyone, then." Augusta's tone closed like a door — politely, finally, with no handle on Rose's side. "Drink your tea, my dear. It is getting cold, and cold tea is the one tragedy I refuse to underwrite."

scenes.synopsis: Texture — Rose alone after Augusta's, turning the de Valcourt flicker over in her mind.
scenes.prose:
> In the carriage home, Rose turned Augusta's flicker over like a coin of uncertain minting — the briefest catch, as of a woman stepping on a stair she had not expected, smoothed away with talk of chocolate.
> *(System: the de Valcourt name — émigré notes, foreign paper, obligations older than the Hartwell ruin — and Augusta, who had caught herself on it like a stair.)*
> Kinship, then — or something adjacent to it. The Dowager Marchioness of Ravencroft had been born into the very papers Rose meant to follow up the chain; the fluency with which Augusta spoke of obligations as treaties, of signatures outlasting sums, had the ease of a native speaker. It explained the French in her phrasing, the continental shrug she had never quite shed, the way she had said *in writing* as though writing were the only place anything true had ever happened.
> It explained nothing else. And Rose, who had learned at some cost when to press and when to wait, knew better than to ask for more. Some doors in Augusta's house were kept locked for reasons that had nothing to do with Rose, and knocking on them would only teach the household to listen for her step — and to report the knocking.
> She made a note in her pocketbook — *de V. papers — ask Quill* — and underlined it twice, and then, feeling the weight of the carriage's motion and the morning's exactness settling into her shoulders, underlined it a third time for emphasis and immediately felt foolish. Twice was resolve. Three times was anxiety. She left it at three, as a reminder that resolve and anxiety were, this season, traveling in the same carriage.
> The carriage rattled on through streets going about their unconcerned business. Somewhere ahead, the money's true shape was waiting, and it had begun, faintly, to cast a shadow — a shadow with a faded continental hand, endorsed against an account that bore her name.

scenes.synopsis: Romance — Julian begins paying his brother's scattered debts, quietly, refusing help.
scenes.prose:
> She found Julian in the Hartwell library at dusk, bent over a spread of papers that were clearly not his own — drafts, notes of hand, a solicitor's letter with a foreign postmark, the whole melancholy apparatus of other people's obligations.
> "You are early for the musicale," Rose said from the doorway, "and those are not your papers."
> He looked up, and for a moment the mask of easy Ashcombe charm did not quite arrive — the smile came late, like a guest who had missed the announcement. "My brother's," he said at last. "Or rather — my brother's creditors'. The debts scattered when he — when the estate matters settled. Someone must gather them before they gather interest, and lawyers, and opinions."
> "Someone," Rose said, coming closer, "or you?"
> "Me." He began stacking the papers with deliberate neatness, squaring the edges as though order on the desk could impose order on the accounts. "They are small debts, mostly. Tradesmen, a tailor in Calais who writes the most reproachful French I have ever been privileged to misunderstand, a note held by a man in Dieppe who writes the most elegant threats I have ever received. Nothing that touches the Ashcombe name if it is paid quietly. Which it will be. By me."
> "Julian — " She could see, now that she was close, the figures in the margins. Small, he had said. The figures did not look small.
> "No." The word was gentle and absolute, and it stopped her the way a hand on her arm would have. "You have your own creditors, Rose — of the social kind, which are worse, because they cannot be paid in coin and receipted. I will not have it said that Lord Julian Ashcombe paid his brother's tailor with Miss Hartwell's money. Some debts a man pays alone, or they are not paid at all."
> He smiled then, the charm arriving late but intact. But Rose had seen the papers, and the papers said what the smile would not: the debts were larger than small, and the paying would take longer than quiet.

scenes.synopsis: ★ FASHION-SELECTION — no coin cost, remembered. Choosing how Rose presents the new alliance at the week's first public appearance.
scenes.prose:
> *(System: fashion-selection — diegetic, no coin cost. The choice is remembered and will surface in Gazette and caller dialogue.)*
> "The musicale is Thursday," Letitia said, laying three options across the bed with the gravity of a quartermaster issuing arms. "And half the ton will be watching to see how the Hartwell–Drummond alliance dresses. Mrs. Aldous will certainly have an opinion before the interval. The Gazette will certainly have one by morning. Choose as if Mrs. Nance Bell herself were holding the swatches — because, my love, in a sense she is."
>
> **A. The Grey Accord** — dove-grey silk, silver trim; harmony made visible, the alliance as a settled fact.
> **B. The Hartwell Declaration** — Hartwell burgundy, worn unapologetically; the house that won, dressing like it.
> **C. The Quiet Parley** — ivory and pearl, cameo at the throat; understatement as confidence, letting Honoria be the color in the room.
>
> *(System: no coin cost. The selection is remembered — callers will comment, and the Gazette will judge.)*
> Rose ran her hand over the three silks — the grey cool and diplomatic under her fingers, the burgundy rich with the memory of the Assembly, the ivory quiet as a held breath — and chose. Letitia nodded slowly, already composing the evening's strategy around the cloth: which entrance, which set, where to stand when Honoria was presented, how to arrange the two of them in the retiring room so the alliance read as fact rather than performance.
> "Well chosen," she said, folding the rejected silks away with something like regret. "Now we shall see whether the ton agrees with your taste or merely with your dressmaker. The two are so rarely the same thing, and the ton so rarely knows the difference."
> Rose looked at the chosen gown, hanging now on the wardrobe door beside the morning's armor. Two dresses. Two performances. One week. The season, she reflected, was becoming a wardrobe with a plot.

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the merge board: the standing order queue, orders always waiting, the free-income engine.
scenes.prose:
> *(System: merge-board texture scene — the standing order queue. The atelier's order book never empties; orders wait, merge, and complete in the background — the free-income engine that funds the season's coins.)*
> At Élise's workroom the next morning, the great order board told its own story: commissions pinned in rows, ribbons and lace and half-finished bodices moving through their stages like ships in a harbor, each at its own pace, each bound for its own completion.
> Three standing orders waited in the queue — a widow's mourning silk to be softened for second mourning, a debutante's ball gown awaiting its final fitting, a riding habit to be remade for a lady who had changed her mind about the color and would change it back by Friday. Each one, completed, would drop its coins into the Hartwell purse: the slow, honest engine of the season, turning thread into money while Rose turned money into standing. No fanfare, no ballroom — just the patient arithmetic of the workroom, pin by pin, stage by stage.
> Élise moved a pin from one column to the next with satisfaction. "The queue never empties, chérie. That is the point. While you are paying Drummond's price in ballrooms, the board is paying your dressmaker in coin. You spend the afternoons; the atelier spends the mornings. Between us, we shall keep the house solvent."
> Rose watched a length of burgundy merino — *her* burgundy, left over from the ritual, the offcuts of the armor — advance one stage along the chain toward becoming somebody's trim. Nothing wasted. Everything merged, mended, moved forward, the workroom's patient arithmetic answering the ballroom's extravagant sums.
> "Then keep it moving," she said. "We shall need every coin. The season is long, the creditors are patient, and the ton — " she smiled, a little grimly — "the ton is always hungry."
> "The ton," said Élise, pinning with finality, "can wait its turn like everyone else."

scenes.synopsis: Rose's private remark about Drummond — the seed of the leak.
scenes.prose:
> That evening, alone with Letitia in the small parlor, the day's exactness finally cracked.
> The fire had burned low. The tea had gone the way of the afternoon's tea, and the evening's after it — cold, and ringed, and reproachful. Rose sat with her feet tucked under her in a way that would have earned a rebuke in any room but this one, and said, low, into her wine: "She is a dragon. A magnificent, exact, daylight dragon — and I am to lead her dull niece about like a prize heifer all season while the ton applauds my gratitude. Augusta calls it an alliance. I call it a leash with better stationery."
> Letitia glanced at the door — closed — and at the window — latched. "Houses leak, Rose."
> "Then let it leak. I am tired of being exact." Rose set down her glass with more force than the parlor deserved. "All day I have been measured, pinned, collared, and presented. The dragon may have my afternoons, but she does not have my private opinions. Those I keep — " she gestured at the empty room, the low fire, the two of them alone in the lamplight — "in here. In the one room in London where I am allowed to be unguarded."
> Letitia said nothing for a moment. Then: "It is never the one room, my love. That is the first thing the ruin taught us, and I had hoped it was the lesson that would keep."
> "The ruin taught me to fight in ballrooms. It did not teach me to whisper in my own parlor." Rose stood, restless, and went to the window, and looked out at the dark square. "I am sorry. I am tired, and the tiredness is making me honest, which is the most dangerous thing a woman in my position can be."
> "Then be tired quietly," said Letitia gently, "and be honest only with me."
> The room was empty. The house was not. Somewhere below stairs, a door closed — softly, the way doors close when the person closing them does not wish to be heard doing it.

scenes.synopsis: The leak — Rose's private remark about Drummond comes back to her, repeated by a caller.
scenes.prose:
> The caller came at four — a Mrs. Aldous, all sympathy and sharp eyes, there ostensibly to admire the Assembly flowers before they quite died, and actually, Rose understood within ninety seconds, to deliver something.
> "My dear Miss Hartwell," she said, settling with her tea and arranging her skirts with the care of a woman laying out instruments, "I was so sorry to hear — that is, one does hear things — that you find the Drummond arrangement something of a *leash*." She smiled. "Your word, I believe. 'A leash with better stationery.' So vivid! So — " the smile sharpened by a degree — "so *unguarded*, for you."
> Rose's cup stopped halfway to her lips.
> The dragon. The prize heifer. The exact words of an empty room — her empty room, her low fire, her wine, her aunt the only witness — carried out and delivered back to her by a woman who had not been in it, wrapped in sympathy like a blade in velvet.
> "People do love to embroider," Rose said evenly, setting the cup down with a hand that did not tremble, because she would not permit it to.
> "Oh, embroidery is the least of it." Mrs. Aldous leaned forward, confidential as a conspirator, delighted as a child. "The question everyone is asking — quite kindly, I assure you, quite as your friends — is who you said it *to*. A confidence kept is a character reference, my dear. A confidence carried — well." She left the sentence, and the implication, hanging in the air like smoke. "One does wonder what else travels, when opinions travel so freely from Hartwell House."
> She stayed twenty minutes more, admiring the dying flowers with great enthusiasm, and left Rose standing at the window long after the carriage had gone. Someone inside the house had carried her private remark out. Someone she fed, paid, trusted — or someone she loved. The empty room had not been empty. The house had not been hers. And the dragon, Rose thought with a cold that started somewhere below her ribs, would hear of this — if she had not heard already.

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE LEAK. Rose decides how to answer the betrayal inside her own house.
scenes.prose:
> Rose told Letitia everything — the remark, the empty room, the low fire, Mrs. Aldous's bright, terrible smile, the blade in the velvet of her sympathy.
> Letitia listened without moving, her embroidery hoop lowering slowly to her lap like a setting sun, and when Rose had finished, she said: "It could have been anyone. Marlow, a footman, a maid with an ear at the keyhole and a cousin who sews for Mrs. Aldous. The passages carry sound the way chimneys carry smoke — upward, and to the neighbors."
> "Or."
> "Or — " Letitia hesitated, and the hesitation was the worst of it. "It could have been no servant at all."
> "You mean someone closer."
> "I mean that houses leak upward as well as down, and that you said it in *my* presence too." Letitia's voice was level, but her hands had gone still. "If you mean to find the carrier, you must be prepared to find anyone. Including me. I will not have you discover that halfway through the hunt, like a second betrayal."
> Rose looked at her aunt — the woman who had kept the household book through the ruin, who had marked Quill's fee in red because it frightened her, who had kissed her forehead like a child of twelve the night before the dragon's summons — and felt the season's second price settle onto her shoulders beside the first. Trust had been the one currency she had not known she was spending. Now it, too, was being counted.
> "Then tell me," she said quietly, "what I should do. Not as my aunt. As the woman who kept this house standing when I could not."
> Letitia met her eyes. "I cannot tell you that, my love. This one is yours. But whatever you choose — choose it knowing that the choosing itself will be heard, all through this house, like everything else."
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The leak:*
- **Confront the household** — *Standing−, household loyalty strained.* Rose questions the staff directly; the carrier may be found, but the house will know it is suspected, and loyalty curdles under accusation.
- **Watch and wait** — *Standing unchanged, information advantage.* Rose says nothing and watches — who repeats what, who lingers at doors — trading swift justice for certain knowledge.
- **Tell no one** — *Standing+, private risk.* Rose buries it entirely, not even warning Letitia further; the ton sees perfect composure, but the leak remains open and the carrier unwatched.

scenes.synopsis: Julian's debts deepen — the brother's creditors are less scattered, and less small, than he admitted.
scenes.prose:
> She found him two evenings later at his club's steps, handing a sealed packet to a man with the unmistakable bearing of a solicitor's clerk — the kind of man who carries other people's ruin in his satchel and calls it business, the kind of man whose boots are always polished because his conscience is not.
> "Julian."
> He turned, and this time the charm did not arrive at all — no late smile, no easy bow, only the arrested look of a man caught at arithmetic. "Rose. You should not be seen — "
> "I am in a carriage, on a public street, at dusk. I am barely even here." She studied the clerk's retreating back, the satchel, the polished boots. "That was not a tailor in Calais."
> A pause, long enough to be an answer. "No."
> "How much?"
> "More than small. Less than ruinous." He came to the carriage window, and the lamplight showed her what the library's dusk had softened: the tiredness around his eyes, the set of his jaw. "My brother's notes — some of them are held with others. Bundled. There is a man in London buying them up, quietly, and I do not like the shape of his quiet. So I am buying faster, and paying more than the paper is worth, because the alternative is letting him assemble whatever it is he is assembling."
> "With what?"
> "With what I have." His smile was thin as a draft. "Which is the point of the exercise, and the reason it cannot be hurried, and the reason it keeps me awake. Do not offer, Rose. I mean it — I could not bear to be grateful to you for this. It is the one account in my life that must balance in my own hand, or I am not the man I have told myself I am."
> The carriage moved on. In the lamplight, his face had looked — for the first time since she had known him — like a man doing arithmetic he could not make come right, and carrying on doing it because stopping would be worse.

scenes.synopsis: Texture — Rose counts what Julian will not let her give; honor as an obstacle.
scenes.prose:
> That night Rose sat at the escritoire and did the arithmetic Julian would not let her do aloud.
> *(System: the Hartwell accounts — the purse shelf, the standing orders' slow coin, the season's costs already committed.)*
> She could cover the Dieppe note. She could cover the Calais tailor twice over, and the reproachful French into the bargain. What she could not cover — what no purse, however deep, could cover — was the shape of his refusal. *Some debts a man pays alone, or they are not paid at all.* It was honorable. It was also, she thought with a flash of something unworthy that she examined and did not quite discard, inconvenient — because the man buying up the brother's notes in London was buying them for a reason, and reasons, in her experience, had teeth, and teeth, in her experience, found throats.
> She closed the ledger. Honor was a currency she understood; she had just spent a season's worth of it on a dull débutante, and would spend a season's more before Christmas. But honor spent on pride, with creditors circling and a stranger assembling a position out of another man's debts — that was a different exchange, and the rate worried her the way Drummond's unwritten ledger entry worried her: a sum not yet named, accumulating interest in the dark.
> And underneath the worry, unworthy and undeniable: he would not be grateful to her. He had said so plainly, kindly, finally. The one account that must balance in his own hand. She understood it. She respected it. She resented it anyway, the way one resents a door locked from the inside by someone one loves — and then feels ashamed of the resentment, which changes nothing about the lock.
> Outside, the Hartwell clock struck eleven. Somewhere across London, Julian was still doing his arithmetic. Rose turned down the lamp, and did hers in the dark.

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — JULIAN'S DEBTS. Rose decides how to answer his honorable refusal.
scenes.prose:
> He came the next afternoon — unannounced, which for Julian was announcement enough — and found her in the morning room with Honoria's first round of invitations spread like a losing hand: the musicale, the presentation, the Aldous at-home, each one a small, gilded obligation.
> "You look," he said from the doorway, "like a woman being billed by the hour."
> "I am being billed by the season. It amounts to the same." She set the invitations aside — they could wait; he, she suspected, could not. "Julian. The man buying your brother's notes. Do you know his name?"
> "I know he pays promptly and asks no questions, which in my experience means he intends to ask them later, all at once, when the asking will cost the most." Julian sat, uninvited and welcome, and the ease of the gesture — the years of friendship in it — made what she had to say harder. "Why?"
> "Because I know something about debts that travel upward. Rackham's did — scattered like shot, and every piece of the shot had a direction. Yours may be doing the same." She leaned forward. "Someone is assembling a position, Julian. Augusta said so herself — it is not debt collection, it is positioning. Let me help. Not as charity — as strategy. Whatever you decide, decide knowing I am decided too."
> He was quiet a long moment. The easy charm, the late-arriving smile — all of it set aside, and what remained was simply a man, tired and proud and cornered by arithmetic, looking at her as though she were the one sum he could not make come right.
> "Rose," he said at last. "Choose carefully. Whatever you do here, I cannot un-know it. And neither — " he glanced at the invitations, at the whole gilded apparatus of her season — "neither can you."
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — Julian's debts:*
- **Offer money** — *Romance+, Julian's pride wounded.* Rose presses coin on him despite the refusal; he takes it badly and the debt between them becomes the other kind — the kind that is owed, not paid.
- **Respect his refusal** — *Romance+, Julian's honor intact.* Rose stands down and lets him pay alone; he is grateful and diminished by it in equal measure, and the creditors keep circling.
- **Investigate the brother's creditors** — *Intrigue+, Julian unaware.* Rose leaves his pride untouched and follows the paper instead — who is buying the notes, and why; the money's chain grows one link longer.
