scenes.synopsis: Quill's warning — "there are other codicils"; and: watch my office, not my clients.
scenes.prose:
> Mr. Quill received her in his chambers at Lincoln's Inn, where the dust lay on the law books like snow on a battlefield and the clerk coughed in a key calculated not to disturb, and where the very air smelled of paper that had been keeping secrets longer than Rose had been alive.
> "Miss Hartwell." Quill set aside a brief with evident relief, as though she were a more interesting problem than the one he had been reading. "The Assembly is won, the ruin reversed, the ton appeased. To what do I owe the honor of a client who no longer requires rescuing?"
> "To the rescuing not being finished." Rose laid his memorandum on the desk, open to her own marginal line. "Rackham's debts scattered. You wrote it yourself — émigré notes, foreign paper, obligations that predate my ruin and will outlast it. I want to follow them up the chain."
> Quill's expression did not change, which in a solicitor is the equivalent of a scream. "Up the chain," he repeated, very quietly. "Miss Hartwell, chains have two ends. The lower end is Rackham, who is destroyed, and may be examined at leisure. The upper end is — " He stopped, and went to the window, and stood with his hands behind his back looking out at the Inn's grey courtyard.
> "Is what?"
> "Complicated." The word fell like a stone into a well. "There are other codicils. To the settlements, to the notes, to arrangements made before your father's time. Codicils that were never read aloud because the rooms they were read in no longer exist — the men are dead, the houses sold, the witnesses scattered to the continent." He turned. "And one piece of counsel, which I give you as a man who values his continued employment and his unbroken windows: watch my office, not my clients. The paper passes through here. The paper always tells the truth, because the paper does not know it is lying."
> "Quill — "
> "That is all I can say in daylight." He sat again, the interview plainly over, the brief reclaimed. "Come back when you have something I can bill you for. Preferably something that does not require me to look over my shoulder while I bill it."

scenes.synopsis: The paper trail — Lucien de Valcourt NAMED in the documents only; he never appears, never speaks. Seeded only.
scenes.prose:
> But Quill, having risen to end the interview, paused with his hand on a deed box — and relented, or appeared to. With solicitors, Rose was learning, there was rarely a difference worth the price of discovering.
> "One thing," he said, "which is not counsel but inventory, and therefore cannot be billed as advice. When my clerk sorts the Rackham papers for the assignees, the émigré notes keep surfacing with the same endorsement." He drew out a folded note, held it so Rose could see the signature without touching it — the paper between them like a specimen in a jar. "There. Read the hand, not the man."
> The endorsement, in a faded continental hand, read: *L. de Valcourt — to be settled against the Hartwell account.*
> Rose stared at it. Twenty years old, the ink gone brown at the edges, the handwriting fluent with the confidence of a world that no longer existed. *To be settled against the Hartwell account.* Her account. Her name, in a stranger's hand, on paper older than her memory of her father.
> "Lucien de Valcourt," Quill said, naming the paper and nothing else. "An émigré name on émigré paper. The notes predate your ruin by twenty years — they predate, I may say, a number of things you currently take for granted. Whether the man is living, dead, or merely well-filed is a question for the documents, not for me." He returned the note to the box with the care of a man handling something that might be evidence, or might be a wasp. "He does not appear in London. He does not write, does not call, does not sue. He is — at present — a signature. I suggest you keep him one."
> *(System: Lucien de Valcourt is seeded — a name in the paper trail only. He never appears, never speaks, this season.)*
> Rose stared at the closed deed box. A signature, twenty years old, endorsed against the Hartwell account. The money's chain had just grown a link — and the link had a name, and the name had Augusta's flicker written all over it, and Quill's warning about codicils, and the man in London buying up notes, quietly, like a collector.
> *Follow it up.* The line in the margin, ticking like the Hartwell clock.

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the tussie-mussie: floriography seeded lightly, a stripped thorn stem.
scenes.prose:
> On the way home, Rose stopped at the flower seller on the corner — an impulse, or the nearest thing to one she had allowed herself all week — and bought a tussie-mussie for Honoria's first call.
> The seller wrapped it in paper and, at Rose's nod, stripped the thorn stems clean before binding them — a small, deft violence, the thorns falling onto the cobbles like punctuation removed from a sentence.
> *(System: floriography thread seeded — the tussie-mussie, the stripped thorn stem. Flowers as messages; this one says: I come unarmed.)*
> "For the young lady?" the seller asked, tying the paper with practiced fingers.
> "For the young lady I am to sponsor," Rose said. "Something that says — " She considered the small, exact bouquet, the blooms bright against the stripped stems. "Something that says I mean it kindly, even if I did not choose it. Something that says the thorns were my idea to remove."
> The seller nodded as if this were a common request. In a season of debts and dragons, perhaps it was — half of London, Rose suspected, was currently sending flowers that meant the opposite of what the card said.
> Rose carried the flowers home like a white flag in miniature — and wondered, climbing the steps, whether Honoria would read the stems or only the blooms. The girl read everything, she had said. It was what one did when one was not interesting. Rose found herself hoping, with a suddenness that surprised her, that the girl would prove interesting after all — if only to give the afternoons something to be about besides the price of them, and the season something to be about besides the paying.
> The stripped thorns lay behind her on the cobbles, small and dark against the stone. Ahead, the house waited, with its leak, and its clock, and its ledger of unbilled options, all ticking — and Rose, for the first time all week, was carrying something into it that was not a bill.

scenes.synopsis: Honoria's first sponsored call — the price in practice; the girl proves less dull than advertised.
scenes.prose:
> Honoria arrived for her first sponsored call at three, punctual to the minute, and accepted the tussie-mussie with both hands and visible pleasure — not the practiced delight of a girl who has been taught to receive, but something warmer and less guarded.
> "Oh," she said, turning it, the paper rustling. "The stems are stripped. How — " she looked up, suddenly less dull and more perceptive than her aunt's ledger-description allowed — "how kind. Thornless. You are telling me you come unarmed."
> Rose blinked. "You read flowers?"
> "I read everything. It is what one does when one is not interesting — one watches the interesting people and takes notes." Honoria smiled, and the smile transformed her: not beautiful, but suddenly, startlingly *present*, as though a lamp had been lit behind a plain shade. "Aunt Agatha says you are to sponsor me. She did not say you were to like me. But I thought — " the courage faltered, the flush rising — "I thought I might try to be worth the afternoons. I know what they cost you. I know I am the price. I only — I should like not to be a waste of it."
> And Rose, who had braced herself for a season of dutiful boredom — for grey gowns and grey conversation and the slow erosion of her afternoons — felt something shift: the faintest rearrangement of expectation, like a pin moved one column over on a board. The girl was not dull. She was *unlit* — and there was a difference, and the difference was everything.
> "Miss Drummond," she said, "I believe we shall surprise your aunt."
> "Oh, I do hope so," said Honoria earnestly. "She so dislikes surprises. She considers them a failure of planning."
> Rose laughed — genuinely, for the first time in days — and Honoria laughed too, a little breathless, as though laughter were a liberty she had not been granted before. The price, Rose thought, had just acquired a face. And the face, against all the odds and all the ledgers, was beginning to look like a person.

scenes.synopsis: The household takes stock — Letitia's quiet audit of the week's costs, and the leak unresolved.
scenes.prose:
> "The musicale is Thursday," Letitia said over the household book that evening, "Honoria's presentation Friday, the Aldous at-home Saturday — at which Mrs. Aldous will certainly repeat your remark about the leash to anyone who missed it the first time, with improvements."
> "You think she will."
> "I think she has already, and Saturday is merely the encore." Letitia made a notation in her neat, unhurried hand. "The staff are — careful. Since Mrs. Aldous's call, the house has the atmosphere of a courtroom between sessions. If you confronted them — " she glanced up — "they do not know whether you have. The footmen are polishing with unusual vigor. Marlow has taken to appearing in doorways without being summoned, like a conscience with keys."
> "I have not decided." Rose watched the lamplight move on the page. "Confrontation, watching, silence — each one costs something different, and I cannot yet tell which currency I can afford."
> "No. And indecision, in a house, is its own kind of accusation." Letitia closed the book with a soft, final sound. "Whatever you chose — the choosing itself is the cost. There is no unbilled option, Rose. There never was. That is what the Assembly bought us: the end of unbilled options. From now on, everything is itemized — the afternoons, the trust, the silence. Even the silence has a price, and the house is keeping the account."
> Outside, a carriage passed — unrecognized, unremarked, gone. Rose had stopped trying to place them. London was auditing her now; the carriages were merely the auditors' clerks, and the audit, like Drummond's ledger, would be presented in daylight.
> She thought of stripped thorn stems, and signatures twenty years old, and a dragon's exact smile, and a girl who read flowers because she was not interesting enough to be read herself — and understood, all at once, that these were not four separate troubles. They were one trouble, wearing four different collars.
> "Then we pay," she said, "and we pay in daylight. It is the only currency the ton cannot counterfeit."

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the evening before the musicale; Rose dresses her resolve along with her gown.
scenes.prose:
> The gown for the musicale — the remembered choice, grey or burgundy or ivory — hung ready on the wardrobe door, and Rose stood before it the way a general regards a map: not admiring, but memorizing.
> *(System: the week's first public appearance approaches — the Hartwell–Drummond alliance on display, the Gazette watching, Mrs. Aldous certainly watching.)*
> Everything now was performance: the sponsorship, the composure, the collar that said paid in full, the smile that would say it again on Thursday in a different key. The only things that were not performance were the things she could not show — the leak in her own house, still open, still unanswered; the signature in Quill's deed box, twenty years old and newly urgent; Julian's arithmetic, done alone by lamplight; Augusta's flicker at a twenty-year-old name, smoothed away with talk of chocolate.
> She touched the silk. It was only cloth — warp and weft, dye and thread, Élise's pins and Letitia's strategy, the whole exact edifice of the week's second performance. But cloth, properly chosen, was the one armor the ton could not pierce. They could only describe it, and description was Mrs. Nance Bell's business, not hers. *Miss Hartwell's gown spoke of settled accounts.* Let the gown speak. Rose had said enough this week; her words had traveled farther than her carriage.
> "Paid in full," Rose told the gown, very quietly, the way one tells a horse to stand before mounting.
> The gown, like the papers, declined to comment. But it hung very straight — collar exact, skirt falling in its rehearsed line, every pin where Élise had left it. And Rose, looking at it, felt the week's scattered costs draw together into something like order: the dragon's price, the leak's price, the pride's price, all itemized, all to be paid in daylight.
> Tomorrow the alliance would be displayed. Tonight, the armor waited, patient as a second self.

scenes.synopsis: The Gazette watches — Bell's paper notes the alliance, the gown, and the price, without cruelty and without mercy.
scenes.prose:
> The Gazette arrived with the morning post, and Letitia read the society column aloud with the air of a woman defusing a second device in as many days.
> "'Miss Hartwell,'" she read, "'was observed in close attendance upon Miss Honoria Drummond at — well, at everywhere. The alliance, so unexpectedly struck, appears to prosper. Miss Hartwell's gown' — " Letitia paused, and looked up with the particular expression of a woman who has found the fuse — "'spoke of settled accounts; whether the accounts are in fact settled, the ton awaits to learn.'"
> "Settled accounts," Rose repeated. "She liked the gown, then."
> "She liked the *question*. That is Mrs. Nance Bell's particular genius — she never asserts, she inquires. An inquiry cannot be answered and cannot be sued. 'Whether the accounts are in fact settled' — she has taken your collar, your pins, your whole exact edifice of a morning, and turned it into a question mark the size of the season." Letitia folded the paper with crisp finality. "The ton awaits to learn, Rose. They are learning in public, at your expense, and the tuition is non-refundable."
> Rose took the paper and read the paragraph herself, twice. No cruelty — Bell never dealt in cruelty; cruelty was for pamphlets and caricaturists. No mercy either — mercy was for sermons. The paper judged taste — the gown, the alliance, the performance, the visible spending of reputation on the deserving — and left the verdict to its readers, who would render it over dinner tables all across London by nightfall, each verdict slightly different, all of them final.
> Which was, she reflected, exactly how a proprietor survives every regime: never the author of the judgment, only its publisher. The Gazette inquired. The ton answered. And Miss Hartwell — observed at everywhere, in close attendance, her gowns speaking — paid the tuition, in daylight, as agreed.

scenes.synopsis: Julian at the musicale's edge — the debts follow him into the ballroom.
scenes.prose:
> He was at the musicale, of course — Julian was always where the ton was thickest, charm deployed like a screen, the easy bow and the ready laugh — but Rose found him in the card room during the interval, alone, turning a letter over in his hands with the air of a man reading his own sentence.
> The card room was half-empty, the tables abandoned for the music, the candles burning low in their sconces. Through the doorway came the quartet, bright and oblivious.
> "Dieppe?" she asked quietly, closing the door behind her.
> "Dieppe," he confirmed, and did not offer the letter. "The elegant threats have become less elegant and more frequent — the French, I find, deteriorates under financial pressure, like everything else. My prompt friend in London has bought the note — the whole bundle, I think. He writes to introduce himself." A dry sound, not quite a laugh. "He introduces himself as a man of business. They always do, just before the business turns out to be personal."
> "What does he want?"
> "A meeting. Next week." Julian pocketed the letter with a finality that did not quite conceal the tremor in his hand. "Do not look like that, Rose. It is only money. Money is the one problem in this town that can actually be solved — counted, borrowed, repaid, receipted."
> "Can it?" She thought of Drummond's price — reputation, not money — and of Quill's codicils, and of a signature twenty years old endorsed against her own account, and of Augusta saying *positioning*, with her fan stopped mid-motion. "I am no longer certain money is the solvable kind. I am beginning to think money is merely the kind that keeps the best accounts."
> The music resumed in the next room — the interval ending, the ton returning to its seats, Honoria somewhere out there being charming on schedule. Julian offered his arm, the charm arriving at last, on schedule, like everything else about him that evening.
> But his hand, on her sleeve, was cold. And Rose, walking back into the music on the arm of a man doing arithmetic he could not make come right, understood that the debts had followed him into the ballroom — and that ballrooms, for all their candlelight, were no protection at all.

scenes.synopsis: Augusta's warning about the note-buyer — and a second flicker at the émigré paper.
scenes.prose:
> Rose mentioned the note-buyer to Augusta in the retiring room, lightly, as one mentions weather — and watched the Dowager's fan stop mid-motion, like a bird arrested in flight.
> "Buying up scattered notes," Augusta repeated. "In London. Quietly." The fan resumed, a fraction faster than before. "My dear, that is not debt collection. That is *positioning*. Someone is assembling a position — against whom, and to what end, the notes themselves will tell you, if you read them the way Quill reads them."
> "The way Quill reads them?"
> "As paper that does not know it is lying." Augusta's gaze was level over the rim of her teacup. "The émigré notes, Rose — the old endorsements, the continental hands — they were bundled once before, thirty years ago. Bundled and bought, by men who understood that a debt is a lever and a lever needs a fulcrum, and that the fulcrum is always someone else's name." She paused. "I was — there were — " The flicker again, brief as a skipped stitch, there and gone before Rose could be certain she had seen it — but she had seen it before, over chocolate, at the mention of the same papers. "It ended badly. For everyone except the men who had bought quietly."
> "Augusta — " Rose leaned forward. The retiring room was empty but for them, the musicale's murmur beyond the door.
> "Enjoy the musicale, my dear." The door of the subject closed — politely, finally, with the soft click of a lock turned by an expert hand. "And tell your young Honoria her grey gown is very becoming. Dull girls in becoming gowns are the safest investment in London — they appreciate, they do not depreciate, and they never, ever surprise their sponsors."
> Rose watched her go back to her circle, fan moving at its normal, unhurried pace, the Dowager Marchioness of Ravencroft once more entire and unassailable. But the flicker had been real — twice now, at the same papers — and Rose added it to the pocketbook's account: *Augusta — knows the émigré bundling. Thirty years ago. Ended badly.* Underlined twice. She was learning, this season, to keep books of her own.

scenes.synopsis: Texture — Rose alone on the terrace; the season's threads gather: the leak, the notes, the signature, the dragon.
scenes.prose:
> Between the sets, Rose stepped onto the terrace alone, and London spread below her in lamplight and rumor.
> *(System: the chapter's threads drawn together — Drummond's price being paid in ballrooms; the leak still open in her own house; Julian's notes being bought by a stranger; Quill's codicils; a twenty-year-old signature; Augusta's flicker.)*
> The night air was cool after the heat of the music room, and it cleared her head the way cold water clears a glass. Below, the street glittered; above, the sky showed the particular indifference of a September night to the affairs of heiresses. She had won. The ruin was proved engineered, Rackham destroyed, the Assembly survived — every closed arc of Season One, sealed and ribboned, applauded by the ton and printed by the Gazette.
> And yet the house had woken to what winning cost, and the cost was still being counted: in afternoons given to Honoria, in a private remark carried out of an empty room by hands she could not name, in émigré paper surfacing from deed boxes like bodies in a river, in Julian's cold hand on her sleeve, in Augusta's fan stopping mid-motion at the mention of a buyer.
> *Follow it up.* The line from the memorandum, ticking like the Hartwell clock, ticking like everything else in her life now.
> Up the chain. To whoever was buying Julian's brother's notes, quietly, in London. To whatever the other codicils said, in rooms that no longer existed. To the signature — twenty years old, faded, fluent — endorsed against the Hartwell account before she was old enough to sign her own name. To the bundling, thirty years ago, that had ended badly for everyone except the men who had bought quietly.
> The season was called The Money. Rose understood, suddenly and completely, standing alone on the terrace with London glittering below, that it was not about having it.
> It was about being had by it — and about learning, before the season ended, how to be the holder rather than the held.

scenes.synopsis: The drive home — Letitia names the chapter's true subject: winning was the easy part.
scenes.prose:
> In the carriage home, Letitia was silent for a full three streets — a record, broken only by the rattle of the wheels and the occasional snort of the horses — before she spoke.
> "You were magnificent," she said at last. "Honoria was charming — did you see Lady Aldous's face when the girl answered her about the music? The gown was exactly right. Mrs. Nance Bell will inquire approvingly tomorrow, which is the highest praise the press of this town is capable of."
> "But."
> "But magnificent is not the same as finished." Letitia turned to her in the lamplight, and her face was serious in a way Rose had seen only twice before — once at the height of the ruin, once the night before the Assembly. "Season One was about surviving the ruin. This — all of this, the dragon's price, the leak, Julian's notes, Quill's papers, Augusta's thirty-year-old ghosts — this is about surviving the *rescue*. Nobody warns you, when you win, that the victory is only the first installment. The rest comes due in pieces, all season, and every piece has your name on it, and the ton stands by with its account book open, checking the arithmetic."
> Rose looked out at the dark squares rolling past, the houses shuttered, the streetlamps burning for no one. "Did we win, Letitia? Truly? Or did we merely change the nature of the losing?"
> "We survived the Assembly." Letitia smiled, thin as Drummond's. "The ton waits to see what survival costs. I believe I read that somewhere — in a paper of no particular cruelty and no particular mercy."
> The carriage turned into their street. The house was dark, the clock ticking within — paid in full, the collar had said, all those pins ago.
> The house declined to confirm. And Rose, climbing the steps in the gown that had spoken of settled accounts, felt the week's itemized costs settle onto her shoulders like a cloak she would wear until Christmas: the afternoons, the trust, the pride, the signature. All due. All in daylight.

scenes.synopsis: ★ GAZETTE STING — the paper's verdict on the week: survival, priced.
scenes.prose:
> *(System: the Gazette sting — delivered as the paper itself, the chapter's public verdict.)*
>
> *From the Gazette, under Mrs. Nance Bell's imprint:*
>
> *"Miss Hartwell survives the Assembly. The ton waits to see what survival costs.*
>
> *The Hartwell–Drummond alliance — so unexpectedly, so visibly struck — prospers in ballrooms. Miss Honoria Drummond, sponsored, gowned, and much improved by the association, does her patroness credit. The patroness's gowns speak of settled accounts.*
>
> *Whether the accounts are in fact settled, the ton awaits to learn. Dragons, after all, keep ledgers — and ledgers, unlike ruins, are never proved engineered. They are merely presented.*
>
> *Miss Hartwell is expected to continue paying. In daylight. The ton will be watching the coin."*
>
> *(System: the sting lands — no cruelty, no mercy. The paper judges taste and leaves the verdict to its readers. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, inquires; she never asserts. The week is priced in public, and the price is now a matter of record.)*
>
> Rose read it at breakfast, twice, and set it down beside her plate with unusual care. *Miss Hartwell is expected to continue paying.* Expected — Drummond's word, returned to her by way of the press, engraved now not on heavy paper but on the public record, where every subscriber in London could read it over coffee. The ton would be watching the coin. Let them. The coin, at least, was honest — counted, spent, receipted.
> It was the other currencies that worried her: the afternoons, the trust, the pride — uncounted and uncountable, accumulating interest in the dark, compounding like debts and leaks. *Whether the accounts are in fact settled, the ton awaits to learn.* Bell's inquiry, hanging over the breakfast table like a question mark the size of the season.
> "Well," said Letitia, pouring the tea with the steadiness of a woman who had survived worse paragraphs, "it could have been worse."
> "Everyone keeps saying that," said Rose. "I am beginning to suspect it is the motto of the season — printed small, at the bottom of every page."
scenes.sting: Miss Hartwell survives the Assembly. The ton waits to see what survival costs. The Hartwell–Drummond alliance — so unexpectedly, so visibly struck — prospers in ballrooms. Miss Honoria Drummond, sponsored, gowned, and much improved by the association, does her patroness credit. The patroness's gowns speak of settled accounts. Whether the accounts are in fact settled, the ton awaits to learn. Dragons, after all, keep ledgers — and ledgers, unlike ruins, are never proved engineered. They are merely presented. Miss Hartwell is expected to continue paying. In daylight. The ton will be watching the coin.

scenes.synopsis: ★ CLIFFHANGER — Drummond's terms, restated at the door: sponsor Honoria, or the ton hears the Hartwells are finished.
scenes.prose:
> The knock came at nine the next morning — not the post, not a caller, but a footman in Drummond livery, with a note on the same heavy paper as the summons. The house, which had just begun to breathe again after the musicale, held its breath once more.
> Rose opened it in the hall, Letitia at her shoulder, the morning light falling across the engraved sheet like a judgment.
>
> *Miss Hartwell —*
>
> *Mrs. Aldous has been most entertaining. It seems your private opinions of our arrangement travel faster than your carriage. A pity. Leaks, like debts, compound.*
>
> *I write to restate my terms, that there be no misunderstanding between us: you will sponsor Miss Honoria Drummond — your name, your invitations, your dances, your afternoons — visibly, repeatedly, and without reservation, for the season.*
>
> *Or the ton will hear, from no one in particular, as these things travel, that the Hartwells are finished after all.*
>
> *The choice, as ever, is yours.*
>
> *— A.D.*
>
> Rose read it twice. The leak — her empty-room remark, the dragon, the leash with better stationery — had reached Drummond herself, carried by hands Rose could not name out of a house she could not seal. And Drummond had done what dragons do: she had not roared. She had restated. The terms, the price, the alliance — all of it set down again in that absolute hand, with the alternative stated as plainly as a sum at the bottom of a column.
> *Leaks, like debts, compound.* Drummond knew. Of course Drummond knew. Drummond knew everything, and charged for the knowing.
> Letitia's hand found Rose's shoulder. "The terms," she whispered, "restated at the door. In daylight. Before witnesses." Her fingers tightened. "She means the footman to report back what he saw."
> Rose folded the note with exact, unhurried hands — the collar holding, the armor intact — and looked at the Drummond footman, still waiting in her hall like a ledger entry that had learned to walk.
> "Tell Lady Agatha," she said, "that Miss Hartwell has received her terms."
> The door closed. The house exhaled — slowly, raggedly, like a patient after bad news well delivered.
> Somewhere upstairs, the Hartwell clock ticked on — paid in full, the brief had demanded.
>
> *(System: Chapter 1 ends. Drummond's terms stand restated: sponsor Honoria, or the ton hears the Hartwells are finished. Season Two has named its price.)*
---

scenes.synopsis: Open from Chapter 1's cliffhanger — Drummond's terms restated at the door, in writing, before breakfast is cold. No new summons, no new naming; the threat simply made paper.
scenes.prose:
> *(Hartwell House, breakfast room. The morning after the Last Assembly. Rain stippling the windows in grey appliqué. A footman in Drummond livery — grey and silver, the colors of a thundercloud with pretensions — has come and gone before the chocolate was poured; his card sits on the silver tray like a small grey accusation, and the whole room has arranged itself around not looking at it.)*
> "Read it aloud, Aunt, and spare me nothing. I find bad news improves when it is given a voice." — Rose
> *(Letitia takes up the card, finds her spectacles, and reads — and Rose watches her aunt's face perform the entire correspondence course of emotions between the first line and the last.)*
> "My dear Miss Hartwell will do me the honour — blah — my niece Honoria will wait upon you at eleven — blah — *your name, your invitations, your dances, your afternoons* — and should these attentions lapse, the town will hear, before dinner, precisely how the Hartwells stand. My God, Rose. She has written the word *dances*. It is underlined. Twice." — Letitia
> "Then we shall give her dances. Pour the chocolate, Aunt. A woman threatened before breakfast may still be formidable by eleven." — Rose
> *(Letitia pours with a hand that trembles only slightly — the tremble of fury, Rose knows, not fear; she has seen that exact tremor at christenings, weddings, and one memorable funeral. Outside, a carriage passes on the wet cobbles; every carriage in Mayfair sounds, this morning, like a verdict being delivered to the wrong address.)*
> "She cannot do it, you know. Ruin us with a sentence. The ton has heard worse about better families and yawned itself to sleep by the second course." — Letitia
> "She can do it because we are not a better family. We are a family with a mortgaged estate, a solicitor who speaks of codicils the way other men speak of weather, and a reputation held together by your excellent chocolate. Drummond has counted our coins, Aunt. She would not threaten idly — idleness is the one luxury Lady Agatha has never permitted herself." — Rose
> "Then we launch the girl." — Letitia sets down the pot with the finality of a gavel. "Dull, is she? Deserving, is she? We have launched duller and deserved less. Fetch the good calling cards, Rose. If we are to be held to ransom, we shall be held to ransom *elegantly* — and we shall make the ton pay admission to watch."
> *(Rose takes the card, folds it once along its threatening crease, and slides it into her workbox — not hidden, filed, between a ribbon sample and a tradesman's bill. The first lesson of the chapter, learned before the chocolate is cold: a threat, once written down, becomes an appointment. And appointments, Rose reflects, can be managed.)*

scenes.synopsis: The household takes stock — the leak from Chapter 1 is named, the terms are translated into a campaign, and Rose begins following the money in her head.
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room. Letitia winds wool with the ferocity of a woman winding a plan — the ball of grey yarn growing rounder and more militant by the minute. Rose stands at the window, workbox open, Drummond's card laid beside a stack of unpaid tradesmen's bills she has been quietly auditing since dawn, her pencil moving down the columns like a general surveying a battlefield she already knows she is losing.)*
> "It was Tibbs, by the way. The second housemaid." — Letitia does not look up from the wool. "She told the butcher's boy that Mr. Quill had been here twice in a week, and the butcher's boy told his mother, and his mother tells everyone — she is the town crier with a better bonnet. That is your household leak, Rose. I have spoken to Tibbs. She wept. I kept her — a weeping servant is a loyal servant, and a dismissed one is a newspaper."
> "Sound household management and sound strategy in a single sentence. I shall have that embroidered on a cushion." — Rose
> "Do. — Quill twice in a week, Rose. That is not a social call."
> "Quill twice in a week means the codicils are breeding. Rackham's debts, Julian quietly paying his brother's — everyone in this town is paying someone else's money, and nobody will say whose. It is a positive orgy of other people's money, and I am beginning to suspect I am the only person in London paying my own."
> *(Letitia's winding slows. She regards her niece over the spectacles with the expression she reserves for sermons and creditors.)*
> "Do not follow the money before eleven, my dear. Follow the girl. Honoria Drummond is coming to be sponsored, and she will arrive terrified — I know her sort. I *was* her sort, before I married your uncle and learned to be terrifying instead."
> "You were never a wallflower, Aunt."
> "I was a wallflower with opinions, which is worse. The ton forgives a girl who says nothing. It never forgives a girl who says something dull. Now — strategy." — The wool is abandoned; the general takes the field. "You will give her your name, your invitations, your dances, your afternoons. Very well. We shall make each of those things worth having. Your name shall open doors, your invitations shall be the ones that matter, your dances shall be with men who can be trusted to look pleased, and your afternoons — your afternoons, my love, shall be a campaign."
> *(A knock below — the area bell, then the front door, then the particular hush of a caller being admitted. The eleven o'clock call, early by nine minutes. Terror, Rose reflects, folding away the bills, is always punctual.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 1 — Honoria calls. The wallflower, the stammer, and the good heart, all arriving nine minutes early in a bonnet two seasons out of date.
scenes.prose:
> *(The drawing room. Miss Honoria Drummond stands just inside the door as though the carpet might object to her presence and she has prepared a defense in advance. She is plain the way a winter field is plain — nothing to catch the eye, everything honest underneath. Her bonnet is two seasons old, its ribbon re-pressed with visible care; her gloves are mended at the thumb, mended well, by hands that knew the work mattered.)*
> "M-Miss Hartwell. Mrs. Hartwell. My aunt — my aunt said I was to — that is, she said you would be so k-kind as to —" — Honoria
> "As to receive you, my dear, which we do, with chocolate. Sit before you fall. You look as though the stairs argued with you, and lost." — Letitia
> *(Honoria sits — perches, rather — on half the chair, as if the other half were reserved for someone more deserving. She produces, with great and visible care, a small tussie-mussie: violets and a sprig of rosemary, tied with plain thread, the stems trimmed with a precision that suggests she cut them herself that morning.)*
> "For — for your drawing room, ma'am. I — the violets are for modesty. That is what the flower book says. And the rosemary is for remembrance. I thought — a lady's drawing room ought to have something that means something." — Honoria
> *(Letitia takes the posy as though it were orchids from a hothouse. Rose watches the girl's hands — red-knuckled, the hands of someone who does her own mending and her own flower-cutting — and feels the first crack in her armor, and notes with professional interest that the crack is irritation at Drummond, not at this girl, who has done nothing in the world but be born to the wrong aunt.)*
> "It shall live on the mantel, where the modesty of the household is most in need of reinforcement." — Letitia, finding it a sherry glass at once. "Now, Honoria — may I call you Honoria? — tell me, do you take chocolate with cream? There is no wrong answer, but there is a right one, and I shall judge you entirely upon it."
> "W-with cream, please. Oh — I mean — thank you." — Honoria
> *(The stammer eases a fraction, the way a held breath eases. Rose makes a note — the campaigner's note, filed alongside Drummond's card: the girl is not stupid. She is frightened. Those are different problems, with different cures, and only one of them can be fixed with chocolate and cream.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 2 — what Honoria wants. Not a Season. Just not to be laughed at. Dialogue-heavy; let the stammer do the work of showing terror, and the plain sentences do the work of showing sense.
scenes.prose:
> *(The garden behind Hartwell House, after chocolate. Letitia has tactfully developed a headache — a headache that arrived, Rose notes, precisely as the second cup was poured, and will depart precisely when the campaign planning begins. Honoria walks beside Rose among the rain-wet roses, her mended gloves clasped hard enough to whiten the knuckles, her eyes on the path.)*
> "Your aunt wishes me to sponsor you. Into society. Balls, dances, afternoons — the whole apparatus. I am to lend you my name, my invitations, my dances, my afternoons. It is quite a list. She underlined it." — Rose
> "I know. She — she explained it. At length. With diagrams, almost. She drew a — a sort of chart. Of the Season." — Honoria
> "A chart. Of course she did. And what do you wish, Honoria? Not your aunt. You. If no one were managing you — and I assure you, you are being managed by experts on all sides — what would you ask for?"
> *(A long pause. A rose petal falls, sodden, and lands on the path between them like a full stop. When Honoria speaks, the stammer is worse — the truth costs more than politeness, and she is paying in full.)*
> "I d-don't want a Season, Miss Hartwell. I know what I am. I am not — people do not look at me twice, and when they do, they — at the assemblies last year, two girls laughed. Not at me, exactly. Near me. It amounts to the same thing, only it is worse, because you cannot — you cannot answer laughter that is near you. There is nothing to answer."
> "Girls laugh near everyone, Honoria. It is their principal exercise. They would laugh near the Archbishop if he stood still long enough."
> "I only want —" She stops, gathers herself, and the next sentence comes out plain and whole, the plainest sentence Rose has heard all Season. "If I am to be taken about, and stared at, I want not to be laughed at. That is all. I don't expect to be admired. I should like to be — unremarkable without being ridiculous. Is that a very small thing to want?"
> *(Rose stops walking. This is the moment the chapter turns on: the dragon's niece has asked for the smallest thing in the world — smaller than a Season, smaller than a husband, smaller than admiration — and Rose, who has been calculating in dances and invitations and afternoons, understands that the price Drummond named is denominated in a currency she hadn't considered. Not coin. Not credit. Kindness, carefully spent, in public, where it can be seen.)*
> "It is the largest thing anyone has asked of me this Season, Honoria. Larger than money, larger than marriages. To be unremarkable without being ridiculous — I shall have to be very clever indeed, and I am not always clever before luncheon."
> "You are clever. Everyone says so. Even my aunt says so, and she says so as though it were a fault. As though it were — consumption, or radical politics."
> "Your aunt says many things as though they were faults. Come — we will walk back, and you will tell me which flowers you like, and I will pretend this is merely a morning call and not the beginning of a campaign. Campaigns, I find, go better when nobody admits they have begun."
> *(They turn. The rain has stopped. Somewhere above them, Letitia's headache is presumably lifting, right on schedule.)*

scenes.synopsis: Texture micro-beat — the after-echo of Honoria's visit. Seed the tussie-mussie floriography thread: flowers as messages.
scenes.prose:
> *(The drawing room, empty now. The tussie-mussie sits on the mantel in a sherry glass, violets already loosening their hold on the stems, rosemary upright and soldierly beside them. Rose stands before it, turning Drummond's card over in her fingers — threat, appointment, threat, appointment — and finds her eyes returning, again and again, to the small plain posy.)*
> "Violets for modesty. Rosemary for remembrance." — Rose
> *(She says it to the empty room, testing the weight of the words the way one tests a coin for counterfeit. A girl who brings flowers that mean something to a house she fears — who consulted a flower book, who tied the stems with plain thread because she has no ribbon to spare, who carried it nine minutes early through the rain — that is not dullness. That is a language. The ton speaks in glances and guest lists and underlined words; Honoria speaks in posies. And Rose, standing in the quiet drawing room with a dragon's threat in one hand, understands that she has been handed, quite by accident, the beginnings of a code.)*
> *(She takes a violet between thumb and forefinger — gently, the way one handles evidence — breathes it in, and sets it back with unusual care. From the street below: the cries of a flower seller, a carriage on the cobbles, a dog with opinions. London going about its magnificent indifference, quite unaware that a wallflower has just declared war in the language of flowers.)*
> *(Rose folds Drummond's card into the workbox and closes the lid with a click that sounds, in the quiet room, like a decision being filed rather than made. On the mantel, the violets nod in their sherry glass. Modesty. Remembrance. The campaign, Rose thinks, has acquired a motto — and she did not even have to invent it. Somewhere below, Letitia is telling the cook about the posy, in the tone of a woman reporting a military honor; the house, Rose reflects, has already adopted the girl's flowers as its own small flag. Let her. A campaign needs its colors.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — HONORIA'S TRUTH. Honoria asks the question outright; Rose must decide what the girl is allowed to know about why she is being sponsored.
scenes.prose:
> *(The garden again, the next morning — the roses drier, the light thinner, the hour earlier than any call of politeness would justify. Honoria has come to return Letitia's borrowed shawl and stayed for a turn about the roses, and Rose has let her stay, because the girl walks the paths the way other girls walk ballrooms — as if they might, at any moment, be hers. Halfway down the path Honoria stops, and the question comes out all at once, stammer and all, the way a cork comes out of a bottle.)*
> "Miss Hartwell — why are you doing this? For me, I mean. Nobody does things for me. My aunt says it is your Christian duty, but I am nineteen and I know when I am being — being managed. My aunt manages me. Mrs. Hartwell manages me kindly. You —" She looks up, and her eyes are clear and frightened and entirely adult. "Am I being managed?"
> *(Rose looks at the girl — the plain face, the honest eyes, the mended gloves clasped hard — and understands that whatever she says now will be the foundation everything else is built on. A launch founded on a lie will wobble at the first ball; it will list, and take on water, and go down with all hands. A launch founded on the whole truth may never stand up at all — the truth being, as truths go, a peculiarly unseaworthy vessel. The garden is very quiet. Somewhere, a gardener's barrow squeaks. Rose chooses her words the way Élise chooses silk — for strategy, not for beauty.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — Honoria's truth:*
- **Tell her plainly** — *Honesty+, Honoria stricken but trusting.* "Your aunt holds a letter — a debt of my family's — and the price of her silence is your Season. I will not lie to you, Honoria. But I will also not fail you." She weeps, then straightens; the trust between them becomes iron.
- **Let her believe it's friendship** — *Kindness+, the lie accrues interest.* "Because I like you, and because the ton is wrong about you, and because someone ought to have done it sooner." She glows; and every kind hour afterward compounds the debt of the untruth.
- **Deflect, kindly** — *Wit+, the question waits.* "Because your aunt terrifies me slightly less than you terrify yourself, and I have always backed the braver horse." She laughs through the stammer; the question retreats, but it will return better armed.

scenes.synopsis: Beat 3 — the first commission. Honoria's wardrobe; the atelier hears everything. Fashion as intelligence: Élise already knows about Drummond's terms.
scenes.prose:
> *(Élise's atelier, Bond Street. The workroom hums — three girls at machines, a cutter chalking sarcenet with the concentration of a cartographer, the good smell of pressed linen and French soap and hot irons. Élise herself, tape about her neck like a general's sash and chalk dust on her cuffs like battle honors, looks Rose up and down and smiles the smile of a woman who has already read the morning's post, the afternoon's post, and several letters that were never posted at all.)*
> "So. The dragon's niece." — Élise folds her arms. "You will dress her, and I will dress her, and all London will watch you do it. Sit, chérie. You look like a woman who has been threatened before chocolate. The worst kind of threatened — the kind that arrives in a grey livery and leaves a card."
> "How do you know about Honoria? Drummond's card arrived not four hours ago. Four hours, Élise. The ink was barely dry on the threat."
> "Four hours is a lifetime." — Élise pours two small cups of something dark and restorative. "Lady Agatha's maid told my finisher's cousin, who told my finisher, who told me while pinning a hem. The atelier hears everything, Rose. We are the confessional with better lighting. Brides confess here. Bankrupts confess here. Fools confess everywhere, but here we write it down in the order book, with measurements."
> "I need a wardrobe." — Rose sets down the cup. "Not a Season's worth — a campaign's worth. Everything she wears must say *unremarkable* in a voice so assured that no one thinks to laugh. Do you understand the commission? It is the opposite of everything you have ever been asked to do."
> "Ah." — Élise's eyes narrow with professional interest, the interest of a general offered an impossible siege. "The hardest commission. To dress a girl to be overlooked beautifully. It will cost — not only money. Half the ton will come in to stare at the muslins and ask questions with their eyes. Questions I shall answer with pins in my mouth, which is the atelier's way of saying nothing at all."
> "Then we shall give them muslins worth staring at, and answers worth nothing. Measure her Thursday. And Élise —" Rose lowers her voice, though the machines cover it well enough. "Whatever your workroom hears about the Drummonds, about debts, about paper changing hands — I want to hear it too. Consider it part of the commission."
> *(Élise's chalk pauses, mid-air, over a length of grey sarcenet. The general considers the new orders — their scope, their danger, their price.)*
> "That is a different commission, chérie. But the atelier keeps books for all its clients." — Élise
> *(She marks the order book with a flourish. Rose watches the pen move and understands that she has just hired, for the price of a wardrobe, the best-informed woman in London.)*

scenes.synopsis: The commission deepens — Honoria's figure, Honoria's colors, and the first piece of atelier intelligence: an unpaid bill with a name attached.
scenes.prose:
> *(The fitting room, the inner sanctum, where the light is kinder and the talk is not. Élise unrolls bolts across the chaise — dove grey, jonquil, a deep rose damask, a green sarcenet — and talks while her hands work, the way surgeons talk while cutting: steadily, precisely, without looking up.)*
> "She is short-waisted, long in the leg — we build up, never across. High necklines; the throat is her best feature and she hides it like a sin, poor child. No white — white on a frightened girl is a surrender flag, it says *I have given up, pray be kind*. We want colors that hold the eye gently. Grey that is almost blue. Yellow like late sun on a wall. Rose, but the deep rose, the one that has made up its mind and is not asking permission."
> "You have thought about her." — Rose watches the bolts accumulate, each one a sentence in the argument. "You have thought about her a great deal, for a woman who met her only in my description."
> "I think about everyone. It is my profession. A dressmaker who does not think about the girl inside the gown is a mere seamstress, and I am not a mere anything." — Élise selects the grey, holds it to the light. "Now — intelligence, since you asked, and since you are paying for the commission that carries it. The Vicomtesse de Brie's bill is three months unpaid, and she has ordered a ball gown regardless — ordered it as a woman orders who has no intention of paying. Someone is lending her money, or she is lending it to someone, and either way the atelier is financing a mystery."
> "And?"
> "And Mr. Rackham's man was here yesterday, asking after a coat left for alteration in 'thirteen. Thirteen, chérie. A coat abandoned for three years, suddenly wanted back. Debts leave coats behind, Rose. It is practically their signature — the one thing a ruined man cannot bear to collect, until the day he must."
> *(Rackham. The name sits between them like a dropped pin on a marble floor — small, bright, impossible to ignore. Rose files it alongside Quill's codicils and Julian's quiet payments and the vicomtesse's gossip: the money thread, tangle by tangle, knot by knot.)*
> "Keep the book open, Élise. And the ears."
> "The book is always open." — Élise chalks a decisive line. "It is the ears that charge extra. Though for you, chérie — for you, I may offer a discount. You amuse the workroom."

scenes.synopsis: The chapter's single fashion-selection scene — Honoria's first public gown. 2–3 diegetic options, no coin cost, remembered by the game and by the ton.
scenes.prose:
> *(Three lengths of silk lie across the chaise, each pinned with a paper tag in Élise's decisive hand. The fitting room is quiet — the machines muffled beyond the door, the cutter's chalk stilled. Honoria's first public appearance — the calls, the teas, the being-looked-at — will be made in one of these three, and everything that follows will be built on the choice. Élise waits, arms folded, the oracle of the fitting room, and lets the silence do the selling.)*
> "Choose, then. Not for beauty — any fool can choose beauty, and half the ton does, badly. For *strategy*. The gown is the first sentence of the argument we are making, and the ton reads first sentences the way judges read indictments. Choose the sentence."
> *(Rose lays her hand on each bolt in turn — the grey cool under her palm, the jonquil warm as late sun, the rose deep and certain. She thinks of the girl: the mended gloves, the stammer, the plain brave sentence in the garden — *unremarkable without being ridiculous*. She thinks of Augusta's doctrine, still unheard, and of Drummond's underlined words, and of the ton waiting like a cat at a mousehole. Then she chooses.)*
*★ Choice (remembered — no coin cost; the Gazette, the callers, and Honoria herself will remember):*
- **The dove-grey sarcenet** — *Restraint+, Augusta approves.* Grey that is almost blue; the color of a girl who expects nothing and deserves better. Honoria will look composed, forgettable in the kindest way — and the ton will have to work to find fault.
- **The jonquil silk** — *Warmth+, Letitia applauds.* Yellow like late sun; a risk, a small defiance. On Honoria's coloring it will catch candlelight and make her look, for an evening, like someone's happy thought. The ton will notice — which is the point, and the danger.
- **The deep-rose damask** — *Presence+, Élise's private favorite.* Rose that has made up its mind. It borrows a little of Rose's own armor and lends it to the girl. Wearing it, Honoria will look sponsored — which is true, and which the ton will read exactly as it pleases.
> *(Rose rests her hand on one bolt — finally, decisively — and Élise marks the tag with a single stroke of chalk, the way a judge signs a sentence.)*
> "Noted. In ink, in the book, and in my memory." — Élise folds the chosen silk with reverence. "Go on, chérie — the ton is already choosing its adjectives. We have merely chosen first, which is the whole of the advantage in this town."
