scenes.synopsis: Beat 4 setup — the Dowager's card arrives. Not a summons in Drummond's style; an invitation that cannot be refused.
scenes.prose:
> *(Hartwell House, late afternoon. The light going amber across the hall. A card on the tray — heavy stock, the Ravencroft crest blind-embossed, the kind of card that does not ask but assumes. Letitia reads it over Rose's shoulder, her spectacles catching the light.)*
> "The Dowager Marchioness of Ravencroft requests the pleasure of Miss Hartwell's company at tea tomorrow. *Alone.* Underlined once." — Letitia looks up. "Augusta underlines the way other women weep — rarely, and to devastating effect. This is not a summons, Rose. Drummond summons. Augusta *invites*, which is infinitely more compulsory."
> "She knows about Honoria."
> "Everyone knows about Honoria, my dear. By now the fishmonger knows about Honoria, and the fishmonger's wife has opinions about the gown. The question is what Augusta *intends*, which is never the same as what she knows. Augusta's knowledge is the map; her intentions are the territory."
> "Augusta intends to be amused. I intend to be instructed. It amounts to the same afternoon, with better cake."
> *(Rose turns the card over. On the back, in Augusta's formidable upright hand, the ink still faintly glossy: *Bring the girl's measurements. We shall do this properly or not at all.*)*
> "She wants the measurements." — Rose stares at the line. "She is already campaigning. She has been campaigning since breakfast, probably. Possibly since the card arrived — possibly she knew before the card arrived. I would not put it past her."
> "Of course she is." — Letitia is already moving toward the writing desk. "Augusta has launched eleven goddaughters, three nieces, and one extremely unlikely cousin — the one with the laugh like a donkey, you remember — and she regards a wallflower as a personal insult to the order of things. Go, be instructed, and do not — I beg you, Rose, I beg you on my knees, which at my age is a serious undertaking — do not try to be cleverer than Augusta. It wastes everyone's tea, and the tea at Ravencroft House is too good to waste."
> *(Rose copies the measurements onto a fresh sheet in her clearest hand. On the back of Augusta's card she writes, for her own amusement: *tomorrow: be instructed*. Then she underlines it once, in tribute.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 4 — Augusta's strategy. How to launch a girl the ton has decided to overlook: the doctrine of being seen three times by the right eyes.
scenes.prose:
> *(Ravencroft House, the morning room that has ended more Seasons than most ballrooms have begun. Augusta, Dowager Marchioness of Ravencroft, sits enthroned among correspondence like a queen among dispatches — Honoria's measurements already spread on the table like a battle map, annotated in Augusta's hand with observations Rose can read upside down: *short-waisted*, *throat good*, *frightened — remedy: certainty*.)*
> "Drummond's niece. Plain, stammers, good heart, mended gloves." — Augusta does not look up from the measurements. "I have had her whole history by ten o'clock — the assemblies last year, the two girls, the laughter *near* her. Sit, Rose. You look like a girl who has been handed a siege and told it is a Season."
> "I have been handed both. They appear to be the same thing this year. The siege has better refreshments."
> "Listen, then, for I shall say this once, and I dislike repeating myself even to people I like." — Augusta sets down her pen. "The ton does not hate wallflowers, Rose. Hate would be a compliment — it requires attention, and attention is the one currency the ton never spends on the undeserving. The ton *forgets* them, which is fatal, because a forgotten girl becomes a joke the moment anyone remembers her. Our task is not to make Honoria admired. Admiration is for beauties and heiresses and girls with ten thousand a year. Our task is to make her *seen* — three times, in one week, by the right eyes, doing the right unremarkable things beautifully."
> "Seen doing what, precisely?"
> "Arriving with you. Leaving with you. Dancing once — once only, and well — with a partner who has been instructed to look as though he is enjoying himself. A girl seen three times in good company ceases to be a curiosity and becomes a fixture. Fixtures are never laughed at, Rose. One laughs at accidents, not furniture."
> *(Rose laughs despite herself — a short, surprised sound — and then stops, because Augusta is not joking, and because the doctrine is, in its brutal way, perfect: a complete theory of social survival in four sentences.)*
> "Furniture." — Rose tests the word. "You intend to make her furniture."
> "I intend to make her *safe*. There is a difference, and you will learn it, and the learning will cost you." — Augusta takes up the measurements. "Now. We shall do this properly or not at all. You have brought the girl's measurements, as instructed. Good. The first lesson of launching anyone, Rose: the Dowager is always obeyed, especially when she is right."

scenes.synopsis: The plan's currency — the campaign week takes shape: names, dances, afternoons. The price Rose pays, itemized as strategy.
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta draws a list down the margin of Honoria's measurements, each name a small detonation in her formidable hand.)*
> "Tuesday: my at-home. She arrives with you, leaves with you, speaks to exactly four people, all chosen — chosen by me, which means chosen correctly. Thursday: the Ashcombe ball — Julian's mother has agreed, do not ask me what it cost, to put Honoria's name on the list and a reliable partner on her card for the second country dance. A reliable partner, Rose, means a man who can be trusted to smile as though the smile were his own idea. Friday: calls. You will take her to the only three houses that matter and let the rest of the town hear about it from their servants, which is how the rest of the town hears about everything."
> "My name, my invitations, my dances, my afternoons." — Rose looks at the list. "Drummond's price, itemized. She underlined the words; you have supplied the particulars."
> "Drummond's price is the beginning of wisdom, not the end." — Augusta's pen pauses. "Here is the part she did not name, because she does not understand it: you will also give the girl your *certainty*. When the ton looks at her — and it will look, Rose, the way a cat looks at a new piece of furniture, deciding whether to sharpen its claws on it — she must see in your face that there is nothing to see. Your composure is her gown. Wear it well, and wear it every day, and do not let it slip at the crucial moment, which will be the moment you least expect."
> "And if they laugh?" — Rose asks it quietly. "If, despite everything, they laugh?"
> "Then you laugh first, at something else entirely — at Letitia's bonnet, at the weather, at your own reflection — and the ton, which follows laughter the way hounds follow a scent, will laugh with you and forget what it was laughing at. That is the whole art. I have practiced it for forty years, and I have never once been laughed at, which tells you everything about the efficacy of the method and nothing about my character."
> *(She folds the list with precision, crease to crease, and hands it to Rose. A campaign, in Augusta's hand, on the back of a girl's measurements — the most valuable piece of paper Rose has handled all Season, codicils included.)*
> "One more thing." — Augusta rises, which means the audience is ending. "The Gazette will have its say. Nance Bell's paper judges everyone, and it will judge this — it judges taste, Rose, and nothing else, which is why the ton fears it more than the debt collectors. Give it nothing to judge but elegance, and it will judge the elegance. Give it a girl being laughed at, and it will write the laughter down in ink, and ink is forever."
> *(Rose takes the list, and the warning with it, and understands that she has just been given both the campaign and its terms of surrender.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 5 — Letitia's kindness. The comic aunt disarms the terrified girl: a lesson in entering a room, with business.
scenes.prose:
> *(The Hartwell drawing room, cleared for rehearsal — the small tables pushed back, the footstool strategically placed, the air of a theater before the house opens. Letitia, armed with a shawl, a fan, and the authority of a woman who has entered a thousand rooms badly and survived to tell the tale, regards Honoria with the eye of a drill sergeant who adores her recruits and intends to make them suffer beautifully.)*
> "Entering a room is a science, my dear. Chin up — not *up* up, you are not a horse being shown at Tattersall's — eyes on the hostess, smile as though you have just remembered something pleasant, and for heaven's sake do not clutch your reticule as though it contained the crown jewels." — Letitia advances. "What *does* it contain? Let me see."
> "A h-handkerchief. And — and a peppermint. In case of — of faintness." — Honoria produces both like evidence.
> "Excellent. A girl prepared for faintness never faints — it is the unprepared who oblige us with scenes. Now — walk to me. No, do not hurry, you are not escaping a fire. Glide. *Glide*, child. Pretend the floor is a ballroom and you are slightly bored by it, as all the best people are."
> *(Honoria glides, with immense concentration — chin at the approved angle, eyes on the hostess, smile faintly pleasant — and collides gently with the footstool, which has been placed, Rose suspects, precisely for this purpose. There is a terrible pause. The footstool rocks. Honoria's face performs a tragedy in three acts. And then Letitia laughs — a great warm unladylike laugh, the laugh of a woman who has collided with furniture in every drawing room in London — and Honoria, to her own astonishment, laughs too, stammer and all, the laugh shaking out of her like water from a shaken cloth.)*
> "There." — Letitia wipes her eyes. "You have survived the worst thing that can happen in a drawing room — looking foolish in front of someone kind. It is excellent practice. The unkind ones matter less than you think; they are too busy being unkind to each other to spare you more than a glance. Again — and this time, step *over* the footstool as though you had placed it there yourself, as a test for the unwary."
> *(Honoria steps over the footstool with immense dignity, chin at the approved angle, and does not look down. It is, in its small way, a triumph — the first of the campaign, won in an empty drawing room with no audience but a footstool and an aunt. Letitia applauds with her fan, smartly, twice.)*
> "Furniture, my dear. Augusta's word, and she is never wrong about these things. From now on, you are excellent furniture — well-placed, well-polished, and entirely unlaughable."
> "I — I think I should like to be furniture." — Honoria considers this. "Furniture is — furniture is never sent away. It is just — there. It belongs."
> *(Letitia's fan stills. For a moment the comedy drops from her face like a dropped shawl, and what is underneath is something fierce and maternal and entirely serious.)*
> "Yes, my dear. That is exactly what it is. Now — again, from the door, and this time do not apologize to the footstool."

scenes.synopsis: The merge-board texture scene — the atelier's standing order queue. Orders always waiting: the free-income engine, diegetic.
scenes.prose:
> *(Élise's workroom, late — the lamps lit, the machines silent, the day's work folded and shelved. The great order book lies open on the cutting table, its pages ruled into columns in Élise's decisive hand: client, commission, stage, due. Rose, waiting for a hem to be finished, reads it over Élise's shoulder — and understands, suddenly and completely, the economy of the whole war.)*
> "The standing queue. Read it to me — all of it. I want to hear the shape of it." — Rose
> "Lady Calthorpe's sash — half done, pays on delivery. The Misses Fenwick's gloves — cut, pays on delivery. A reticule for Mrs. Alder, a habit-shirt for the Countess, six handkerchiefs hemmed for a bride who wept on them in advance — wept, chérie, before the wedding, on the handkerchiefs, which I consider optimism." — Élise turns a page. "Orders always waiting. That is the atelier: a machine that turns waiting into money. While the ton waits to be amused, we wait to be paid, and we are paid."
> *(As they watch, a finisher ties off the sash — a few swift practiced knots — folds it in tissue with the care of a woman wrapping a child, and sets it on the finished shelf. Élise draws a line through the entry — one stroke, decisive as a signature — and writes the sum in the paid column in figures that make Rose blink.)*
> "And there — income. No drama, no dragon, no ton. A sash, finished, paid for. While you fight your war in ballrooms, my girls fight it in buttonholes, and the book balances either way. This —" she taps the order book, "— this is the only honest ledger in London, Rose. Everything else is promises."
> *(Rose looks at the queue — the waiting orders, the patient columns, the sash on the finished shelf — and feels something settle in her chest like a stone finding the bottom of a pond. This is the other economy: not debts and codicils and Rackham's abandoned coats, not threats in grey livery, but work, finished, paid. The atelier does not threaten. It delivers. She will need both economies before the Season is out — the ballroom's and the workroom's — and she is beginning to suspect the workroom's is the one that will save her.)*
> "Keep the queue full, Élise. Whatever else happens — whatever the dragons do, whatever the papers say — keep it full."
> "It has never been empty." — Élise closes the book with a soft finality. "Not in twenty years. Not even in the Terror, when the clients paid in assignats and wept on the handkerchiefs in advance. The queue, chérie, is eternal. It is the ton that is temporary."

scenes.synopsis: Beat 6 setup — the studio sitting is arranged. Octavia Wren paints Rose; the studio is where the émigrés talk.
scenes.prose:
> *(A card from Mrs. Octavia Wren, the portraitist, delivered by a boy with paint on his cuffs: *I am returned from Bath and require your face, which has improved with trouble. Sit for me Thursday. Bring no opinions about the nose; I have already decided. — O.W.*)*
> "Octavia is back." — Rose holds up the card. "She requires my face. It has, she says, improved with trouble."
> "The painter?" — Letitia looks up from her correspondence. "The one who made Lady Jersey look merciful? That woman could flatter a gargoyle into a marriage settlement. She once painted my late husband and made him look — well. She made him look *possible*, which was beyond the powers of the clergy."
> "She wants me to sit Thursday. Her studio is — it was, last Season, the place where the émigrés waited their turn and talked while they waited. Half the news of the French money came through her waiting room — the vicomtesses gossip the way other women breathe, and Octavia lets them, and remembers everything."
> *(Letitia sets down her pen with the air of a woman reaching a conclusion.)*
> "Then sit, and listen. You are following Rackham's debts up the chain, are you not? Chains are made of talk, my dear — talk, and paper, and the little pauses between the talk. Go and collect some links. And for heaven's sake, hold your chin the way she tells you. She is always right about chins, even when she is wrong about noses."
> *(Rose writes her acceptance — *Thursday, with pleasure, and I shall bring no opinions about anything* — and in the margin of her mind adds a note in her campaigner's hand: Octavia's sitters gossip; Octavia herself misses nothing; a portrait studio is an atelier with better light and worse secrets. And secrets, Rose reflects, folding the note, are the one commodity London never runs short of.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 6 — the studio sitting. An émigré sitter gossips about de Valcourt money; Rose listens. (Lucien de Valcourt named in gossip only — never appears, never speaks.)
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia Wren's studio, Thursday. North light through the tall windows, turpentine and linseed on the air, the good disorder of genius — canvases stacked three deep, draperies over everything, a skull on the mantel wearing a feathered hat. Rose sits for her portrait, chin at the prescribed angle, while in the waiting corner an émigré vicomtesse — all bones and old lace and magnificent ruin — waits her own turn and talks, as émigrés do, to fill the silence that exile leaves behind.)*
> "You have the Hartwell chin, ma chérie. Hold it — so, exactly so. The vicomtesse will talk; let her. She pays in gossip what she cannot pay in coin, and her gossip is better than most people's money." — Octavia, brush moving.
> "— and I tell you, ma chère Octavia, the de Valcourt money is moving again." — the Vicomtesse, to the room at large. "Moving, always moving. It does not rest, that money. It travels."
> *(Rose's hands still in her lap — Octavia's brush does not. The name lands in the quiet studio like a coin dropped on marble: Lucien de Valcourt. Gossip only, a name in someone else's mouth, a direction on a map rather than a man in a room — but a name attached to money, and the money is moving.)*
> "De Valcourt?" — Rose keeps her voice carefully casual, the voice of a woman making conversation about the weather. "The family that lost everything in '93 and found it again in — what was it — sugar? Shipping? I never can keep the restorations straight."
> "Found it, lost it, found it." — the Vicomtesse waves a bony hand. "Money like that does not sit still, mademoiselle. It travels. It pays debts that are not its own. It buys paper — notes, mortgages, the little promises men write when they are desperate and sign when they are drunker. Your Mr. Rackham's paper, they say, has traveled through interesting hands. Very interesting hands."
> *(Rackham's paper. In interesting hands. Rose holds her chin exactly as Octavia placed it — lifted, thoughtful, composed — and files the sentence away with the care of a woman handling a live coal, to be examined later, with tongs.)*
> "Do not look so interested, chérie. It ruins the mouth." — Octavia, without looking up from the canvas. "Think of something dull — Drummond's niece, perhaps. Think of her bonnet. That should flatten the expression nicely."
> *(Rose thinks of Honoria's bonnet — two seasons old, ribbon re-pressed with such care — and the mouth obeys, and Octavia paints on, and the vicomtesse talks on, and the chain grows one link longer.)*

scenes.synopsis: The money thread tightens — debts, paper, and whose hands the notes are passing through. Rose follows Rackham's debts one link up the chain.
scenes.prose:
> *(The sitting continues. The vicomtesse, having delivered her news like a dispatch rider, dozes among the draperies, her old lace rising and falling with magnificent indifference. Octavia paints, and talks in the low voice she uses for truths — the voice beneath the flippancy, the one Rose has learned to listen for.)*
> "She is right about the paper, you know." — Octavia mixes a grey with great attention. "Half the distressed notes in London have changed hands this spring — bought up quietly, by agents, for principals no one names. Your friend Julian has been buying his brother's back, poor honorable boy, paying full price for paper worth half — it is the most expensive honor in London, and he pays it gladly. Someone else is buying cheaper, and faster, and without the inconvenience of honor."
> "De Valcourt?" — Rose asks it softly, to the canvas, to the north light.
> "A name in gossip, nothing more. I paint faces, chérie, not pedigrees of money." — The brush pauses. "But ask yourself, Rose: who profits when a family's debts are gathered into one hand? The holder of the paper holds the family — the mortgages, the notes, the little promises. Rackham's creditors are being — consolidated. That is the word the agents use. Consolidated, as though debt were an empire and someone were building one."
> *(Rose is very still. Quill's codicils, breeding. Julian's quiet payments, full price. The vicomtesse's moving money. Élise's abandoned coat from 'thirteen. The chain is taking shape, link by link, and every link is paper — paper bought, paper gathered, paper held by hands no one will name.)*
> "If someone is gathering the Hartwell paper —" — Rose begins, and stops, because the sentence finishes itself.
> "Then Drummond's threat is not the only paper that matters. Yes." — Octavia studies the canvas. "Now lift the chin — you are thinking again, and thinking ruins the mouth worse than interest. Think of the bonnet. The re-pressed ribbon. There."
> *(Rose lifts her chin. She is thinking, furiously — of paper, of hands, of empires built from debt — and Octavia, who misses nothing, paints the thought right into the portrait, where it will hang in Hartwell House for a hundred years, thinking.)*

scenes.synopsis: Texture micro-beat — the walk home from the studio. Seed the stripped-thorn-stem floriography thread, lightly.
scenes.prose:
> *(Bond Street, late afternoon. The light going gold on the shopfronts. Rose walks home alone, declining the carriage — her head too full of paper for the confinement of a carriage, her feet needing the honest work of walking. At the corner a flower girl holds up roses, their stems stripped of thorns, the bare green stems neat as peeled willow.)*
> "Stripped of their thorns, miss. Safe as daisies." — the flower girl, hopefully. "No pricks, miss. Ladies like 'em without the pricks."
> *(Rose buys one — a deep red, thornless, faintly absurd in its defenselessness — and carries it home turning it in her fingers, the stripped stem smooth and strange against her glove. A rose without thorns: beautiful, and defenseless, and not quite a rose anymore — a rose that has been made safe for ladies who do not wish to be pricked. She thinks of Honoria — the ton wants its wallflowers thornless too, safe as daisies, never pricking anyone's comfort, never drawing blood with an opinion or an awkwardness. And she thinks of Drummond, who keeps all her thorns, every one of them, and uses them — and of Augusta, thorned like a briar and twice as formidable — and of herself, somewhere between, deciding daily which thorns to keep.)*
> *(At home she puts the stripped rose in water on her desk, beside Drummond's card and Augusta's campaign list. Three objects, three economies: the threat, the strategy, and the girl they are all, in the end, about. The rose nods in its glass, thornless and absurd, its stripped stem pale against the dark wood. Rose looks at it for a long moment — at the threat beside it, underlined twice, and the strategy beside that, folded crease to crease — and makes a note in the campaigner's hand, not in the workbox but in her memory, where the important things go: *the ton wants them thornless. We shall disappoint the ton.* Outside, the street cries on without her: the flower seller, the carriages, a dog with opinions. London, magnificent and indifferent, has no idea what is being decided on a desk in Hartwell House.)*

scenes.synopsis: The first fitting — Honoria in the atelier, terrified and, for a moment, delighted. The campaign becomes cloth.
scenes.prose:
> *(Élise's fitting room. The Thursday measuring has become a fitting — the chosen silk from the [F] commission, half-made, pinned and chalked, hanging on Honoria like a promise. Honoria stands on the dais while Élise circles with pins in her mouth, muttering in French — instructions, endearments, threats, all in the same tone — and Rose watches from the chaise, her hands folded to keep them from fidgeting.)*
> "Do not breathe in so, chérie, you will faint and I will have to catch you, and I am too expensive to catch people. Breathe *out*. There. Now — look." — Élise turns Honoria to the glass with the flourish of a magician revealing the rabbit.
> *(Élise steps back. The girl in the mirror is — not beautiful. The mirror is honest, and Élise has not asked it to lie. But she is composed. The gown holds her upright the way good architecture holds a wall — not by ornament, but by structure. Color in her cheeks that is not terror, for once. Her hands, in the half-finished sleeves, have unclasped.)*
> "Oh." — Honoria
> *(It is the smallest sound — a breath, a syllable, nothing. But the stammer is gone from it, and Rose — watching from the chaise — feels something complicated tighten in her chest, something between triumph and grief. This is what the price buys. Not dances. Not afternoons. This: a girl looking in a glass and seeing, for the first time, someone the ton will have to work to overlook.)*
> "You look," Rose says carefully, choosing the words the way Élise chooses silk, "like a girl the ton will have to work to overlook. And I mean that as the highest praise in my power."
> "Is that — is that good? To be — overlooked? Only with — with work?" — Honoria turns from the glass, and her eyes are bright.
> "It is the best thing anyone has looked all Season. It is the whole campaign, in cloth." — Rose rises. "Élise, she will need — everything. The calls begin next week. The teas, the at-homes, the ball. We launch her properly or not at all — Augusta's words, and for once I agree with every syllable."
> *(Élise meets Rose's eye over Honoria's head — the look of two generals watching a recruit discover she can march. The atelier hears everything — including, now, the sound of a campaign being sewn, stitch by stitch, into silk.)*
> "Properly." — Élise nods, already chalking. "Or not at all. There is no third option, chérie. Not in my workroom."

scenes.synopsis: ★ DRESSING RITUAL — Afternoon Calls with Honoria. Elegance that flatters by restraint; never outshine the niece. Twenty micro-decisions at 5 coins each (~100 coins, NOT free); jewels from owned pieces only; the reveal coda lands in S21.
scenes.prose:
> *(The ritual opens the morning of the first calls — the campaign's first public day. Hartwell House, Rose's dressing room, the light thin and honest. On the stand: the occasion brief, published — pinned where Rose can read it while the maid waits, the pins in her cushion, the morning holding its breath.)*
> **OCCASION BRIEF — Afternoon Calls with Honoria (first campaign calls)**
> *Editorial criterion: elegance that flatters by restraint. You are the frame, not the picture. Every choice must make Honoria look assured without making Rose look dimmed — the ton smells self-effacement and calls it guilt. Be the more beautiful woman in the room, quietly, so that standing next to you feels like safety, not comparison.*
> *Direction — choose one (remembered):*
> - **The Quiet Frame** — dove greys, soft blues; you recede half a step so she advances one. *(Augusta's doctrine, worn.)*
> - **The Warm Escort** — jonquil, cream, rose; you glow gently, and she glows by standing near the light. *(Letitia's instinct, tailored.)*
> - **The Assured Sponsor** — deep rose, slate, black accents; you look like a woman whose sponsorship is a prize, and she looks prized. *(The bold play — the ton reads confidence as truth.)*
> *(Rose reads the brief twice, and chooses. Twenty micro-decisions, five coins each — restraint, itemized. The pins come out one by one, and with each pin, a small deliberate quiet is built.)*
> 1. The gown's neckline — high, to echo Honoria's and make modesty look like fashion. *(5 coins)*
> 2. The sleeve — long, fitted, no flounce; nothing that moves when you do not. *(5 coins)*
> 3. The gown's color depth — one shade deeper than Honoria's, never paler; the frame is darker than the picture. *(5 coins)*
> 4. The sash — narrow, self-fabric; no contrasting color to steal the eye. *(5 coins)*
> *(Four pins in, and the criterion holds: nothing here asks to be looked at. Rose watches the maid's hands work and thinks of Augusta's doctrine — *your composure is her gown* — and understands, with the clarity that comes from being dressed by someone else, that she is being sewn into a strategy.)*
> 5. The shawl — cashmere, folded thrice; warmth you can offer her if she shivers. *(5 coins)*
> 6. The shawl's drape — over one arm, ready; a sponsor carries comfort visibly. *(5 coins)*
> 7. The gloves — kid, plain, immaculate; your hands do the reassuring, let them look capable. *(5 coins)*
> *(Story morsel — between pins, the maid tying the sash: "Miss Honoria's maid says she was sick this morning, miss. Nerves. She wore the peppermint." Rose's fingers still, half a second, then finish the knot. Sick with nerves, and coming anyway. The girl is braver than the campaign deserves.)*
> 8. The reticule — small, dark; nothing that glints or swings. *(5 coins)*
> 9. The handkerchief — plain linen, tucked where you can reach it for her, not you. *(5 coins)*
> 10. The bonnet's brim — wide enough to shade, not to hide; you are not hiding either. *(5 coins)*
> 11. The bonnet's trim — a single ribbon, Honoria's gown color; a quiet rhyme between you. *(5 coins)*
> 12. The ribbon's knot — to the side, not the front; asymmetry reads as ease. *(5 coins)*
> *(Twelve pins, and the woman in the glass is becoming someone else — someone quieter, someone whose beauty has been put, deliberately, at half-mast. It is the hardest thing Rose has ever worn: not the gown, but the restraint. The ton will look at her today and see nothing to discuss, and that nothing is the most expensive thing she owns.)*
> 13. The hair — low chignon, severe; severity in the hair permits softness in the face. *(5 coins)*
> 14. The hairpin — tortoiseshell, invisible; no ornament that competes with the girl's courage. *(5 coins)*
> *(Story morsel — the maid at the hair: "Lady Agatha's carriage was seen in the square, miss. Slowed past the house. Didn't stop." Rose meets her own eyes in the glass — severe chignon, quiet face. "She is checking her investment," Rose says. "Let her look. Investments that perform are left alone.")*
> 15. The shoes — kid slippers, low heel; you will stand a great deal, and stand still. *(5 coins)*
> 16. The stockings — silk, clocked discreetly; detail for the close observer only. *(5 coins)*
> 17. The pelisse for the carriage — wool, dark; the street sees the sponsor, the drawing room sees the friend. *(5 coins)*
> 18. The pelisse's collar — turned up against the wind, down in the hall; transitions matter. *(5 coins)*
> 19. The scent — none. No perfume today; let the rooms smell of themselves, and you of nothing that distracts. *(5 coins)*
> 20. The final check — the glass, full length; ask it one question: *does she look safe standing next to me?* *(5 coins)*
> *(Jewels: from OWNED pieces only — the pearl studs, the thin gold chain. The jewel shelf is always open, but it is never a ritual step; what you own is what you wear.)*
> *(Total: 100 coins. Not free — restraint, it turns out, must be paid for like everything else.)*
> *(The maid steps back. In the glass: a woman composed entirely of deliberate quiet — the frame, not the picture, darker than the picture by exactly one shade. The criterion holds. The reveal coda follows — S21.)*

ritual.occasionBrief: Afternoon Calls with Honoria (first campaign calls)
directions: The Quiet Frame: dove greys, soft blues; you recede half a step so she advances one. *(Augusta's doctrine, worn.)*
The Warm Escort: jonquil, cream, rose; you glow gently, and she glows by standing near the light. *(Letitia's instinct, tailored.)*
The Assured Sponsor: deep rose, slate, black accents; you look like a woman whose sponsorship is a prize, and she looks prized. *(The bold play — the ton reads confidence as truth.)*

scenes.synopsis: The reveal-coda beat — the ritual's payoff. Rose revealed in the glass, worn complete; then the first call. The coda is the acquisition asset: Rose, fully dressed, with hair and composure — never a bare dress form.
scenes.prose:
> *(The reveal coda: Rose stands before the full-length glass in the finished ritual — gown, shawl over one arm, bonnet's single ribbon knotted to the side, pearl studs catching the light, the thin gold chain at her throat. The maid is gone. The dressing room is quiet. For a held breath it is only Rose and the woman the ritual made — and the woman the ritual made is a study in deliberate quiet, every pin a decision, every decision a small act of war.)*
> *(Mirror moment: she turns — slowly — and the gown moves exactly as much as she does, no more; the sleeve does not flounce, the sash does not swing, the shawl stays folded over her arm like a flag at rest. The criterion holds: elegance that flatters by restraint. She looks like safety. She looks like the kind of woman a frightened girl could stand beside and not be diminished — the frame, darker than the picture by exactly one shade, asking nothing of the eye.)*
> "Does she look safe standing next to me?" — Rose, to the glass
> *(The glass declines to answer, which is the glass's job — mirrors are honest about hems and silent about everything else. A knock at the door: Honoria is below, in the chosen gown, clutching the peppermint reticule, early by nine minutes as always. Rose descends. In the hall, the girl looks up — and her face does what the glass could not: it answers. The color rises in her cheeks; the stammer, for once, has nothing to say; she looks, Rose thinks, like a picture that has just realized it is hanging in a good frame.)*
> "Oh, Miss Hartwell. You look — you look like the answer to something." — Honoria
> "I look like a frame, my dear. You are the picture. Shall we go and be looked at?" — Rose
> *(They step into the carriage together — the sponsor and the sponsored, the frame and the picture, the woman who paid a hundred coins for restraint and the girl who is about to be worth every one. The reveal is complete: not a dress, but a woman, dressed for war and calling it afternoon calls. The carriage door closes. The campaign goes public.)*

scenes.synopsis: The campaign calls begin — Augusta's doctrine in action: seen three times by the right eyes. The ton looks, the way a cat looks at furniture.
scenes.prose:
> *(Lady Calthorpe's drawing room, first of the three houses that matter — the room all amber and old portraits, the company all consequence. Rose enters with Honoria half a step behind — the rehearsed glide, the footstool long since conquered, the peppermint reticule carried like a sidearm. The room's conversation dips, the way water dips around a stone, and then resumes, a fraction louder, as if to prove it had never dipped at all.)*
> "Miss Hartwell — and this is Miss Drummond. Lady Agatha's niece. Honoria, Lady Calthorpe." — Rose
> *(Honoria curtsies — low, correct, unhurried, the chin at Letitia's approved angle. She speaks when spoken to, in complete sentences, the stammer surfacing only once, on the word "pleasure," which everyone pretends not to notice and one kind old general loudly does not hear, asking her to repeat it so he may admire the sentiment properly. The room, Rose notes, is watching — the cat-and-furniture assessment Augusta predicted — and finding, to its evident surprise, nothing to sharpen its claws on.)*
> "Your aunt was telling me — that is, I heard — you are fond of flowers, Miss Drummond." — Lady Calthorpe, over the tea.
> "I — I keep a book of them, ma'am. Their meanings. Violets are for modesty. I brought some for Mrs. Hartwell's mantel — for remembrance, the rosemary. A drawing room ought to have something that means something. That is what I — that is what I think." — Honoria
> *(A small silence — the dangerous kind, the kind that precedes either laughter or warmth. Then Lady Calthorpe — who has buried two husbands and outlived three reputations and never once been surprised by anything — smiles with genuine warmth, the real article, unrehearsed.)*
> "Modesty on the mantel. We could use more of it in this town, and on more mantels. You must tell me what rosemary means, child, when we are better acquainted — and we shall be better acquainted, I think." — Lady Calthorpe
> *(First sighting: survived. More than survived — approved, by a woman whose approval is quoted. In the carriage between houses, Honoria exhales as though she has been holding her breath since Tuesday, and possibly since birth.)*
> "She did not laugh." — Honoria
> "No one is going to laugh, Honoria. That is the entire campaign — three sightings, the right eyes, and not one laugh. We are one third of the way to furniture." — Rose
> *(Honoria leans back against the squabs and closes her eyes, and smiles — a small, private, unpracticed smile, the first Rose has seen on her face that was not braced for impact.)*

scenes.synopsis: The small triumph — the third house, and the ton's verdict beginning to turn. Furniture, becoming fixture.
scenes.prose:
> *(The third house, the Ashcombes' — the drawing room all pale green and family portraits, Julian's mother presiding with the ease of a woman who has never doubted her place in any room. The call goes as the others went: the glide, the curtsy, the complete sentences, the flower book. And then, as they rise to leave, Julian's mother mentions it — casually, as though it were the most natural thing in the world, as though girls like Honoria were put on ball lists every day of the week.)*
> "We shall expect you Thursday, Miss Drummond. The second country dance — I have taken the liberty of securing you a partner. A reliable young man. You will enjoy it, I think." — Julian's mother
> *(Honoria's hand tightens on Rose's arm hard enough to leave marks. She does not speak until they are in the carriage, and then it comes out in a rush.)*
> "A dance. At a ball. With — with a partner who knows? Who has been — told?" — Honoria
> "A partner who has been instructed to look as though he is enjoying himself. Augusta's words, not mine — though I suspect he will enjoy himself, the instructions being, in your case, redundant." — Rose pauses, choosing honesty over comfort, because the garden taught her the price of anything else. "You have been — excellent furniture, Honoria. The ton is revising its opinion. The ton always revises; it has nothing else to do between meals."
> *(Honoria laughs — a real laugh, stammerless, surprised out of her like water from a rock — and then, abruptly, cries: two tears and no more, dabbed fiercely with the plain linen handkerchief, the peppermint reticule clutched in her lap.)*
> "I am sorry. It is only — nobody has ever — campaigned for me before. Nobody has ever — made lists. About me." — Honoria
> "Dry your eyes, my dear. Furniture does not weep in carriages. Fixtures weep at home, like everyone else — it is one of the privileges of being a fixture." — Rose
> *(But Rose's own throat is tight, and she looks out at the passing square so Honoria won't see — at the houses going by, at the ordinary miracle of a London afternoon. The price Drummond named is being paid in full — name, invitations, dances, afternoons, every underlined word — and it is buying something Rose hadn't expected to care about this much: a girl, laughing and crying in a carriage, because someone made lists about her.)*

scenes.synopsis: Debrief at home — Letitia's comic accounting of the campaign's first day, and the first shadow: who else is watching.
scenes.prose:
> *(Hartwell House, evening. Letitia, in her wrapper, her hair in a nightcap that would frighten the ton, demands the full report with the appetite of a general after a first engagement — chocolate, the good biscuits, and no detail spared.)*
> "Three houses. No laughter — not a giggle, not a smirk, not even the *near*-laughter the girl dreads. One general who pretended not to hear the stammer and then asked her to repeat herself out of admiration. One smile from Calthorpe — Calthorpe! — who has not smiled genuinely since the Regent's birthday. And a dance at the Ashcombe ball, the second country dance, with a reliable partner. Rose, you are a miracle worker. When this is over I shall have you canonized, or at least given a very good seat at the opera, which is nearly the same thing."
> "When this is over I shall sleep for a week, and then I shall sleep for another." — Rose accepts the chocolate. "Aunt — did you notice the carriage? Grey, no crest, slowed past Calthorpe's while we were inside. Slowed, and looked, and went on."
> "Drummond's, checking her investment. Or Cecilia Vane's, checking her entertainment — the girl does love a spectacle, especially one she did not have to pay for. Or nobody's, and you are seeing spies in carriages because you have been reading too much —" — Letitia stops, because Rose is not smiling.
> "Quill's letter this morning said the codicils are 'multiplying.' His word, underlined — everyone underlines at me this Season, I am beginning to feel like a school exercise. And Octavia's vicomtesse says distressed paper is being consolidated — bought up, quietly, by agents for unnamed principals. Someone is gathering debts the way Augusta gathers goddaughters: systematically, and without asking permission."
> *(Letitia sets down her teacup. When she is serious, the comedy drops like a dropped fan — suddenly, completely, and the woman underneath is formidable.)*
> "Then guard the girl, Rose. Whatever the money is doing — whatever paper is moving in the dark, whatever hands are gathering it — do not let it touch Honoria. She is the one clean thing in this campaign. The one thing that is not a debt or a threat or a codicil."
> "She is the campaign, Aunt."
> "Then keep her clean." — Letitia's voice is quiet and absolute. "That is an order from your comic aunt, and I do not give many. Guard the girl."
> *(Rose nods, and drinks her chocolate, and thinks of grey carriages slowing past houses, and of paper consolidating in the dark, and of a girl who cried in a carriage because someone made lists about her.)*

scenes.synopsis: Julian, lightly — the honorable suitor quietly paying his brother's debts. One link of the money chain, shown not told.
scenes.prose:
> *(The park, the next morning — the hour when London walks off its evenings. Rose walks early to clear her head, the campaign's first day still ringing in it like a struck bell, and finds Lord Julian Ashcombe on the same path, also walking early, also clearing his head. They fall into step with the ease of people who have been allies longer than they have been anything else, and for a while they simply walk, which is its own conversation.)*
> "Your mother has put Miss Drummond on the ball's list." — Rose breaks the silence first. "And found her a partner for the second country dance — a reliable partner, instructed to look as though he is enjoying himself. I am — grateful is too small a word, Julian. It is a thimble for an ocean."
> "My mother collects causes the way other women collect china. Yours collects strays." — Julian smiles, tiredly. "Between you, London's overlooked are in capable hands. Though I warn you, Rose — my mother's causes have a way of becoming permanent fixtures. You may find you have acquired a goddaughter by Thursday."
> *(A pause. He looks tired — the particular tiredness of a man paying money he does not owe, the tiredness Rose is beginning to recognize as the Season's true epidemic.)*
> "You are still buying your brother's paper." — Rose says it gently, as a statement, not a question.
> "Someone is buying everyone's paper, Rose. I buy my brother's to keep it from worse hands — full price, which my man of business calls honorable and my banker calls insane, and I call necessary." — He looks out across the park. "Quill tells me Rackham's notes have nearly all changed hands now — consolidated, the agents say. Into whose hands, no one will tell me, and I have asked everyone it is proper to ask, and several it is not."
> "Into hands that hold the family, once they hold the paper." — Rose watches a rider go by. "Octavia said something like that, over a portrait sitting. She is always right about money."
> "Octavia is always right about money and always wrong about noses." — The old joke, worn smooth between them. Then, quieter: "Rose. Whatever Drummond holds over you — my mother would want me to say that the Ashcombes stand with the Hartwells. I want to say it myself. Without my mother. It is my own sentence."
> *(He bows — the formal bow, the one that means he is serious — and walks on, his step unhurried, his shoulders square under the tiredness. Rose watches him go — honorable, tired, paying full price in a market where everyone else is buying cheap — and adds another link to the chain in her mind: whoever is consolidating the paper is in a hurry, buying fast and cheap; and Julian is the only man in London buying slowly, and dear, and for love. In a war of paper, she reflects, the honorable man is always outnumbered.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 7 setup — tea at Cecilia's. Honeyed, sly, never overt. The villain dangerous in defeat, laying the table for the leak.
scenes.prose:
> *(Miss Cecilia Vane's drawing room — all pale silk and paler smiles, the light filtered through muslin to flatter everyone and reveal nothing. Cecilia, defeated last Season in the matter of a certain engagement and never quite recovered — never quite forgiven, either, though no one can say for what — receives Rose with the warmth of a woman who has been practicing this exact temperature of welcome in front of her glass.)*
> "Rose! How brave of you — how *good* of you — to take up the Drummond girl. The whole town is talking of nothing else. Charity, they call it. I call it courage. Though I suppose charity *is* a kind of courage, when the object is — well." — Cecilia pours, the silver pot catching the light. "Sugar?"
> *(Tea is poured. The room is full of the soft clink of the almost-innocent — cups, spoons, the murmur of a room that has heard everything and admitted nothing.)*
> "Honoria is — a sweet girl. Deserving. The ton has decided to overlook her, and I have decided not to. It seemed the least — the least interesting thing to do would have been to agree with the ton." — Rose, carefully, watching.
> "Deserving. Yes." — Cecilia's smile does not move. "Dull, of course — but deserving. One does feel for the dull ones, doesn't one? They try so hard, and the trying shows. It is the showing that is so — painful. For everyone."
> *(Rose feels the sentence land — her own private words, *dull, deserving*, shaped in her own mouth in this very campaign, in confidence, in her own drawing room — now returned to her slightly rearranged, like a letter read by someone else and refolded wrong, the creases not quite matching. The room is very still. Cecilia sips her tea.)*
> "I said something like that once. Privately." — Rose keeps her voice level.
> "Did you? How candid of you." — Cecilia's eyes are bright and empty as porcelain. "But then, you are always candid, Rose — it is your great charm, and your great danger. Everyone says so. Sugar? You take two, I think. I remember everything about everyone. It is my particular talent."
> *(The tea continues, honeyed, hour after hour of it — the weather, the opera, the ball, the girl. Rose drinks it watching Cecilia over the rim of her cup, and understands — with the cold clarity that comes too late to be useful and just in time to be filed — that everything said in this room is being memorized for future recitation. Every sentence is being copied, in Cecilia's perfect hand, into a book Rose will never see. She sets down her cup, smiles, and resolves to give the room nothing more worth copying.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 7 — the second leak. Cecilia repeats Rose's private words about Honoria at the tea table, before witnesses. Sly, never overt.
scenes.prose:
> *(The tea has drawn its usual audience — three callers, all with excellent hearing and no pressing engagements, arranged about the pale silk room like an audience that has paid for its seats. Cecilia, refilling cups with the grace of a woman performing a sacrament, tells a story about the campaign — fondly, warmly, with the air of a woman sharing admiration so sincere it could not possibly be anything else.)*
> "— and Rose said to me, only yesterday, that the girl is *dull but deserving*, and that one must simply make the best of it. Such honesty! Such *devotion* to a hopeless cause — to take up a girl one privately despairs of, and to do it so beautifully. I told Lady Calthorpe exactly what Rose said — I hope you don't mind, Rose, I praised your candor to the skies. I said, 'If only we were all so honest about our charities.'" — Cecilia
> *(The words hang in the perfumed air: *dull but deserving*. Rose's private sentence — spoken in confidence, in her own drawing room, to her aunt — now making its rounds of the ton with Cecilia's fond smile attached like a gift tag. The second leak. The first was Tibbs and the butcher's boy, and cost nothing but embarrassment; this one wears silk, and pours the tea, and will cost Honoria.)*
> *(The three callers are very still — the stillness of people witnessing something and deciding, simultaneously, how to retell it. Rose feels the sentence traveling already, out of this room, into other rooms, growing embroidery with every retelling. She smiles. She has been smiled at by experts; she knows the countermove.)*
> "I did say something of the sort," Rose says evenly — pleasantly, even, as though discussing the weather. "In private. I find private sentences have a way of traveling when they are carried by friends. It is the great advantage of friendship — the distribution."
> "Oh, but we are all friends here!" — Cecilia laughs, delighted. "And it is *true*, isn't it? The poor child *is* dull. To deny it would be — well, it would be unkind to pretend otherwise, would it not? Honesty is the kindest policy with girls like that. Everyone knows it. Everyone says it. I am only saying what everyone is thinking, with love."
> *(Never overt. Never a raised voice, never a bared tooth. Just the sentence, placed like a pin in a cushion, where everyone can see it — and the pin, Rose notes, is Cecilia's own now; she has handled it so fondly it bears her fingerprints. Rose smiles, and files the moment the way she files everything now — as evidence, in the campaigner's hand, in ink.)*
> "You are kindness itself, Cecilia." — Rose rises, smooths her skirts. "I shall remember exactly how kind. I have an excellent memory for kindness. It is my particular talent."
> *(The callers look from one to the other, sensing — without understanding — that something has just been decided. Cecilia's smile does not waver. Neither does Rose's. The tea is over.)*

scenes.synopsis: The leak spreads — by dinner the sentence is everywhere. Quill's note arrives: the codicils, multiplying.
scenes.prose:
> *(Hartwell House, evening. The sentence has traveled faster than any carriage in London: *dull but deserving* — quoted at two teas, murmured at a musicale, embroidered by retelling until it has acquired adjectives it never possessed. Letitia paces the drawing room, her wrapper snapping; Rose sits very still by the mantel, watching the tussie-mussie — violets for modesty, rosemary for remembrance — as though it might offer counsel.)*
> "It is everywhere." — Letitia wheels. "*Dull but deserving.* As though the girl were a charity sermon with legs. Quoted at Lady Calthorpe's — Calthorpe's, Rose, where the girl was *approved* yesterday — murmured at the musicale, embroidered at the Hendersons'. Oh, Rose — your own words, turned into a label and hung round her neck like a placard. Your own private sentence, retailing by the yard."
> "My words, Cecilia's mouth, the ton's ears." — Rose does not move. "The second leak. The first was Tibbs and cost us nothing but embarrassment — a weeping servant, a butcher's boy, a mother who tells everyone. This one costs Honoria. It costs her the one thing the campaign was built to give her: the right to be unremarkable without being ridiculous. She is now remarkable — as a charity case."
> *(A letter arrives — the evening post, the footman, the tray. Quill's hand, the solicitor's cramped urgency, the seal pressed crooked in haste: *The codicils multiply. Three now reference the Rackham paper specifically. Someone is not merely buying debts, Miss Hartwell — they are buying the instruments that enforce them. Come Thursday.*)*
> "Quill wants me Thursday." — Rose reads it twice. "The codicils are breeding, the paper is consolidating, and Cecilia is retailing my private sentences by the yard. It is quite a week to be a Hartwell. It is quite a week to be anyone's anything."
> *(Letitia stops pacing. She looks at her niece — very still, very pale, very upright — and her voice, when it comes, is the voice underneath the comedy, the one she uses for funerals and creditors.)*
> "What will you do about Cecilia?"
> "That," Rose says — and touches the tussie-mussie, lightly, the violets nodding — "is the question the chapter has been saving for last. The money can wait until Thursday. The girl cannot. Cecilia has chosen her weapon — my own words, returned to me. I shall choose mine. But not tonight. Tonight I am going to sit here, and look at Honoria's flowers, and decide what kind of woman I am when someone uses my own sentences against a nineteen-year-old girl."
> *(Letitia nods, and pours the chocolate, and does not pace again. Outside, the carriages go by — every one of them, tonight, carrying the sentence.)*

scenes.synopsis: The leak lands — Honoria has heard what the ton is saying. The girl's hurt, plain and unadorned.
scenes.prose:
> *(The garden, the next morning — the roses wet again, the light thin. Honoria is already there when Rose comes down — she has walked, she says, because the carriage felt too conspicuous, because the very wheels seemed to be saying it. Her eyes are red. The peppermint is gone from the reticule; she has stopped pretending she might not need it, and the absence of it is the saddest thing Rose has seen all week.)*
> "They are saying it." — Honoria does not turn from the roses. "*Dull but deserving.* At Lady Calthorpe's yesterday, someone said it where I could hear — where I could *hear*, Miss Hartwell, deliberately, the way you place a card on a table — and then pretended they hadn't. As though — as though I were deaf. Or furniture that couldn't hear." — She turns, and her face is composed, which is worse than tears. "Furniture hears, you know. It just cannot answer."
> *(No stammer. Grief, Rose notes — filing it away even now, the campaigner in her never quite silent — speaks more fluently than fear. Fear stammers. Grief enunciates.)*
> "Honoria —" — Rose
> "Did you say it?" — The question comes out whole, plain, adult. "Miss Hartwell — please. I can bear the ton thinking it. I have always known the ton thinks it — I have known since I was fifteen and the laughter started being *near* me. But did *you* say it? You, who — you, who made the lists. I need to know if the lists were — if I was —"
> *(She stops. The garden is very quiet. The question hangs between them — unfinished, unadorned, unbearable — and Rose understands that this is the true price of the campaign. Not the dances, not the afternoons, not the hundred coins of restraint. This: the girl's trust, held up to the light to see if it is genuine. Everything depends on the answer — the campaign, the Season, the friendship that may or may not have been a lie — and the answer depends on the decision made in the garden days ago, when Honoria asked why and Rose chose what to tell her.)*
> "Sit with me," Rose says — and her voice, to her surprise, is steady. "And I will tell you exactly what I said, and to whom, and what it has cost us both. No management, Honoria. Not today. Today you get the truth, whatever it costs us both."
> *(Honoria sits. The roses nod above them. Rose begins.)*

scenes.synopsis: Dialogue-heavy repair — Rose tells Honoria the whole truth of the leak, and Honoria's good heart answers. The stripped thorn stem returns, transformed.
scenes.prose:
> *(The garden bench, the roses dripping. Rose tells it plainly — the whole of it, no evasion, no softening, no management: the private sentence spoken to Letitia in confidence (*dull, deserving* — the lazy words, the careless words); Cecilia's tea, the pale silk room, the three callers with excellent hearing; the retelling, the embroidery, the label hung round a girl's neck. Honoria listens the way she does everything: completely — both hands folded in her lap, eyes on Rose's face, not interrupting, not looking away.)*
> "So it was true." — Honoria, when Rose finishes. "I am dull. You said it, and she repeated it, and the ton believes it. It is — it is a complete chain. Like a — a proof."
> "You are not dull." — Rose stops, discards three polite lies in succession — *you are not, you mustn't, the ton is wrong* — and chooses the fourth thing, the true thing. "You are unpracticed. There is a difference, and the ton is too lazy to learn it, and I was too lazy when I spoke. I said a lazy thing, Honoria, in a private moment — a sentence I would not defend in daylight — and I am sorry in a public way, which is the only way that counts. I cannot unsay it. I can only outlive it, and so can you."
> "Cecilia said it to be cruel." — Honoria's voice is flat.
> "Cecilia said it to be *seen* saying it." — Rose is precise, because precision is the only honesty left. "The cruelty was incidental — which is worse, in a way, because it means she will do it again, to someone else, without even meaning this. She collects sentences the way other women collect china. She will do it again."
> *(Honoria is quiet a long time — so long that a blackbird finishes an entire aria in the roses. Then, from her reticule — the peppermint is back, Rose notices, the small armor resumed — she takes something: a rose stem, its thorns stripped, a little wilted from carrying, the bare green stem neat as peeled willow.)*
> "The flower girl gave me this. On Bond Street. She said they strip the thorns so ladies won't prick their fingers." — The stammer returns, gently, like an old friend. "I thought — I thought I didn't want to be stripped of my thorns either. Even if — even if nobody thinks I have any. Even if the thorns are — small. And dull. And deserving."
> *(Rose takes the thornless stem — turns it in her fingers, the same absurd, defenseless rose she carried home from Bond Street, the same smooth strange stem — and hands it back, deliberately, like returning a sword.)*
> "Keep your thorns, Honoria." — Rose closes the girl's fingers around the stem. "The ton wants its wallflowers safe as daisies — thornless, prickless, never drawing blood. We shall disappoint the ton. We shall disappoint it thoroughly, and often, and on purpose."
> *(Honoria looks at the stem in her fist — and laughs, a small wet sound, half grief and half something else. The repair, Rose understands, is not complete. But it has begun. And it began, as all repairs do, with the truth.)*

scenes.synopsis: The portrait sitting continues — another money thread. The de Valcourt name surfaces once more in gossip; Rose pulls it, gently.
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia's studio, the portrait nearly done — Rose on canvas, chin lifted, thinking furiously, exactly as in life, the thought painted right into the oils where it will hang for a hundred years. The vicomtesse is back in the waiting corner, wakeful today, her old lace arranged for company, and full of news — the particular fullness of a woman who has been saving it up.)*
> "— the de Valcourt agent was at the bank again, they say." — The vicomtesse does not bother with preamble. "Buying, always buying. Paper, mortgages, the little promises men write when they are desperate. Mademoiselle Hartwell, you look pale — is it the light, or the money? With you English it is so often the money."
> "The light, I assure you." — Rose holds the pose, the chin, the thinking mouth. "This agent. Does he buy for de Valcourt himself, or for — interests? There is always a difference, though no one ever admits it."
> "For interests, always for interests." — The vicomtesse waves the distinction away. "Money that moves like that belongs to no one and everyone — it is like the wind, mademoiselle, it blows where it wishes. But I will tell you what the émigrés say, what we say among ourselves when the English are not listening: the de Valcourt money remembers who it lent to, and it is calling the memories in. One by one. Like debts. Like — how do you say — like old friends one has not seen since the Terror."
> *(Octavia's brush pauses — a rarity, a full stop, the equivalent of a gasp from anyone else.)*
> "Careful, chérie." — Octavia's voice is low, the truth-voice. "You are following a chain, and chains have owners, and owners have hands. Rackham's paper, your family's paper — if one hand is gathering it all, that hand intends to *use* it. Paper is not collected for decoration. Ask Quill what the codicils enforce. Then ask yourself who benefits from enforcement. Then —" the brush resumes, "— then come back on Thursday and tell me, because I am a painter, and I live for other people's disasters."
> "You miss nothing, Octavia."
> "I miss the nose. I told you I had already decided about the nose — it is finished, it is perfect, do not argue." — Octavia stands back from the canvas. "It is the money I never miss. Money, chérie, is the only sitter that never lies about its age."

scenes.synopsis: Quill's warning deepens — the other codicils. The money plot's floor drops one level: enforcement instruments, not just debts.
scenes.prose:
> *(Quill's chambers, Thursday — the room all dust and precedent, the air thick with the smell of old paper and older secrets. The solicitor spreads documents across his desk like a man laying out evidence at a trial: codicils, assignments, memoranda, each one weighted with a brass seal, each one smelling of dust and urgency and other people's money.)*
> "Three codicils now reference the Rackham paper specifically, Miss Hartwell." — Quill's finger moves down the pages. "Three. And this —" he taps a memorandum, the paper crackling, "— this is an assignment of enforcement rights. Not the debt itself. The *right to enforce it*. Do you understand the distinction? It is — it is the difference between owning a sword and owning the arm that wields it."
> "The debt is the chain." — Rose studies the memorandum. "The enforcement right is the hand that pulls it."
> "Precisely." — Quill looks at her with something like respect, and something like pity. "Someone is not merely buying what is owed, Miss Hartwell. They are buying the power to *call it in* — the mortgages, the notes of hand, the little promises men write when they are desperate. Your family's paper among them, I regret to say. I regret to say it more than I can express, which is why I express it so briefly."
> *(The chambers are very quiet. Outside, London goes about its business — the business, Rose reflects, of writing little promises and signing them when drunk.)*
> "Can you learn whose hand?" — Rose asks it directly. "Whose hand pulls the chain?"
> "Agents, Miss Hartwell. Always agents — men in snuff-coloured coats, men with notebooks, men who are paid to have no names." — Quill hesitates, the professional hesitation of a man about to say something unprofessional. "But the money moves like —" another hesitation, "— like émigré money. Patient, vengeful, and in no hurry to explain itself. Money with a memory, Miss Hartwell. That is the most dangerous kind."
> *(Rose thinks of the vicomtesse's words — *the de Valcourt money remembers who it lent to* — and says nothing. Some chains are followed in silence, lest the links hear you coming.)*
> "Thursday next, then." — Rose rises. "And Quill — whatever you learn, bring it to me before it reaches the ton. I am tired of being the last to know my own ruin. It is —" she manages a smile, "— it is bad for the complexion."
> *(Quill bows her out, and Rose walks home through the afternoon with the memorandum's words in her head: not the debt, but the right to enforce it. Drummond wants her afternoons. The consolidator wants everything the paper can take. And somewhere between the two, a girl is learning to glide over footstools.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — CECILIA'S LEAK. Rose confronts Cecilia — not at tea, but on the neutral ground of the park — and decides what becomes of the woman who retailed her sentences.
scenes.prose:
> *(The park, morning — the hour of riders and duels and decisions. Rose has asked Cecilia to walk — a summons Cecilia accepted with the delight of a woman who mistakes a reckoning for attention, who arrived in a walking dress of particular perfection, as though for a levee. They walk among the early riders, alone enough for honesty, public enough for safety — the neutral ground, where neither drawing room's rules apply.)*
> "You repeated my private words about Honoria. At your tea, before witnesses, with a smile — with *fondness*, which was the masterstroke. Do not deny it — denial would bore us both, and I am not bored yet. I am, in fact, excessively interested."
> "My dear Rose — it was admiration! I praised your candor — I told Lady Calthorpe —" — Cecilia
> "You hung a label round a nineteen-year-old girl's neck and called it praise." — Rose does not raise her voice; the riders go by, indifferent. "I know what you are, Cecilia. You are dangerous in defeat — last Season taught you that losing quietly gets you nothing, so you have decided to be *remembered* instead, at any cost, on any terms. It is a strategy. I understand strategies. I am offering you one chance to choose what you are remembered for — because the ton's memory is long, but mine is longer."
> *(Cecilia's smile does not move — it is porcelain, it does not move — but something behind it recalculates, the way a gambler recalculates when the cards turn. The villain, sly to the end, waits to see which weapon Rose has brought to the park. The riders pass. The decision waits.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — Cecilia's leak:*
- **Cut her** — *Society+, Cecilia dangerous.* "You are not received at Hartwell House, nor at Augusta's, nor anywhere my name carries. The ton will notice. Let them." Cecilia's smile finally cracks; a cut enemy is an honest enemy — and a vengeful one.
- **Warn her** — *Wit+, she smiles.* "Do it again, and I will tell the ton exactly what you said, and where, and why — with the same fond smile you used on me. We understand each other." She laughs, genuinely delighted; the game between them is now declared, and therefore almost honorable.
- **Feed her false words** — *Cunning+, the trap is set.* "You love a private sentence, Cecilia. Here is another: tell Lady Calthorpe that I said Honoria is to marry imminently — to whom, I cannot say. Watch what the ton does with it, and wonder why I told *you*." Cecilia glows; the lie is launched, and its fuse is in Rose's hand.

scenes.synopsis: Rose brings the Cecilia decision to the atelier — and Élise, who hears everything, has already heard it.
scenes.prose:
> *(Élise's workroom, evening — the lamps lit, the day's work put away. Élise is pinning the Ashcombe ball gown — Honoria's gown, the chosen silk made glorious, restraint made radiant — and does not look up when Rose enters, which is how Rose knows she knows.)*
> "It is done, then." — Élise's pins move steadily. "Whatever you decided about Cecilia, it is done — my finisher's cousin's sister was at the park with a dog, and the dog heard everything. Dogs are the new newspapers, chérie. More reliable, and they do not expect to be paid, only walked."
> "Then you know before I tell you." — Rose sinks onto the chaise. "The atelier hears everything, including, apparently, parks. Including dogs."
> "I know. And I know the gown will be ready Thursday —" she stands back, surveys the silk, "— and I know Lady Calthorpe has asked after Honoria twice, which is the ton's way of revising an opinion without admitting it had one. What I do not know —" Élise looks up, pins in her mouth, eyes sharp as needles, "— is whether you want this workroom to be merely a workroom, chérie. Or something more."
> *(The question hangs among the muslins — among the half-made gowns, the chalk dust, the good smell of pressed linen. Rose looks at the order book on the cutting table — the standing queue, the patient columns, the honest ledger — and understands what Élise is offering: not gossip, but intelligence. The atelier as an ear. The confessional with better lighting, turned — deliberately — into a listening post. The decision the chapter has been carrying since the first commission, since *whatever your workroom hears, I want to hear it too*.)*
> "I want to think about it tonight." — Rose rises. "A workroom that listens is a weapon, Élise. Weapons need deciding — carefully, and once. I will not decide it tired, and I will not decide it here, among the muslins, where everything sounds reasonable."
> "They do need deciding." — Élise returns to her pins. "Sleep on it. The muslins will keep your secret either way — they are excellent at secrets, the muslins. It is the silk you must watch."
> *(Rose walks home through the evening, and thinks about ears, and weapons, and the difference between a workroom and a war room — and whether there is one, anymore.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE ATELIER'S GOSSIP. Rose returns at dawn and decides what the atelier becomes in this war: an ear, a bystander, or something in between.
scenes.prose:
> *(The atelier, dawn — the grey morning light through the workroom windows, the machines shrouded, the muslins ghostly on their stands. Élise alone, chalking a pattern in the half-light, her tape about her neck even at this hour. Rose has come before the workroom wakes — this decision, she has decided in the sleepless small hours, belongs to no audience, not even an audience of muslins.)*
> "I have thought all night, Élise." — Rose does not sit; the decision is a standing one. "Your workroom hears everything — debts, bills, who is paying whom, whose paper is moving, whose man asks after coats left in 'thirteen. In this Season, that is not gossip. That is the war — the money war, underneath the ballroom war. And I must decide what I am asking of you, because asking is a kind of spending, and I am already spending a great deal."
> *(Élise sets down the chalk. For once — entirely, completely — the general is serious. The flippancy drops like a dropped shawl, and what is underneath is a woman who has run a workroom for twenty years and knows exactly what ears cost.)*
> "Ask carefully, chérie." — Élise's voice is quiet. "A workroom that listens for you listens *against* others. There is no neutral ear — not in this town, not in this Season. The confessional with better lighting becomes the courtroom with better lighting, and I must know, before I agree, which one you are building."
> *(The dawn light strengthens. The muslins wait. Rose thinks of the order book — the honest ledger, the sash finished and paid for — and of the chain of paper growing link by link in the dark, and of a girl with a stripped rose stem in her fist, keeping her thorns. Then she asks.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The atelier's gossip:*
- **Task Élise to listen** — *Intelligence+, the atelier becomes an ear.* "Then listen — deliberately. Who orders, who cannot pay, whose man asks after old coats. Bring it all to me, and I will make it worth the hearing." Élise nods slowly; the order book gains an invisible column, and the war gains its listening post.
- **Keep it casual** — *Charm+, the gossip comes unforced.* "No orders. No tasks. Just — if the workroom hears things, as workrooms do, I would like to hear them too. As a friend." Élise smiles; the intelligence will come, but on friendship's schedule, not war's.
- **Keep the atelier out of the war** — *Honor+, Élise's relief.* "No. Your workroom is a sanctuary — brides, bankrupts, fools, all confessed in safety. I will not make it a weapon." Élise exhales, and something in her face softens; the atelier stays clean — and Rose fights with one ear fewer.
