scenes.synopsis: Augusta's verdict — the launch plan confirmed, the leak assessed, the Dowager's doctrine applied to Cecilia.
scenes.prose:
> *(Ravencroft House, the morning room that has ended more Seasons than ballrooms have begun. Augusta hears the whole of it — the calls, the three sightings, the leak, the park, the decisions — with the stillness of a woman who has heard everything before and judged most of it, and found most of it wanting. Rose finishes. Augusta pours — herself, a rare honor, a rarer tenderness — and speaks.)*
> "Cecilia retailed your sentence. Of course she did." — Augusta settles back. "Defeated girls retail sentences the way defeated armies retail ammunition — it is all they have left, and they spend it lavishly, and it never quite wins the war. You confronted her in the park. Good. The park is the correct venue for such conversations — public enough for safety, private enough for honesty. What did you decide about her?"
> *(Rose tells her. Augusta listens, and nods once — the nod of a commander approving a subordinate's dispositions.)*
> "The campaign survives it." — Rose looks into her cup. "Honoria survived it — the girl has more steel in her than the ton suspects. But the ton has its label now — *dull but deserving* — and labels, once hung, are hard to remove. They hang them round girls' necks like placards, and the girls carry them to their graves."
> "Then we hang a better one beside it." — Augusta is brisk; sentiment is for after the war. "Thursday's ball: she dances the second country dance, she dances it well, and she is seen to enjoy it. A girl who enjoys a ball cannot be merely deserving — enjoyment is the one thing charity cases are never permitted, and the ton knows it. The ton will revise — the ton always revises, it has nothing else to do between meals, and it hates to be wrong in public."
> "And Drummond?" — Rose sets down the cup. "She has slowed past the house twice. Checking her investment. The grey carriage, no crest."
> "Let her check." — Augusta waves it away. "Investments that perform are left alone — it is the first law of dragons, and of bankers, who are much the same. Rose." — Her voice changes, the tenderness surfacing again. "You are paying her price with interest — your name, your invitations, your dances, your afternoons, and now your composure, your sleep, and your private sentences. And the girl is worth it. I have launched eleven goddaughters, three nieces, and one extremely unlikely cousin, and I tell you plainly: this one has the best heart of any of them. Hearts, in the end, are the only thing the ton cannot counterfeit — it can counterfeit beauty, and wit, and even virtue, but never a good heart. It does not know the pattern."
> *(Augusta refills Rose's cup herself — again, the rare honor — and Rose understands that she has just been given both absolution and orders, in that order.)*
> "Now go. Thursday. The ball. Furniture becomes fixture — and fixtures, my dear, are forever."

scenes.synopsis: The small triumph confirmed — the ball, the dance, the girl's joy. The stammer nearly gone for a moment. The campaign's dividend.
scenes.prose:
> *(Hartwell House, the morning of the Ashcombe ball. The gown has arrived — the chosen silk, finished, glorious in its restraint, laid out on the bed like a promise kept. Honoria stands in it before the glass, the peppermint reticule in her hand, her hair dressed and redressed by Letitia's own maid — and for a long moment nobody speaks, because there is nothing to say that would not diminish it.)*
> "I look —" Honoria begins, and stops — because the stammer has, for once, nothing to say, because the girl in the glass has silenced it. "I look — like someone. Like — a person the glass was expecting."
> "You look like a girl the ton will have to work to overlook," Rose says — the campaign's motto, the highest praise in her power. "And tonight, for one dance, it will not even try. Tonight, for one dance, the ton will simply — look. And see."
> *(Honoria turns from the glass, and her face — plain, honest, radiant, the face of a winter field in sudden sun — does something to the room. Letitia, watching from the door, presses a hand to her mouth and does not trust herself to speak, which for Letitia is the equivalent of a scream.)*
> "Miss Hartwell — Rose —" Honoria catches herself, color rising like a flag. "May I call you Rose? Just — just for tonight? Just — when it is only us?"
> *(The question hangs in the quiet room — small, enormous, the whole campaign in a single sentence. Rose looks at the girl — the mended gloves replaced by new ones, the bonnet two seasons old exchanged for Élise's making, the stammer nearly gone — and understands that whatever the sponsorship began as, whatever Drummond's underlined words demanded, it has become something else entirely, something no dragon charted.)*
> "For tonight, and for every night after it." — Rose's voice is steady, which surprises her. "We are past *Miss Hartwell*, you and I. We were past it in the garden, the morning you asked me why — the morning you asked if you were being managed, and I answered. Whatever I answered, we were past it then."
> *(Honoria hugs her — sudden, fierce, the hug of a girl who has never presumed and now presumes everything, arms tight around the woman who made the lists. Rose holds her — holds her hard — and over the girl's shoulder meets Letitia's eyes: *the campaign's dividend*, Letitia mouths silently, *paid in full, with interest*.)*
> "Now." — Rose steps back, smooths the girl's sash. "The ball. Remember — glide, not hurry. Chin at the approved angle. And if anyone laughs —"
> "— you will laugh first, at something else entirely." — Honoria's eyes shine. "I remember. Augusta's doctrine. The whole art."
> "My excellent furniture." — Rose kisses her cheek. "My fixture. Go and be seen."

scenes.synopsis: The quiet before the storm — Letitia's wisdom, an evening ritual, the household at peace for one night.
scenes.prose:
> *(Hartwell House, late. The ball is hours away; the house is quiet in the particular way of houses holding their breath — the servants moving softly, the lamps lit early, the whole building braced for the evening the way a ship is braced for weather. Letitia and Rose sit with chocolate in the drawing room, the tussie-mussie still on the mantel — violets for modesty, rosemary for remembrance, a little faded now, and all the more precious for it — the stripped rose still on Rose's desk beside Drummond's card and Augusta's campaign list.)*
> "Do you remember," Letitia says — cradling her cup, her wrapper comfortable, her nightcap nowhere in evidence yet — "when you were nineteen, and terrified of everything? When you hid in the library during your own come-out ball and read sermons?"
> "I was never terrified, Aunt. I was merely — strategic about my fears. I deployed them where they would do the most good."
> "You hid in the library and read sermons. I remember — I brought you chocolate, and you pretended you had gone in for a book, and we both knew you were hiding, and we both pretended otherwise, which was the beginning of our entire relationship." — Letitia smiles. "Honoria is braver than you were, my love. She walks into rooms that have already decided to laugh at her. You only hid from rooms that *might*."
> "She has you to walk in with." — Rose looks at the tussie-mussie. "That is the difference between your nineteen and hers — between my nineteen and hers. She has — she has us. The lists, the gowns, the doctrine. No one ever made lists about me."
> *(Letitia is quiet a moment — the comedy set aside, the woman underneath surfacing.)*
> "Rose. Whatever Drummond holds — whatever Quill's codicils say, whatever paper is consolidating in the dark, whatever Cecilia retails by the yard: tonight a good girl dances at a ball. A girl who was sick with nerves this morning, who walked because the carriage felt too conspicuous, who keeps a book of flower meanings and brings posies to houses she fears — tonight she dances the second country dance at the Ashcombe ball, in a gown made for the purpose, and she will dance it well. That is not nothing, my love. That is, in fact, nearly everything."
> *(Rose looks at the tussie-mussie — violets for modesty, rosemary for remembrance — and the thornless rose beside Drummond's card, and understands that Letitia is right, and that being right is the aunt's most annoying habit, and her most valuable one.)*
> "Nearly everything," Rose agrees. "The Gazette will decide the rest — Nance Bell's paper judges taste, and taste only, and tomorrow morning it will judge ours."
> *(They drink their chocolate. The house holds its breath. The ball waits.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ GAZETTE STING — the paper judges. Mrs. Nance Bell's masthead; the verdict on the campaign, neither kind nor cruel, but exact. No mystery, no unmasking — the Gazette judges taste, and that is all it has ever done.
scenes.prose:
> *(Morning. The Gazette arrives with the chocolate, as it always does — folded, crisp, smelling of ink and judgment. Letitia reads the society column aloud, her voice flattening with each line, the way a road flattens before a cliff.)*
> **THE SEASON GAZETTE** — *Mrs. Nance Bell, Proprietress*
> *"Miss Hartwell takes up Miss Drummond. Charity, or the dragon's errand? The ton has watched Miss Hartwell parade Lady Agatha Drummond's niece through three drawing rooms and a ballroom, and the ton — which misses nothing and forgives less — asks the question on every lip: does Miss Hartwell love the girl, or does she owe the aunt? The gowns are exquisite (Élise, of course). The girl is — improved. Whether she is improved enough, and whether the improvement is kindness or commerce, remains, like so much this Season, an open ledger."*
> *(Silence. The chocolate cools, untouched. Somewhere below, Honoria is arriving for the post-ball call — Rose can hear her on the stairs, humming, the sound of a girl who danced well last night and knows it. The humming stops at the drawing-room door, which means she has seen their faces.)*
> "An open ledger." — Letitia sets down the paper carefully, as though it might detonate. "Well. At least it did not call her dull. It called the gowns exquisite. It called the girl — improved. It could have been — it could have been so much worse, Rose."
> "It called *me* into question instead." — Rose takes the paper, reads the paragraph again. "*Charity, or the dragon's errand?* — the paper has asked, in print, the exact question Honoria asked in the garden. *Does Miss Hartwell love the girl, or does she owe the aunt?* Nance Bell does not accuse, does not unmask, does not hunt — she judges. Taste, and nothing else. And her judgments, once printed, become the ton's memory."
> *(Rose folds the paper with care — crease to crease, the way Augusta folds lists. The campaign has its verdict: neither kind nor cruel, but exact. Whether it is kindness or commerce is now, officially, an open question — an open ledger, in the one paper the whole ton reads. And ledgers, Rose reflects, have a way of demanding to be balanced.)*
scenes.sting: Miss Hartwell takes up Miss Drummond. Charity, or the dragon's errand? The gowns are exquisite (Élise, of course). The girl is — improved. Whether she is improved enough, and whether the improvement is kindness or commerce, remains, like so much this Season, an open ledger.

scenes.synopsis: ★ CLIFFHANGER — Honoria's whisper. The price, seen by its object. Everything the chapter built converges on one sentence.
scenes.prose:
> *(The drawing room, moments later. Honoria enters — radiant from the ball, the dance danced well, the ton revised, the second country dance a triumph of gliding and reliable partners — and stops when she sees their faces. The Gazette lies folded on the table. The chocolate sits cooling. She has read the paper at home. Of course she has. Everyone has. Her aunt sent it round with her breakfast, underlined.)*
> "You have seen it." — Rose rises.
> "My aunt sent it round with my breakfast. She —" Honoria's voice is steady, which is somehow worse than tears. "She underlined the question. *Charity, or the dragon's errand.* She underlined it twice, the way she underlines everything. The way she underlined —" She stops. "She was pleased, I think. It is the kind of question she likes. The kind with no good answer."
> *(Honoria crosses to the mantel — to the tussie-mussie, violets for modesty, rosemary for remembrance, faded now but still standing — and touches it gently, as though checking that something in the room is still true, as though the flowers might have changed their meanings overnight.)*
> "Rose —" she says, and the stammer is gone — completely gone, burned away — and what replaces it is worse, because it is calm, the calm of a girl who has finally understood something. "They say you only do it because you must."
> *(The sentence lands in the quiet room like a pin dropped on marble — small, bright, ringing. Everything the chapter has built — the calls, the gown, the dance, the garden truths, the decisions in the park and the atelier at dawn — narrows to this single point: the girl knows. Whether Rose told her plainly in the garden, or let her believe it was friendship, or deflected kindly — the ton has told her anyway, in print, underlined twice. The price, seen by its object. The sponsorship, priced in public.)*
> "Honoria —" — Rose
> *(But Honoria is looking at her — not angry, not weeping, just waiting, with the terrible patience of the young — and the chapter ends on the wait: on the question of what, exactly, is owed to a girl who knows she was purchased, and loves her purchaser anyway. The tussie-mussie nods on the mantel. The Gazette lies folded on the table. And Honoria waits.)*
---

scenes.synopsis: Open from Chapter 2's cliffhanger — Honoria's whisper becomes Rose's warrant to go below stairs.
scenes.prose:
> "They say you only do it because you must." — Honoria, and the words had stayed in the carriage all the way home, sitting between them on the squabs like a third passenger, and up the stairs, and into Rose's bedchamber, where they now sat like an uninvited guest who had taken the best chair.
> "Must what?" — Rose
> *(She had asked it too late, in the carriage, and Honoria had only shaken her head and looked out at the rain, which was answer enough. They say. They — the ton, the tea-tables, the girls who had laughed at Honoria's hem last Season and would laugh again this one. They say you only do it because you must. As if kindness were a confession. As if a wardrobe commissioned out of friendship were a debt exposed.)*
> *(All the way home Rose had watched the rain draw lines down the glass and thought about the second leak — Cecilia's words, heard at tea, repeated below stairs before the cups were cold. Above stairs, Augusta was launching Honoria like a ship of the line. Octavia was sitting for her portrait while émigrés gossiped about de Valcourt money over the painter's shoulder. Everybody talked. Nobody heard. That was the whole of it, and the whole of it was intolerable.)*
> "Jenny." — Rose
> "Miss?" — Jenny
> "The plain grey. Not the dove — the ash. The one with no trimming at all." — Rose
> *(Jenny's hands stopped in the middle of laying out the evening things — silk, ribbon, the armour of the drawing room — and Rose watched the girl's face do the small arithmetic of a servant: miss is not going out, miss is going somewhere, miss is going somewhere no silk is required for.)*
> "Miss is not going out?" — Jenny
> "I am going down." — Rose
> "Down, miss?" — Jenny
> "Below stairs. Where the talking happens before it becomes — they say." — Rose
> *(She stood at the window and watched the area steps where the tradesmen came and went like blood through a vein — the butcher's boy, the laundress, the fishmonger with his basket, all of them carrying the town in and the house out. The house ran on people she had never seen. That was the point of them, and it was also the danger of them, and it was also, if she was honest with herself at three in the afternoon with Honoria's whisper still in her ears, the only place left where the truth had not yet been dressed up for company.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ THE DRESSING RITUAL — church/chapel plainness; humility with spine. Full ritual: occasion brief, editorial criterion, 3 directions, ~20 micro-decisions at 5 coins each (~100 coins), story morsels between pins.
scenes.prose:
> *(OCCASION BRIEF, published: A lady goes below stairs to be among servants as a supplicant, not a mistress. The brief is humility with spine — plain as church, but cut well enough that the plainness reads as choice, not poverty. No performance of piety. No costume of the poor. EDITORIAL CRITERION: every decision must answer one question — would this let her be forgotten in a room full of people paid to notice? If the answer is no, it does not go on the body.)*
> **Three directions:**
> — *Mourning severity:* black bombazine, widow's restraint, the plainness of grief — spine as marble. Risk: grief performs too loudly below stairs, where real mourning is common.
> — *Country Quakerish:* ash-grey stuff gown, white cap, the plainness of the meeting-house — warmth inside the severity. Risk: the cap reads as costume on a lady.
> — *Clerical reserve:* dove-grey merino, high collar, the plainness of a clergyman's daughter — dignity without display. Risk: too fine; merino whispers money.
> *(Rose chooses the country Quakerish — the ash-grey stuff, no cap, hair her own. Below stairs, borrowed humility insults; only the real article, cut well, will pass.)*
> **The ritual, 5 coins a pin:**
> 1. The ash-grey stuff gown, untrimmed — *5 coins.* 2. Bodice high to the throat, no fichu — *5 coins.* 3. Long sleeves to the wrist, plain cuffs — *5 coins.* 4. The merino petticoat beneath, undyed — *5 coins.* 5. Hem let down a full inch for the back stairs — *5 coins.* 6. Side seams taken in — not for vanity, for silence; loose cloth rustles — *5 coins.* 7. *(Story morsel: Jenny pins the waist and says, very low, "My mother wore grey like this to chapel, miss. She said the Lord sees the stitching." Rose does not answer, but her throat closes.)* 8. Woollen stockings, undyed — *5 coins.* 9. Half-boots, black kid, the soles softened so they do not strike the stone — *5 coins.* 10. Hair drawn back plain, no ornaments — *5 coins.* 11. No cap — a lady in a cap below stairs is a lady in disguise, and disguise insults — *5 coins.* 12. The plain linen collar, starched once only — *5 coins.* 13. *(Story morsel: Letitia's maxim, unbidden: "Servants forgive a great deal, my dear, except being managed. Never let them catch you managing them." Rose checks her own face in the glass for management, and finds it, and smooths it away.)* 14. A grey wool shawl, fringeless — *5 coins.* 15. No reticule — a lady carrying nothing carries no errand they can read — *5 coins.* 16. Plain gloves, grey kid — *5 coins.* 17. No rouge, no powder — *5 coins.* 18. The wedding-ring finger bare of everything but her mother's thin gold band — owned, no cost, and the jewel shelf is never a ritual step — *5 coins for the fitting of the sleeve over it.* 19. *(Story morsel: Jenny steps back and her eyes shine, and Rose understands that the girl is seeing not a mistress in costume but something she recognises — her mother's chapel grey — and that recognition is either the whole victory or the whole danger.)* 20. A final turn before the glass: forgettability, cut well — *5 coins.* *(Total: ~100 coins. No Crown SKUs touch rituals.)*

ritual.occasionBrief: The brief is humility with spine — plain as church, but cut well enough that the plainness reads as choice, not poverty.

scenes.synopsis: The reveal coda — the plain dress shown worn on Rose, not a dress form; invisibility, cut well, becomes real.
scenes.prose:
> *(The coda: Rose stands before the glass in the ash-grey stuff gown, and the glass gives her back a stranger — no, not a stranger; a version of herself with the varnish off. The dress does not flatter. That is the point. It fits — Jenny's stitching lies flat as water — and in fitting perfectly it refuses to be looked at, which is the hardest thing a well-cut garment can do. Above stairs, every gown she owns is an argument. This one is a withdrawal of all arguments, and she feels the silence of it go through her like cool water.)*
> "Well?" — Rose
> "Miss looks — " — Jenny, and stops.
> "Say it." — Rose
> "Miss looks like somebody it would be a sin to lie to." — Jenny
> *(Rose laughs before she can stop herself, and the laugh cracks the solemnity like an egg, and they are both the better for it — the maid and the mistress, standing in a bedchamber that suddenly feels less like a dressing room and more like a chapel vestry. Then she sobers, because Jenny is right and Jenny does not know how right she is: below stairs, the plain dress is not camouflage. It is a confession. It says: I have come down to your country, and I know it is a country, and I know I am a foreigner in it, and I am asking — not commanding — to be let across the border.)*
> "Jenny. If anyone asks where I am — " — Rose
> "Miss is lying down with a headache." — Jenny, prompt as a conspirator.
> "No." — Rose
> *(She sees the girl's face fall, and is sorry, and is also certain — because the whole of the day's philosophy is in this one refusal. No more managing. No more being managed into alibis. The ash-grey gown was cut for plainness; let the errand be plain too.)*
> "If anyone asks where I am, tell them the truth. I am below stairs. I am tired of being talked about by people I have never thanked." — Rose
> *(The words land in the quiet room like a dropped pin. Jenny curtsies — deeper than usual, and not from training; from something older, something the girl's mother would have recognised. Rose takes up the grey shawl, settles it fringeless over her shoulders, and goes to the back stairs, where the stone is worn in the middle by two hundred years of feet that were never introduced to anybody — and today, for the first time, by hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 2 — the housekeeper shows Rose the hall's order: who hears what, who carries what, who is paid by whom.
scenes.prose:
> *(The back stairs come out at the servants' hall, and the servants' hall at half past three is a parliament in session. The long table, scrubbed white as bone. The upper servants at the high end, the lower at the foot, and every place as fixed as a pew in church. Conversation stops the way a flock of starlings stops — all at once, mid-note. Twenty faces turn. Rose stands in the doorway in ash-grey, and feels every one of those faces decide what she is.)*
> "Mrs. Pye." — Rose
> "Miss Hartwell." — Mrs. Pye
> *(The housekeeper rises — she alone does not stare; she assesses, the way a general assesses weather. Mrs. Pye is fifty-five, iron-grey, apron starched into architecture, and has run this house since Rose was in short coats. Rose has spoken to her perhaps a hundred times, always about linen, and has never once seen her — really seen her — until this moment.)*
> "I have come to learn the house." — Rose
> "The house, miss?" — Mrs. Pye
> "Who hears what. Who carries what. Who is paid by whom." — Rose
> *(A sound goes round the table — not quite a laugh, not quite a gasp. Mrs. Pye looks at Rose for a long moment, and then she does something Rose has never seen her do: she smiles, and the smile is not respectful. It is interested.)*
> "Sit down, miss." — Mrs. Pye
> *(She indicates a place — not at the high end, not at the foot, but a stool by the dresser, the visitor's place, the place for someone who belongs to no table and is therefore, paradoxically, trusted by all of them. Rose sits. The parliament resumes, cautiously, like water closing over a stone — and Rose, perched on her stool with her hands folded, understands that she has been granted something no drawing room ever granted her: a seat with no performance attached.)*
> "Bess, pour for Miss Hartwell. Will, you may finish your story — the one about the fishmonger's boy, and mind your language." — Mrs. Pye
> *(And just like that, Rose is inside the government — not admitted, exactly, but permitted to observe the session. Mrs. Pye leans on the dresser beside her and begins, in a low voice, to name the order of things: who takes the letters up, who takes the gossip down, who is paid by the house and who is paid, quietly, by somebody else.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 3 — the canon line: "The house runs on people, miss. You never saw us. That's the point of us."
scenes.prose:
> "You keep a list, Mrs. Pye." — Rose
> "I keep the house, miss. The house keeps the list." — Mrs. Pye
> "Who hears what, then. Tell me plainly." — Rose
> "Bess hears everything said above stairs before dinner, because she lays the fires and the quality talk as if the grate were deaf. Parrish hears everything after dinner, because the gentlemen drink and the valet stands behind the chair like a piece of furniture, and furniture has ears. The kitchen hears what the tradesmen say at the area door, and the tradesmen hear the whole town." — Mrs. Pye
> "And who carries what?" — Rose
> "Letters go by Will, because he is quick and honest — the two qualities you want in a messenger, and seldom found together. Gossip goes by anybody with a mouth, which is everybody. Money — " — Mrs. Pye
> *(She pauses. Across the hall, the footman called Ned is cleaning plate, and his new boots gleam in the lamplight like a confession.)*
> "Money goes where it is sent, miss. The question is always who sent it." — Mrs. Pye
> "And who is paid by whom?" — Rose
> "By the house, most of us. By the house, and glad of it." — Mrs. Pye
> "Most." — Rose
> "Most." — Mrs. Pye
> *(Rose looks at her — really looks, for the first time in twenty years — and sees not a function but a woman: tired eyes, a mouth that has kept ten thousand secrets, hands that have folded a generation of linen.)*
> "Mrs. Pye. I have lived above you all my life and I never — " — Rose
> "The house runs on people, miss. You never saw us. That's the point of us." — Mrs. Pye
> *(It is not said unkindly. That is the worst of it. It is said the way one states the weather — a fact of the architecture, like the worn step on the back stairs. Rose feels the rebuke go through her like a draught under a door, and she does not resent it.)*
> "Then I am here to see you now. All of you. If you'll have me." — Rose
> "We'll see, miss." — Mrs. Pye
> "That's fair." — Rose
> "It's more than most get." — Mrs. Pye

scenes.synopsis: Texture of the hall as a country — its hierarchy, humor, loyalties, and Christian names.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose stays for the servants' tea, and learns more in an hour than in a Season of drawing rooms. The hall has its own precedence, as rigid as the peerage: Mrs. Pye at the head by right of office; Parrish the valet by right of proximity to power; Mrs. Hollis the cook by right of everyone being afraid of her; then the upper housemaids, the footmen by seniority, the kitchen maids, and Tom the hall-boy at the foot, twelve years old and already learning to be invisible on purpose.)*
> "Miss Hartwell wants to know our Christian names." — Mrs. Pye, dry as toast.
> "I want to know everything. Starting there." — Rose
> *(They tell her, and the telling is a ceremony: Bess. Will. Ned. Parrish — "James, miss, but only my mother calls me that, and she's dead." Mrs. Hollis — "Martha, and you'll call me Mrs. Hollis." Tom, who goes scarlet. Dolly the stillroom maid. Kit the second footman. And the laughter that goes round the table is not the laughter of the ton — it is warmer, quicker, and it has teeth; these people are funny the way people are funny who have nothing to lose by it.)*
> "Tell Miss Hartwell about the vicar's pig." — Will
> "Will." — Mrs. Pye, warning.
> "It's clean, Mrs. Pye, it's only a pig — " — Will
> *(The story is told, and it is very funny, and Rose laughs until her eyes water, and she realises she has not laughed like this — unguarded, unobserved, unjudged — since she cannot remember when. Above stairs, laughter is a performance with an audience. Here it is just laughter. The distinction sits in her chest like swallowed light.)*
> "You love them." — Rose, to Mrs. Pye, very low.
> "They're mine, miss. Every quarrelsome one of them." — Mrs. Pye
> *(And Rose understands, with a clarity that rearranges something in her: this is what a household is. Not the drawing room. Not the Season. This — the long table, the tea going cold, the vicar's pig, the boy asleep at the foot with his head on his arms. She has been living in the attic of her own house, mistaking the roof for the residence.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 4 — the footman paid too well: new boots, no explanation.
scenes.prose:
> *(It is Bess who says it, without meaning to, over the second pot — "Ned's got new boots," she says, "and will you look at the shine on them," and the table goes quiet in the particular way of people who have all noticed the same thing and agreed not to notice it. Rose follows their eyes. Ned, the second footman, twenty-two, pleasant-faced, honest-looking — and shod like a guards officer. Hessians, or near enough to pass. New. Not a scuff on them.)*
> *(Rose knows what footmen are paid. She has signed the wage book — or rather, she has watched Mrs. Pye sign it while she initialled beside it, which is the extent of her acquaintance with the economics of service. A footman does not buy Hessians on his wages. A footman does not buy Hessians, full stop, unless — )*
> "Ned." — Rose, pleasantly. "Fine boots."
> "Thank you, miss." — Ned
> *(Too quick. The thanks comes too quick, and his eyes go to Mrs. Pye, and Mrs. Pye's face does nothing at all, which is itself an answer — the housekeeper knows, and the housekeeper has decided, for now, to know privately.)*
> "A present?" — Rose
> "A lucky turn at cards, miss." — Ned
> *(The hall is very still. Somewhere in the kitchen, a pot lid rattles, and the rattle is deafening. Rose smiles — the drawing-room smile, the one that has ended a hundred conversations — and lets it go, for now. But she has marked it: the boots, the quickness, the glance at Mrs. Pye, the lie about the cards told too smoothly to be a first lie. A footman paid too well. New boots. No explanation — or rather, an explanation that explains nothing, which is the same thing with the varnish on. Below stairs, she is learning, everyone knows everything; the question is never what happened. The question is always who is allowed to say so.)*
> *(Later, in the margin of her mind, she writes it down the way Mrs. Pye would: Ned. Boots. Cards — ? Who pays a footman in footwear, and what did the footman do to earn it?)*

scenes.synopsis: Rose watches the footman more closely — the area steps, a letter, a man waiting.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose does not go back upstairs. That is the first decision, and she makes it without quite making it — she simply stays, and staying becomes the afternoon. She shells peas with Dolly in the stillroom, which Dolly finds hilarious and Rose finds meditative — the small green weight of them, the rhythm, the honest work of hands. She carries a tray as far as the baize door with Bess, and learns that the baize door is a border crossing: on one side, the country of the hall; on the other, the empire of the drawing room, where everyone speaks a second language and no one says what they mean.)*
> *(It is from the stillroom window that she sees it: Ned, sent out with a message for the saddler, taking the long way past the area steps — and at the area steps, a man in a snuff-coloured coat, waiting as if by arrangement. No greeting. No surprise on either face. Ned passes him something — small, white, a folded paper — and the man passes something back. Not paper. Something that winks in the afternoon light. Coin, or — Rose narrows her eyes — no. Too large for coin. Too flat. It winks like leather. Like a bootmaker's token, perhaps. Like payment in kind, the second instalment.)*
> "Dolly." — Rose, keeping her voice level. "Who is the man in the snuff-coloured coat?"
> "Never seen him, miss." — Dolly
> "He was waiting for Ned. By arrangement, I'd say." — Rose
> "Aye." — Dolly, and says nothing more, and shells peas with great concentration, and Rose understands that she has asked a question above her clearance — that Dolly knows something, or suspects something, and has decided that a lady in an ash-grey gown has not yet earned the answer.
> *(That is the second thing Rose learns about the hall: silence is also a currency here, and she has not yet earned enough of it to spend. She watches Ned come back up the area steps, whistling, new boots striking the stone with a confidence that wages never bought. The folded paper is gone. The winking thing is in his pocket. Somebody is paying the second footman of Hartwell House, and paying him well, and whatever he is buying, it is not boots — the boots were only the visible part, the armour. What he is really buying is news. News of her.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE FOOTMAN.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose finds Mrs. Pye in the housekeeper's room, ruling lines in the linen book with the steady hand of a woman who has never mislaid anything in her life — not a sheet, not a servant, not a secret. The room smells of lavender and ruled paper and twenty years of competent mornings. Rose lays it out plainly: the boots, the cards that were not cards, the man in the snuff-coloured coat at the area steps, the folded paper going one way and the payment coming the other. Mrs. Pye listens without lifting her pen. When Rose finishes, the housekeeper blots the page, sets down the pen, and folds her hands — and Rose understands that she has just delivered a report to the only other government in the house, and that the response will be a policy decision.)*
> "What would you have me do, miss?" — Mrs. Pye
> *(And Rose understands that this is the true test — not of Ned, but of her. The hall is watching to see what kind of power she is: the kind that commands, or the kind that — what? The kind that asks? The kind that waits? She thinks of Letitia's maxim: servants forgive a great deal, except being managed. She thinks of the ash-grey gown, cut for plainness. She thinks of Honoria's whisper: they say you only do it because you must. Well. Let them say it. The question is what she will do because she chooses to.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The footman:*
- **Question him directly** — *Boldness+. Mrs. Pye wary; Ned cornered may lie, or may break.* Confront Ned yourself, plainly, and demand the truth about the boots and Cecilia's runner.
- **Watch him longer** — *Patience+. The hall approves of patience; but the paper trail cools.* Say nothing; follow Ned's errands, learn the runner's name and the paper's contents before you move.
- **Tell Mrs. Pye everything and let her handle it** — *Trust+. Mrs. Pye's loyalty deepens; but you cede the investigation to the hall's own justice.* Put it in the housekeeper's hands and abide by what she decides.

scenes.synopsis: The footman decision lands — whichever path, the hall's verdict on Rose begins to form.
scenes.prose:
> *(The choice is made — Rose makes it standing in the housekeeper's room with the smell of lavender and ruled paper around her — and the afternoon rearranges itself around the decision like water around a stone. What follows, she will learn, is the same whichever courtesy she chose: the hall has its own pace, and the hall has decided to let her see a little of it.)*
> *(By supper, Mrs. Pye has had words with Ned — or Rose has, or nobody has and everybody knows; below stairs, these distinctions blur like ink in rain. What is certain is this: Ned comes to the hall for his supper with his eyes red, and he does not look at Rose, and Mrs. Pye carves the mutton with unusual precision, and the talk at the table is unusually careful, the way people talk when something has been decided in the next room and the decision has not yet been announced.)*
> "Miss." — Mrs. Pye, later, in the passage. "A word."
> "Mrs. Pye." — Rose
> "The boy's wages are what they've always been. The boots were not bought with wages." — Mrs. Pye
> "I know." — Rose
> "Cecilia's people pay him for news." — Mrs. Pye
> *(The name lands in the passage like a dropped tray. Rose stares — and then, with the sick clarity of hindsight, sees it all at once: the second leak, Cecilia's words at tea carried below stairs before the cups were cold; Cecilia, dangerous in defeat, who had lost the tea-table and bought herself a window into the kitchen instead.)*
> "Cecilia." — Rose
> "Mrs. Cecilia keeps a runner at the area steps — the fellow you saw, in the snuff-coloured coat. News of you, miss. What you do below stairs. Who you talk to. What you ask about." — Mrs. Pye
> *(Rose stands very still. She had come down to hunt the leak, and all the while she has been the thing being watched — her plain dress, her questions, her ash-grey descent, all of it carried up the area steps in a folded paper to one of Cecilia's runners. Somebody is paying to watch her watch them, and the somebody is not a stranger at all. The game, she understands, has a second board, and the second board is Cecilia's, and she has been playing on it blind.)*
> "Thank you, Mrs. Pye." — Rose
> "Don't thank me yet, miss." — Mrs. Pye

scenes.synopsis: Beat 5 — Henry calls; Horse Guards whispers; the army's money once moved like dispatches. Romance stays slow and honorable.
scenes.prose:
> *(Henry comes at five, as he said he would — no, as he wrote he would; his note arrived by Will, who is quick and honest, and Rose notes the choice of messenger with a new, below-stairs eye. A gentleman who sends his note by the honest footman is a gentleman who has nothing to hide in the sending — or who knows exactly what the hall will make of it. He is shown to the morning room, and he stands when she enters, and for a moment they are simply two people who are glad to see each other, which is rarer than it sounds and more precious than it looks.)*
> "Major." — Rose
> "Miss Hartwell." — Henry
> *(He looks tired — the particular tiredness of a man who has been listening to things he cannot repeat. Horse Guards has that effect; Rose has seen it on officers since she was a girl, the look of carrying sealed orders in the head. He accepts tea. He does not touch it. Below stairs, she has learned today, an untouched cup means something; above stairs, with Henry, she suspects it means only that his mind is elsewhere, on channels and dispatches and old money moving in old ways.)*
> "You asked me once how money moved in the Peninsula." — Henry
> "I asked how dispatches moved." — Rose
> "The same channels." — Henry
> *(He says it simply, and the simplicity is the whole of the intelligence: in wartime, the army's money moved like dispatches — sealed, routed, carried by men whose names never appeared on any manifest. Bills drawn on London paid in Lisbon; gold landed at Corunna that had been promised in Whitehall; debts assigned and reassigned until the original creditor was a rumour. The system was built for speed and secrecy, and systems built for speed and secrecy do not dismantle themselves when the guns stop. They find new cargo.)*
> "And now?" — Rose
> "Now the war is over, and the channels remain, and men who learned to move money like dispatches have not unlearned it." — Henry
> *(He looks at her directly — the honorable look, the one that asks permission before it offers anything, and Rose feels the difference between this and every other offer she has received this week like a change in the weather.)*
> "There are whispers at the Guards. Old money, moving in old ways. I thought you should know — Rackham's debts did not begin with Rackham." — Henry

scenes.synopsis: Henry's whispers deepen — a name surfaces in the orbit (de Valcourt, named only, never appearing); the honorable offer.
scenes.prose:
> "Say it plainly, Henry." — Rose
> *(She uses his Christian name without thinking, and his expression does something complicated — pleasure and alarm in equal measure, the way a man looks when a door he has been knocking on opens suddenly, and he is not sure whether to step through.)*
> "The émigré money." — Henry, low. "You heard it at Octavia's sitting — the painters' gossip about de Valcourt funds moving through London. It is not gossip. Or rather, it is gossip built on a true foundation, the way all lasting gossip is."
> "De Valcourt." — Rose
> *(A name only. A name in Henry's whispers, in Quill's orbit, in the émigré chatter over Octavia's portrait. The man himself never appears, never speaks — he is a direction on a map, not a person in the room. Rose marks that carefully: some figures in this affair are to be pursued; some are only ever to be named. De Valcourt is a name to be named, and no more, until the masquerade.)*
> "His money moved through the dispatch channels. Or money like his. Bills, promises, debts assigned and reassigned until no one remembers the original creditor — and Rackham's debts, Rose, are written in that hand. Not his hand. The system's." — Henry
> "You are telling me my debtor's debts are older than my debtor." — Rose
> "I am telling you that if you follow them up the chain, the chain does not end where you expect." — Henry
> *(He sets down his untouched tea. He does not move closer — honorable men, Rose is learning, show their regard by the distances they keep, and Henry keeps his distance the way other men keep their promises: absolutely.)*
> "I can ask further. At the Guards, quietly. It would not be — it need not touch you. Say the word, and I will ask. Or say nothing, and I will not." — Henry
> *(The offer hangs between them, clean as a drawn line: help, freely given, no price named. Above stairs, everything has a price, and the price is named before the help. Rose is beginning to suspect that is the difference between the two countries — above, the price is named; below, it is understood; and Henry, soldier that he is, stands somehow in both countries at once, names nothing, and means the most of all.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — HENRY'S WHISPERS.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose looks at Henry — at the tired eyes, the untouched tea, the careful distance he keeps — and understands that this is the second test of the day, and the harder one. The footman was a question of method: how to govern a country she had never visited, how to wield power without performing it. This is a question of what she will let the war cost her, and what she will let Henry cost himself. He has offered to ask at Horse Guards, quietly. Quiet questions at Horse Guards are never quiet, and never without cost, and he knows it, and he has offered anyway — which tells her everything about the man and nothing about the price, except that he intends to pay it himself, and not tell her. She thinks of Mrs. Pye's warning about money — the question is always who sent it — and wonders what it would mean to let a man's standing be spent on her behalf without ever seeing the account.)*
> *(She thinks of the ash-grey gown. Humility with spine. She thinks of what it would mean to send a good man into the channels where money moves like dispatches — to spend his standing the way other men spend coin. And she thinks of what it would mean to refuse him: whether refusal is protection or pride, and whether a woman who has spent the day learning to accept help below stairs can refuse it above without being a hypocrite in grey.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — Henry's whispers:*
- **Press for the army connection** — *Boldness+. Henry digs deeper at the Guards; the intelligence sharpens, and so does the risk to him.* Ask him to follow the dispatch-money channels wherever they lead, and accept what it costs.
- **Let him volunteer** — *Trust+. The slow thread holds; he gives what he chooses, when he chooses.* Thank him, name no task, and let whatever he brings come freely or not at all.
- **Keep romance out of the war** — *Resolve+. The line is drawn kindly; the work stays hers alone.* Tell him plainly: she will not spend his standing at the Guards on her debts, whatever they are.

scenes.synopsis: The Henry decision lands — honorable, slow; the thread holds whatever she chose.
scenes.prose:
> *(Whatever Rose decides, Henry receives it the way he receives everything — standing very straight, with the attentive stillness of a man accustomed to orders, and to the weight of them. If she pressed him, he nods once, and something in his face both brightens and grieves — the look of a soldier given a mission he wanted and feared. If she let him volunteer, he bows over her hand a fraction longer than protocol allows, and the extra second says everything the protocol forbids. If she drew the line, he looks — relieved? disappointed? — and then he smiles, and the smile is genuine, and that is somehow the worst and best of it: he respects the line even as he regrets it.)*
> "You are careful with people, Rose." — Henry
> "I am trying to be." — Rose
> "It is rarer than courage." — Henry
> *(He takes his leave — no lingering, no pressing of the moment; honorable men ration their own happiness, Rose thinks, the way soldiers ration everything. At the door he turns, and the tiredness is still in his eyes, and underneath it something steadier — the look of a man who has said what he came to say and will not cheapen it by repeating it.)*
> "Whatever the channels carried, and wherever they lead — you are not alone in following them. Whether you ask it of me or not." — Henry
> *(And then he is gone, and the morning room is very quiet, and Rose stands for a long time looking at the two cups — one drunk, one untouched — and thinks about the difference between the countries again. Above stairs, a man offers help and names a price. Below stairs, Mrs. Pye offers nothing and means everything. And Henry — Henry names no price and means the most of all. The slow thread holds. It holds because neither of them will pull it, and Rose understands, suddenly, that this is what courtship is when it is done honorably: two people refusing, daily, to pull.)*

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the chapel bell; below stairs at evening prayer; humility as atmosphere.
scenes.prose:
> *(At six the chapel bell rings for evening prayer, and below stairs the hall empties in a way that is itself a kind of liturgy — no announcement, no herding; the work simply pauses, the pots are covered, the lamps are trimmed, and they go, the whole household moving as one body. Rose follows, because she is following everything today, and finds herself in the small chapel at the end of the servants' passage, where the family pew sits empty — hers, by right, unoccupied for years — and the servants' benches are full, and the candlelight does the faces the kindness the day has not.)*
> *(The prayers are the same words she has heard all her life, and they are not the same words at all. Said here, without an audience, without the rustle of silk to accompany them, they sound — used. Worn smooth, like the step on the back stairs, like Mrs. Pye's hands. Tom the hall-boy fidgets and is gently stilled by Bess's elbow. Bess mouths the responses a half-beat early, the way girls do who learned them at a mother's knee. Parrish — James, whose mother called him James — stands with his eyes closed and his face unguarded in a way Rose has never seen a gentleman's face unguarded.)*
> *(Mrs. Pye does not pray with her eyes closed. Mrs. Pye prays the way she does everything: watching, counting, keeping. Her lips move. Her eyes rest, once, on Rose in the ash-grey gown at the back of the chapel — and Rose understands, with a small cold clarity, that she is being prayed over, or prayed about, and she cannot tell which, and it does not matter. The prayers rise around her, worn smooth as the stair, and for a moment the two countries are one country, and the country is at prayer. Humility with spine. The spine, she is learning, is not hers alone — the whole house has one, and it has been holding her up all her life without her knowing.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 6 — Letitia's below-stairs diplomacy: the aunt knows every servant's Christian name.
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia finds her in the stillroom afterward, which is to say Letitia knew exactly where she would be, which is to say Letitia has known everything all day — the stool, the tea, the boots, probably the folded paper at the area steps. The aunt surveys the ash-grey gown, the unornamented hair, the peas still under Rose's fingernails, and nods once — the nod of a commander inspecting a successful disguise, or a successful truth.)*
> "Mrs. Pye let you stay for tea." — Letitia
> "She let me sit on a stool by the dresser." — Rose
> "High honour. I was never offered the stool." — Letitia
> *(Rose stares. Letitia — takes a seat on an upturned crate with the ease of a woman who has done it a thousand times, and accepts a cup of small beer from Dolly with thanks, by name, and Rose realises she is watching her aunt's true drawing room. The one upstairs is the performance; this is where Letitia actually governs, and has governed since before Rose was born.)*
> "Dolly, dear, how is your sister's baby?" — Letitia
> "Cutting teeth, ma'am, and screaming like a little demon — " — Dolly
> "Give her my regards and a teething ring. I have one somewhere; Rose will find it." — Letitia
> "I will." — Rose, faintly.
> *(And so it goes, and Rose watches, and learns: Bess's mother's rheumatism — twenty years Letitia has asked after it. Tom's lost tooth — "Show Aunt Letitia, Tom, don't be shy, it's a very fine gap," and the boy beams. Parrish's sister in service in Bath, and whether the position suits. Every servant's Christian name, every servant's circumstance, every servant's small affliction and smaller triumph — Letitia carries the whole hall in her head the way other women carry genealogies, and she spends the currency daily, in small beer and teething rings and remembered teeth.)*
> "How long have you — " — Rose
> "Since before you were born, my dear. Somebody in this family had to govern the country we actually live in." — Letitia

scenes.synopsis: Letitia's lesson — the diplomacy of the hall: feed Cecilia the Rose she wants seen (pays off L2's "feed false words").
scenes.prose:
> "You are wondering why I never told you." — Letitia
> "I am wondering a great many things, Aunt. Begin with Cecilia." — Rose
> *(Letitia sips her small beer — a duchess drinking small beer on a crate, entirely at ease — and Rose sees the calculation happen behind the aunt's eyes: how much to say, how plainly, and whether the girl in the ash-grey gown is ready for the whole of it.)*
> "You cannot command below stairs, Rose. You can only — incline it. The hall is not an army; it is a village. Villages are governed by favours, funerals, and who remembers the baby's name." — Letitia
> "Mrs. Pye told you about Ned." — Rose
> "Mrs. Pye tells me everything, in time. The boy is paid for news of you — and the purse behind the payment is Cecilia's. She has bought herself a runner at your area steps, my dear, the way other women buy a bonnet. Dangerous in defeat, our Cecilia: she lost the tea-table, so she purchased the kitchen." — Letitia
> "Then the question is what she wants with news of me." — Rose
> "The question," Letitia says, with the patience of a woman explaining rain, "is what news you wish her to carry. A watched girl may choose what the watcher sees. That is the whole of diplomacy, below stairs or above: decide what you want carried, and then — be seen doing it."
> *(Rose sits very still. It is the most useful thing anyone has said to her all day, and it rearranges the investigation in her head like furniture: she has been trying to stop the leak. Letitia is suggesting she become the source — deliberately, carefully, feeding Cecilia's runner exactly the Rose she wants Cecilia to see.)*
> "You fed her false words at the tea-table, and it was well managed — I heard the whole of it." — Letitia. "Now finish the work below stairs. Give the runner something to carry: the quiet girl, the dutiful girl, the girl with no secrets worth buying. Let Cecilia pay for news of a Rose who does not exist, and spend her money puzzling over her."
> "You are suggesting I lie to my own servants." — Rose
> "I am suggesting you perform for your enemy, my dear, using the stage your servants have kindly provided. There is a difference. One of them is dishonourable — and it is not the one you think." — Letitia

scenes.synopsis: Rose uses the network — a question asked of Bess, answered for kindness, not coin.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose tries it that same evening, because the day has taught her to move quickly or not at all — the hall respects decision the way the ton respects diamonds. She finds Bess in the linen room, folding sheets with the rhythmic precision of long practice, the air smelling of lavender and clean linen and honest work. Rose does not command. She does not manage — she checks her face for management first, the way the ritual taught her, and smooths it away. She asks, the way Letitia asked about the baby.)*
> "Bess. The tea-tray, the day of Mrs. Cecilia's visit. You carried it." — Rose
> "Yes, miss." — Bess
> "And the talk at tea — about Honoria, about the wardrobe — it was below stairs before the cups were cold. I don't want the name of who carried it. I want to know how it travels. Teach me the road." — Rose
> *(Bess folds. Folds. The sheet snaps into its final square with a sound like a small clean decision, and Bess looks at Rose, and Rose sees the calculation in the girl's eyes — the same calculation she has seen in drawing rooms, only honest here, undisguised by manners: is this lady to be trusted with the map of the country?)*
> "It travels on trays, miss. Somebody hears, somebody tells somebody in the passage, somebody tells the kitchen while the tea's drawing. By supper it's the hall's. By morning it's the tradesmen's. By noon it's the town's." — Bess
> "And can it be — steered?" — Rose
> *(Bess's mouth twitches — the hall's grin, quick, warm, with teeth.)*
> "Mrs. Pye steers it, miss. When she wants. Like a barge." — Bess
> "Thank you, Bess." — Rose
> "Miss." — Bess, and hesitates, the sheet forgotten in her hands. "Your aunt asked after my mother's rheumatism. Twenty year she's asked. You — you asked about the road. That's a good question, miss. Most quality asks who's to blame. You asked how it travels."
> *(It is not loyalty bought. It is something better, and rarer, and Rose walks back up the passage feeling as though she has been given something fragile to carry: the beginning of the hall's trust, extended not to the mistress of the house, but to the girl in the ash-grey gown who asked about the road instead of demanding the destination. Letitia's lesson, already working: decide what you want carried. What she wants carried, she realises, is exactly this — that she asked, and asked plainly.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 7 — ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE PLAIN DRESS. Fashion-selection: 2–3 diegetic options, no coin cost, remembered.
scenes.prose:
> *(That night Rose stands before the glass in the ash-grey gown, and the day rearranges itself behind her eyes like the hall's long table at tea: Mrs. Pye's assessing look. Ned's new boots, winking in the lamplight. Henry's untouched tea, and the careful distance he kept. Letitia on a crate, drinking small beer, governing a village with teething rings. Jenny's words — somebody it would be a sin to lie to. Bess's road, mapped station by station. Cecilia's runner at the area steps, buying news of her with bootmaker's tokens.)*
> *(And underneath it all, the question the plain dress has been asking since morning: what is this garment for? Camouflage? Confession? Performance? Diplomacy? The ritual dressed her for humility with spine — the spine, she has learned, belonging as much to the house as to her. But the philosophy — what the dress means, going forward, when the work below stairs is done — that is tonight's decision, and no coin can buy it, and the house will remember what she chooses, the way the house remembers everything.)*
> *(She lays out, in her mind, the diegetic options — not gowns, but meanings. The ash-grey can be:)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The plain dress:*
- **Embrace invisibility** — *Humility+. The hall opens further; above stairs, she becomes harder to read.* Wear the plain dress as a discipline — be forgotten on purpose, let the ton's eyes slide off, do the work unseen. (Diegetic: the ash-grey, worn daily, no ornaments ever.)
- **Keep one fine thing** — *Spine+. A signal to those who know: the plainness is choice, not poverty.* Keep a single owned piece against the plainness — her mother's thin gold band worn openly, or one good shawl — so the hall and the ton alike read intention, not eclipse. (Diegetic: the ash-grey, plus one owned jewel or fine thing, never bought for the purpose.)
- **Refuse the performance** — *Honesty+. No costume, even a virtuous one; the risk is being fully seen.* Put the plain dress aside when the work is done — wear it below stairs as courtesy, but refuse to make humility a uniform. Above stairs, be Rose Hartwell, undisguised. (Diegetic: the ash-grey retired to its peg; her own clothes, her own face.)
