fashionChoices.label: Keep one fine thing
fashionChoices.detail: *Spine+. A signal to those who know: the plainness is choice, not poverty.* Keep a single owned piece against the plainness — her mother's thin gold band worn openly, or one good shawl — so the hall and the ton alike read intention, not eclipse. (Diegetic: the ash-grey, plus one owned jewel or fine thing, never bought for the purpose.)

fashionChoices.label: Refuse the performance
fashionChoices.detail: *Honesty+. No costume, even a virtuous one; the risk is being fully seen.* Put the plain dress aside when the work is done — wear it below stairs as courtesy, but refuse to make humility a uniform. Above stairs, be Rose Hartwell, undisguised. (Diegetic: the ash-grey retired to its peg; her own clothes, her own face.)

scenes.synopsis: The plain-dress philosophy lands — a servant's judgment on what Rose chose.
scenes.prose:
> *(Whatever Rose decides in the night, the morning makes it real — and it is Jenny, laying out the day's clothes with the care of a priest preparing vestments, who gives the verdict of the hall without knowing she gives it. If Rose reaches for the ash-grey again, Jenny's face does something complicated — pride and worry together, the look of someone watching a friend walk back into a burning house on purpose. If she keeps the one fine thing, Jenny nods once, as if a question has been answered to her satisfaction. If she puts the grey aside, Jenny folds it with unusual care and hangs it on its peg like a flag retired, not discarded — honourably discharged.)*
> "Miss." — Jenny
> "Yes, Jenny." — Rose
> "Below stairs — they're saying — " — Jenny, and stops, and starts again, and Rose recognises the particular hesitation of a servant deciding how much of the hall's talk may travel upstairs. "They're saying Miss Hartwell came down yesterday. Really came down. Not visiting. Came."
> "And what do they say about that?" — Rose
> "Bess says — " Jenny drops her voice, though they are alone. "Bess says the grey suited you, miss. Not pretty. True."
> *(Not pretty. True. Rose turns the words over like coins from a foreign country — and finds them better currency than any compliment the ton ever paid her. Above stairs, she has been called beautiful, elegant, striking, all the adjectives of the performance, all of them spent by noon. Below stairs, in a gown with no trimming at all, she has been called true — and the word does not spend. It keeps.)*
> *(She thinks of Cecilia's runner, buying news of her at the area steps, and wonders what he carried home last night: the grey gown, the stool by the dresser, the peas under her fingernails. Let him carry it. Let Cecilia pay for the truth of yesterday — it is the last free sample she will get.)*
> "Tell Bess I said thank you." — Rose
> "I will, miss." — Jenny, and curtsies, and there is something new in the curtsy — not deference. Allegiance. The hall's provisional trust, extended one servant at a time, and Rose receives it the way she has learned to receive everything below stairs: plainly, without performance, as a debt to be honoured.

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the stillroom; a tussie-mussie being made; the S2 floriography thread seeded lightly.
scenes.prose:
> *(Mid-morning, Rose escapes the accounts desk — Rackham's ledgers will keep; they have kept for years, which is the trouble with them — and finds Dolly in the stillroom, surrounded by the sharp green smell of herbs and rosewater, making tussie-mussies for the drawing-room vases. Small tight nosegays, each flower chosen, each stem stripped, each one a sentence in a language Rose is only beginning to learn. Dolly works with the absorption of an artist, tongue caught between her teeth, and Rose watches her hands — quick, sure, kind to the stems.)*
> "What do they say, the flowers?" — Rose
> "Say, miss?" — Dolly
> "In the language. Every flower's a word, isn't it? My aunt says so — she says a lady who can't read a nosegay is illiterate in the only literature that matters." — Rose
> *(Dolly considers this with great seriousness, weighing the claim the way she weighs stems, and then she holds up a stem — a rose stem, and every thorn stripped clean off it, the bark pale where the thorns were, neat as a secret.)*
> "This one's stripped, miss. Thornless. Means — " She frowns, consulting her grandmother's wisdom across the years. "My gran said a stripped stem means safe to hold. No prickles. Or — " and she grins, sudden and wicked, the hall's grin, "it means somebody took the prickles off afore you got there, and you'd best wonder who, and why."
> *(She tucks the stripped stem into the tussie-mussie all the same, neat as a secret kept in plain sight, and Rose takes the little nosegay when Dolly offers it — for the morning room, Dolly says — and carries it upstairs with unusual care. A stripped thorn stem. Safe to hold — or disarmed before she arrived. Below stairs, even the flowers are sending messages, and Rose — who spent yesterday learning that the hall's silence is a currency — understands that the stillroom has its own mint.)*
> *(She sets the tussie-mussie where she will see it while she works the ledgers, and every time her eye catches the pale stripped stem, she thinks: who took the prickles off, and why, and was it for her protection or her handling? And was it Cecilia — smoothing the path below stairs so her runner's news would flow clean? Or was it someone else entirely, someone whose kindness she has not yet learned to price?)*

scenes.synopsis: The leak thread — how Cecilia's tea-time words travelled; the tray-road mapped.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose brings the question to Mrs. Pye directly, in the housekeeper's room, with the tussie-mussie on the desk between them like an exhibit. She does not ask for the name of who carried Cecilia's words — she asks, as she asked Bess, for the road.)*
> *(Not a map of the house, but of the talk: tea-table to tray, tray to passage, passage to kitchen, kitchen to area door, area door to the town. Beside each station, a name. Beside some names, a second name — the person who pays them, when it is not the house. Beside Ned's name: Cecilia's runner at the area steps. There it is — the second board, drawn in ink.)*
> "Cecilia's words were heard by the footman at the door — Kit, not Ned; Ned was below. Kit told the passage. The passage told the kitchen. The kitchen told the town." — Mrs. Pye
> "And the second name beside Kit?" — Rose
> "There isn't one. Kit's only wages are the house's. He's a gossip, miss, not a spy. There's a difference, though the town don't see it." — Mrs. Pye
> "And beside Ned — there is one." — Rose
> "Aye, miss. And now you know whose." — Mrs. Pye
> *(Rose studies the map — the little geography of talk — and understands what Letitia meant about steering barges. The road cannot be closed; talk will travel it whatever she does. But it can be — inclined. A word placed at the tea-table will reach the town by noon. A word placed in the kitchen will reach it by supper. The leak is not a hole to be plugged. It is a river to be navigated.)*
> "Mrs. Pye. If I wanted something to reach the town by noon — " — Rose
> "You'd tell me at breakfast, miss." — Mrs. Pye, without looking up.
> "And if I wanted something to reach Cecilia by evening?" — Rose
> *(Mrs. Pye looks up then, and smiles — the interested smile, the professional's smile.)*
> "You'd tell Ned at luncheon, miss. And you'd make it worth his carrying." — Mrs. Pye

scenes.synopsis: The hall's loyalty tested — will Mrs. Pye say whose errand the runner runs?
scenes.prose:
> "The man in the snuff-coloured coat." — Rose
> "Miss." — Mrs. Pye, warning.
> "I am not asking you to betray the boy. I am asking you to tell me who is buying my footsteps — and what they are buying them for." — Rose
> *(Mrs. Pye sets down her pen. The housekeeper's room is very quiet — the ticking of the clock, the smell of lavender, the weight of twenty years of service pressing on the air between them.)*
> "I don't know his Christian name, miss. That's the truth, and I'll swear it on the Book. He comes to the area steps, Tuesdays and Fridays, regular as the laundry. He pays Ned for news of you — what you do below stairs, who you talk to, what you ask about. And I know whose errand he runs, because there's only one purse in this town that buys news of young ladies by the footman-load." — Mrs. Pye
> "Cecilia's." — Rose
> "One of Mrs. Cecilia's runners, miss. The thin fellow. She keeps two or three of them about the town, the way other ladies keep lapdogs — only hers fetch news instead of slippers." — Mrs. Pye
> *(Rose feels the ground shift — not under her feet, but under the whole investigation. She has been hunting a villain below stairs, and found only a frightened boy in armour, paid in boots by a woman she already knows. Cecilia. Dangerous in defeat. And the question that rises in her now is not who pays the runner — she knows that — but what Cecilia is buying below-stairs news for. What does she want with the stool by the dresser, the peas under the fingernails, the ash-grey gown? What is the use of a lady's footsteps to a woman who has already lost the tea-table?)*
> "Tell Ned — " Rose starts.
> "No, miss." — Mrs. Pye, firmly. "You'll not use me as your messenger, and you'll not frighten the boy further. If you want him, you come to the hall and you ask him yourself, plain, the way you asked Bess about the road. That's the price of this country. Everything plain. Everything face to face."
> *(It is an order — given by a housekeeper to her mistress — and Rose takes it as one, and something in her stands straighter for it. And underneath the order, another question is forming, the one she will carry to the ledgers tonight: Cecilia buys the news — but who buys Cecilia? Is there a deeper purse behind the runner's purse?)*
> "Plain, and face to face." — Rose
> "It's the only government we've got, miss." — Mrs. Pye

scenes.synopsis: Merge-board texture — the standing order queue; orders always waiting; the free-income engine.
scenes.prose:
> *(Between the hall and the ledgers, Rose stops at the atelier board — Élise's commission wall, where the Season's work stands in its ordered rows like regiments on parade. This is the other government she is learning to read: not people, but orders. Honoria's wardrobe stands at the head of the queue — bodices, skirts, trimmings, each piece a mergeable component waiting its turn, each commission a small engine of income that ticks over whether Rose watches it or not. The board does not care about Cecilia's runners or Drummond's letters. The board cares about stitching.)*
> *(The board is never empty. That is the standing rule of it: orders always waiting. A hem to be finished here, a flounce to be matched there, a gown advancing one stage toward completion while Rose was shelling peas in the stillroom. The free-income engine — quiet, patient, indifferent to drama. While she hunted leaks below stairs and followed debts up the chain, the queue worked: Honoria's grey silk bodice merged to its next stage, the silk taking the light like water; two small commissions — a reticule, a fichu — completed and paid out their coins into the purse, unasked, unhurried, the way the hall's trust accrues.)*
> *(Rose touches the edge of the board — Honoria's name at the top, in Élise's neat hand — and thinks of Honoria's whisper: they say you only do it because you must. Well. Let them say it. The board does not care what they say. The board only cares that the work is good and the queue keeps moving. There is a lesson in that, and Rose — who has spent the day learning to read governments — reads it plainly: build the engine, keep it fed, and let the talk travel its own road. The coins will come whether the ton approves or not, and whether Cecilia's runner carries home news of bodices or boots.)*
> *(She collects the completed payouts — small, steady, hers, no one's purse behind them — and returns to the ledgers with the purse a little heavier and her mind a little clearer. Free income. Standing orders. The quietest power in the house, and the only one nobody is trying to buy.)*

scenes.synopsis: The Money thread — Rackham's debts followed up the chain; the chain does not end where expected.
scenes.prose:
> *(The ledgers are waiting where she left them, and Rackham's debts are waiting in the ledgers, and they are — Rose sees it now with her below-stairs eye — exactly like the map Mrs. Pye drew of the talk: a road with stations, and at each station a name, and beside some names a second name, the person who pays them when it is not the house. Rackham owes the tailor. The tailor owes the cloth merchant. The cloth merchant owes — she follows the chain upward, entry by entry, and the entries grow older as she climbs, and stranger: bills assigned, debts reassigned, promises made in one city and payable in another, signatures that are not signatures but relay points.)*
> "Older than Rackham." — Rose, aloud, to the empty study.
> *(Henry's words come back to her: if you follow them up the chain, the chain does not end where you expect. He was right. The debts do not terminate in a creditor; they terminate in a system — the dispatch channels, the wartime machinery of moving money invisibly, still running in peacetime with new cargo. Rackham is not the source of the debt. Rackham is a station on the road, the way Kit is a station on the road of talk: a gossip, not a spy. A debtor, not a villain. The villains in this affair are never where the debts are; they are where the payments come from.)*
> *(She rules a line under the last entry and writes, in her clearest hand — the hand Quill taught her, facts first, conclusions last, no adjectives: CECILIA'S RUNNER — PAID IN BOOTS. WHAT IS SHE BUYING NEWS OF ME FOR? — and under it, the deeper question, the one she is not ready to ask aloud: IS DRUMMOND THE DEEPER PURSE? The name sits on the page like a stone in a shoe. Cecilia buys the runner; but who buys Cecilia? A woman who purchases footmen's loyalty by the pair of boots — is she spending her own money, or someone else's? And if someone else's, whose?)*
> *(Season Two is called The Money, and the money, she is learning, is never about money. It is about who is allowed to move it, and who watches it move, and what they charge for the watching — and whether the watcher at the area steps is himself being watched, by a purse deeper than Cecilia's.)*

scenes.synopsis: Drummond's price — sly, never overt; what this chapter's payment costs her.
scenes.prose:
> *(The letter comes with the afternoon post, on heavy paper, in a hand Rose does not know — but she knows the mind behind it the way one knows a signature without having seen it. Drummond does not threaten. Drummond does not demand. Drummond — proposes. That is his genius, and his slyness: everything he wants arrives shaped like an opportunity, gift-wrapped in reasonableness, and by the time you understand what it cost, you have already said thank you.)*
> *(The proposal is simple, which is how you know it is not simple at all. He will take up one of Rackham's assigned debts — the cloth merchant's, the oldest and ugliest, the one with the most stations on its road — and settle it quietly, no scandal, no town talk, no noon gossip on the tray-road. In exchange, he asks — not money. He never asks for money; money is beneath the transaction, the way the foundation is beneath the house. He asks for access: a standing invitation to the information that passes through Hartwell House. The talk. The road Mrs. Pye mapped. He wants, in effect, to rent a room in the servants' hall — to be told, politely and promptly, what the town will know by noon anyway.)*
> "He wants to buy the river." — Rose
> *(She reads it twice. There is no menace in it — that is the menace. A villain who threatened could be refused with spirit, could be met plain and face to face. Drummond only ever offers, and the offers are always reasonable, and the reasonableness is the trap: each acceptance moves one more piece of her house into his hands, and none of them looks like a piece until it is gone. And now she wonders — with the ledger's question still wet on the page — whether Cecilia's runner is one of his pieces already. Whether the deeper purse behind the boots is the same hand that writes these reasonable letters.)*
> *(She does not answer today. She folds the letter and puts it in the drawer with the ledgers, and the drawer clicks shut like a mouth closing. Drummond's price, this chapter: not coin, but current — the flow of talk itself. And Rose, who has spent the day learning the value of the river, understands exactly what he is asking, and exactly what it would cost, and that understanding is itself a kind of payment — the first instalment, made without signing anything.)*

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the stripped thorn stem carried forward; floriography as quiet warning.
scenes.prose:
> *(That evening Rose takes the tussie-mussie from the morning room and sets it on her dressing table, and she looks at the stripped rose stem for a long time — the pale bark where the thorns were, neat as a secret, Dolly's grandmother's wisdom made visible. Safe to hold — or somebody took the prickles off before you got there, and you'd best wonder who, and why.)*
> *(She thinks of Ned's boots — armour for a footman, paid for by Cecilia's purse. She thinks of Drummond's letter — reasonable as a drawn knife in a velvet sheath, and the question underneath it: is his the deeper purse behind the runner's boots? She thinks of Cecilia's runner at the area steps, buying news of her by the folded paper, and she wonders: is she the rose, or the hand reaching for it? Has someone been stripping the thorns off her path — smoothing her way below stairs, opening the hall's doors, letting her sit on the stool and learn the road — and if so, who, and what do they want her to hold?)*
> *(Mrs. Pye let her sit on the stool. Bess told her the road. Letitia taught her the diplomacy. All of it freely given — or all of it placed, carefully, where she would find it, the way Dolly placed the stripped stem in the nosegay. Below stairs, Rose is learning, nothing is only what it seems; kindness and strategy wear the same ash-grey gown. And Cecilia — Cecilia buys news of her daily. What does a woman do with a lady's footsteps, purchased at the area steps? File them? Sell them? Or simply — hold them, the way one holds a stripped stem, waiting to see what it becomes?)*
> *(She touches the stripped stem with one fingertip. No prickles. Safe to hold. She does not feel safe. She feels — handled. And the difference between those two things is the whole of the game, and the whole of the question she wrote in the ledger: what is Cecilia buying, and who is buying Cecilia?)*
> *(She leaves the tussie-mussie where it is. A reminder. A question without a question mark.)*

scenes.synopsis: Dialogue-heavy — the moral cost of invisibility; being unseen vs. being unknown.
scenes.prose:
> "Jenny." — Rose
> "Miss?" — Jenny
> "When you wear the grey — when I wear it — do you think it dishonest? To be forgotten on purpose?" — Rose
> *(Jenny considers this with the gravity of a theologian, folding Rose's stockings into perfect squares — the small, exact work of hands that have learned patience the way other people learn languages.)*
> "Miss, I am forgotten on purpose every day. It's my trade." — Jenny
> "And is it dishonest?" — Rose
> "It's — " Jenny hesitates, the stockings still in her hands. "It's not dishonest, miss. It's only — it's lonely. Being unseen is a fine thing when you're choosing it. It's a different thing when it's chosen for you. I think — " She looks up, and her eyes are older than her twenty years. "I think the grey is honest if you take it off again. If you wear it for ever, miss, then it's not a dress. It's a disappearance."
> *(Rose sits very still. Out of the mouth of her maid — twenty years old, folding stockings — comes the truest thing anyone has said about the plain dress, truer than the ritual's criterion, truer than Letitia's diplomacy: invisibility is a tool, not a home. Use it, and put it down. The danger was never being seen. The danger was getting comfortable in the dark, the way Cecilia's runner is comfortable in the shadows of the area steps — unseen by choice, unknown by profession.)*
> "You are very wise, Jenny." — Rose
> "I'm very observant, miss. It's my trade." — Jenny, and grins, and the grin is Dolly's grin, the hall's grin — quick, warm, with teeth.
> *(Rose laughs, and the laugh is the unguarded one, the stillroom one, and she thinks: this is what she came below stairs for. Not the leak. Not the money. Not even Cecilia's runner and his folded papers. This — a girl who folds stockings telling her the truth about herself, plain and face to face, because below stairs that is the only government there is. And she thinks of what she will do tomorrow — turn the watcher into the messenger, feed Cecilia the Rose she wants seen — and understands that Jenny has just given her the rule for it: perform, but come home. Wear the grey, but take it off again.)*

scenes.synopsis: The footman thread resolves — Rose faces Ned plainly, per Mrs. Pye's order; the countermove.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose goes to the hall the next morning — plain, face to face, as ordered — and asks for Ned, and Ned comes, white to the lips, and the hall goes quiet in the particular way of people witnessing an execution or a pardon. The boy's new boots are dull this morning, unpolished, as if he tried to make them less visible and only succeeded in making them sad. Rose looks at him in his armour, and she does what Mrs. Pye told her to do, and what Jenny taught her without meaning to, and what the ash-grey gown was cut for: she is plain.)*
> "Ned. I know about Cecilia's runner." — Rose
> "Miss — I — " — Ned
> "I am not going to dismiss you. I am not going to ask you to stop." — Rose
> *(The hall draws breath. Ned stares — and behind him, Rose sees Bess's hand go to her mouth, and Will look down at his plate, and Mrs. Pye carve nothing at all, because there is no mutton at breakfast, only the stillness of a general watching a manoeuvre she ordered.)*
> "You will go on telling him what you see. Only now — you will tell him what I tell you to tell him." — Rose
> "Miss?" — Ned
> "Letitia's diplomacy, Mrs. Pye's river, Bess's road." — Rose, and almost smiles. "A watched girl may choose what the watcher sees. You will carry my news, Ned — the news I want Cecilia to hear. The quiet girl. The dutiful girl. The girl with no secrets worth buying. And in exchange — " She looks at the boots. "In exchange, the house will pay for your boots. Honestly. So you needn't be ashamed of them."
> *(Ned's face does something complicated — shame and relief and something like awe, all at once, the way a boy looks when the execution turns out to be a pardon — and then he does what no footman has ever done in Rose's presence: he laughs, a short cracked sound, and half the hall laughs with him, and Mrs. Pye — Mrs. Pye nods once, slowly, the general accepting a successful manoeuvre.)*
> "Plain, and face to face." — Mrs. Pye, very low.
> "It's the only government we've got." — Rose

scenes.synopsis: Above stairs — Augusta's launch strategy; Honoria's fitting; the atelier as intelligence.
scenes.prose:
> *(Above stairs, the empire continues its business, oblivious: Augusta holds court in the drawing room, launching Honoria with the precision of a naval campaign — this dinner, that ball, the right pew at the right church, the right partner for the first quadrille and the wrong partner nowhere in sight. Honoria sits in the midst of it like a ship being fitted, and Rose — coming up from below with peas still under her fingernails and the hall's allegiance in her pocket and Cecilia's runner turned into her own messenger — sees it all with new eyes.)*
> "Rose! You look — " Augusta surveys the ash-grey, still worn this morning by choice. "Well. Rested, shall we say."
> "I am quite well, ma'am." — Rose
> "Élise comes tomorrow for Honoria's first fitting. You will attend — the atelier is your province, after all." — Augusta
> *(The atelier as intelligence. Rose nods, and thinks: Élise hears everything — the measurements, the fittings, the confidences exchanged in muslin and half-undress. Every wardrobe is a listening post. Augusta is launching Honoria into the ton; Rose will be listening at the fitting, the way Bess listens at the grate. Two campaigns, one house — and Rose, for the first time, is running one of them on purpose.)*
> "Honoria." — Rose, catching the girl's eye across the campaign maps. "Are you — how are you?"
> *(Honoria looks at her — really looks — and something passes between them that is not quite gratitude and not quite alliance, but is warmer than either: recognition. The girl who whispered in the carriage. The girl whose hem was laughed at last Season.)*
> "They say you only do it because you must." — Honoria, very low.
> "Let them say it." — Rose
> "Is it true?" — Honoria
> *(Rose thinks of the stool by the dresser. The vicar's pig. Ned's boots, no longer armour now but only boots, paid for honestly by the house. The stripped thorn stem, pressed between the pages of her prayer book. Cecilia's runner, carrying home the news she chose.)*
> "No." — Rose. "I do it because I choose to. That is the whole difference, and they will never understand it."
> *(Honoria's eyes shine. Above stairs, the launch proceeds. Below stairs, the river runs — and now it runs in the direction Rose inclines it. And Rose stands between the two countries, in ash-grey, belonging — for the first time — to both.)*

scenes.synopsis: Dialogue-heavy — what Letitia really knows about Rackham; a warning about Drummond.
scenes.prose:
> "You knew about the dispatch channels." — Rose
> "I know a great many things, my dear. It is the principal occupation of old ladies — we collect information the way other women collect china, and we break less of it." — Letitia
> "Rackham's debts. The assigned bills. How far up does the chain go?" — Rose
> *(Letitia sets down her embroidery — she has been embroidering all afternoon, which means she has been thinking all afternoon, which means Rose should listen carefully.)*
> "Rackham is a station, as you said. The chain goes up through men who learned their trade in wartime and have not unlearned it — men who move money the way the army moved dispatches: sealed, routed, deniable. Drummond — " She pauses, and the pause is doing work. "Drummond is not the top of the chain, Rose. Drummond is the man the top of the chain employs to be reasonable."
> "Then who is the top?" — Rose
> "That, my dear, is the question you must never ask aloud. Not yet. Ask it of ledgers, ask it of Henry's whispers, ask it of Mrs. Pye's river — but never aloud, and never of Drummond, because the moment he knows you are asking, the price of everything doubles." — Letitia
> "His price." — Rose. "He wants the talk. The road. He wants to rent a room in my servants' hall."
> "Of course he does. Information is the only currency that never debases." — Letitia
> "And Cecilia?" — Rose. "She buys news of me by the footman-load. Is she spending her own money, Aunt — or someone else's?"
> *(Letitia is quiet for a moment — the particular quiet of a woman deciding how much truth the afternoon can bear.)*
> "Cecilia has always had more appetite than income, my dear. It is her defining feature. Whether the appetite is currently being fed by a deeper purse — " She takes up her embroidery again. "That is a question for your ledgers, not for me. But I will say this: a woman who buys footmen's loyalty usually wants something more than gossip. Gossip is cheap. Footmen are expensive."
> *(She takes up her embroidery again — the signal that the audience is ending, and also the signal that the important part is over.)*
> "Rose. You turned her watcher into your messenger. That was well done. But remember: Drummond is sly, never overt. He will not punish you for it. He will simply — adjust the price. Watch for the adjustment. It will arrive shaped like a kindness." — Letitia

scenes.synopsis: Rose at the chapel — prayer as strategy; humility with spine, alone.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose goes to the chapel alone, in the blue hour before dinner — not the servants' service this time, but the empty chapel, the family pew, the silence that belongs to no country, above or below. She does not kneel at first. She stands and looks at the altar, and she thinks about the day: the stool, the boots, the river, the price. The runner at the area steps, turned. Cecilia's purse, mapped. Drummond's letter, unanswered, sitting in the drawer like a loaded pistol wrapped in velvet.)*
> *(Prayer as strategy. It sounds cynical, put that way, and she rejects the cynicism even as she thinks it: no. Prayer as — inventory. An accounting of the soul to match the accounting of the ledgers. What does she have? The hall's cautious trust. Ned's redirected watching — Cecilia's runner, carrying home the Rose she chose. Henry's unasked loyalty. Letitia's counsel, dry as ever and twice as valuable. What does she owe? Drummond's unanswered letter. Rackham's chain, climbing out of sight into the dispatch channels. Honoria's Season, launching like a ship, with Rose required at the fittings. Mrs. Pye's patience, which is not infinite. And underneath it all, the question Jenny asked without asking: will she take the grey off again? Invisibility is a tool, not a home — and she must remember to come home.)*
> *(She kneels. The prayers are the worn-smooth ones, the servants' words, and she says them without an audience — not even, she realises, herself as audience. Humility with spine. The spine, today, was other people's: Mrs. Pye's, Letitia's, Jenny's, Bess's. Her own contribution was only the humility — the willingness to go down, to be plain, to be taught, to be prayed over or prayed about without knowing which. It was enough. It has to be enough, because it is all she has, and she lays it on the altar like the stripped thorn stem: safe to hold, prickles removed, and she does not know by whose hand — Cecilia's, smoothing her path for her runner's convenience, or the house's, in simple kindness.)*
> "Amen." — Rose, into the silence.
> *(The silence, being a chapel, does not answer. Being Rose, she takes that as permission — and as instruction: go on, plain and face to face, and count the price of every kindness.)*

scenes.synopsis: Texture — the hall at night; the bell ropes; loyalty's quiet shape.
scenes.prose:
> *(After dinner — a quiet dinner, Augusta fatigued by launching, Honoria bright with fittings to come, Letitia watchful over her embroidery — Rose walks the passage to the hall one last time, and finds it in its evening state: the lamps low, the table cleared, the servants at their mending and their letters and their small, private hours. Tom the hall-boy is asleep with his head on the table, and nobody wakes him — the hall's mercy, extended without comment. Bess is writing a letter home, tongue caught between her teeth. Parrish is reading a newspaper — yesterday's, much-folded, the ton's news a day late and twice as true. And Mrs. Pye is darning, because even generals darn.)*
> *(The bell ropes hang in their row by the door — one for every room above stairs, each labelled in Mrs. Pye's neat hand. Rose looks at them and thinks of puppet strings, and then rejects the image: no. Not strings. Reins. The house is not pulled about by its bells; it is guided, gently, by people who know which rope to pull and when, and the art of it is in the gentleness. Above stairs, power shouts. Below stairs, it darns. And somewhere out in the town, Cecilia pulls her own ropes — her runners at the area steps — and Rose wonders, not for the first time today, whose hand is on Cecilia's ropes. Who pulls the puller?)*
> "Miss." — Mrs. Pye, without looking up from her darning. "You're hovering."
> "I am admiring the government." — Rose
> *(Mrs. Pye's mouth twitches — the nearest thing to a laugh Rose has ever got out of her, and Rose counts it among the day's great victories, alongside the stool and the road and the redirected runner.)*
> "Go to bed, miss. The government will keep." — Mrs. Pye
> *(Rose goes. Behind her, the hall settles — the lamps, the mending, the sleeping boy — and she understands that she has been admitted to something rarer than a drawing room: the quiet hour of people who have decided, provisionally, to trust her. Provisionally. Everything below stairs is provisional, and that is what makes it honest. Above stairs, trust is performed; here, it is extended, daily, and can be withdrawn by morning.)*

scenes.synopsis: Rose consolidates the debt chain; the next step names Drummond's door.
scenes.prose:
> *(At her desk, by candlelight, Rose rules the final line under Rackham's chain and writes the summary in her clearest hand — the way Quill taught her, years ago, to write a brief: facts first, conclusions last, no adjectives. The chain: Rackham → tailor → cloth merchant → assigned bills → the dispatch channels → the wartime machinery, still running, with new cargo and old discretion. Stations, not villains. Roads, not holes. And at the top of the road — or near the top, for Letitia says never to ask aloud — the reasonable man who wants to rent a room in her servants' hall.)*
> *(She writes: DRUMMOND — PRICE: THE TALK. Then, under it: COUNTER: CECILIA'S RUNNER REDIRECTED. Then, under that, the question for tomorrow, the one she has carried all day from the area steps to the chapel and back: CECILIA BUYS NEWS OF ME — WHAT FOR? AND DOES DRUMMOND PAY CECILIA? Because the runner at the area steps is himself a station — paid by Cecilia, carrying news upward the way Kit carries gossip. And Cecilia — Cecilia may be a station too, paid by someone, carrying something upward that is not gossip at all. Every road has stations. Every station has a payer. Follow the payments and you find the government — above stairs or below, the rule holds.)*
> *(She sands the page, blots it, and sits back, and feels the peculiar satisfaction of a map completed — not the territory, never the territory, but a map, and a map is a beginning. Season Two is The Money, and she has spent the day learning that money is never the subject. The subject is always the watching: who watches, who is watched, and what the watching costs. She has been watched all day — by Ned, by the hall, by Cecilia's runner, by the ton through the Gazette's distant eye — and she has watched back, plain and face to face, and turned one watcher into her own messenger. The books, for tonight, balance — with a question mark in the margin where the deepest purse should be.)*

scenes.synopsis: Drummond's price sharpened — a sly turn: what he wants isn't money; the adjustment arrives shaped like a kindness.
scenes.prose:
> *(The second letter comes at breakfast — no, not a letter. A kindness. That is what makes Rose set down her chocolate and read it twice: Drummond has settled the cloth merchant's debt. Paid it. In full. No conditions named, no price stated — only a short note, in the unknown hand, expressing the hope that Miss Hartwell will remember that old debts, like old friends, are best settled quietly.)*
> *(Letitia's warning comes back to her word for word: he will not punish you for it. He will simply adjust the price. It will arrive shaped like a kindness. Well. Here is the kindness: the ugliest station on Rackham's road, paved over smooth. The chain shortened. The town spared a scandal. And the cost — unstated, unstatable — sitting in Rose's chest like a swallowed stone: now she owes him. Not coin. Gratitude. Obligation. The currencies that never appear in ledgers and always come due, with interest compounded in sleeplessness.)*
> *(And underneath the gratitude, the ledger's question, sharper now: is this the deeper purse? Is Drummond the hand behind Cecilia's runner — the reason a woman of Cecilia's income can afford footmen's loyalty by the pair of boots? Or is the kindness merely what it claims to be, and Cecilia merely what she claims to be — a defeated woman buying news out of spite? Rose does not know. That is the nature of sly men: the kindness and the strategy wear the same reasonable face, the way kindness and strategy wore the same ash-grey gown below stairs.)*
> "Aunt." — Rose, finding Letitia in the morning room. "He paid it. The cloth merchant. All of it."
> "Of course he did." — Letitia, unsurprised. "You turned his watcher — or Cecilia's watcher, whichever purse was behind the boots. So he has made himself your benefactor. You cannot redirect a benefactor's watching, my dear — it would be ingratitude. That is the adjustment."
> "What do I do?" — Rose
> "You accept — graciously, publicly, with thanks. And you remember, privately, exactly what it cost. That is the whole of dealing with sly men: take the kindness, count the price, and never, ever let them see you counting." — Letitia
> *(Rose folds the note and puts it with the first letter, in the drawer with the ledgers. Two kindnesses. No price named. The most expensive correspondence she has ever received — and the question in the margin, still unanswered: who pays Cecilia?)*

scenes.synopsis: Dialogue-heavy — Rose's accounting: who she owes, what she spent, what invisibility cost. (A dialogue with herself, in the ledger's margins.)
scenes.prose:
> "Let us do the accounts, then." — Rose, aloud, to the empty study.
> *(She takes a fresh page and rules it as Quill taught her — two columns, the way all honest books are kept, debits and credits, no adjectives.)*
> "Owed to me: the hall's provisional trust. Ned's redirected watching — Cecilia's runner, carrying home the Rose I chose. Bess's road. Jenny's truth about the grey. Henry's unasked loyalty — though whether that is owed to me or only offered, I cannot say, and I am afraid to ask, which tells me everything about the state of my heart." — Rose
> "Owed by me: Drummond's kindness, price unstated — two letters, one debt settled, gratitude compounding daily. Rackham's chain, shortened by one station and lengthened in obligation. Honoria's Season — Augusta's campaign, Élise's fittings, my attendance required, and Honoria's trust, which I must not break. Mrs. Pye's patience, which is not infinite, and which I have spent freely today. And — " She hesitates, pen hovering. "And the truth, to several people, about several things. Debts of candour. Those come due fastest, and I am overdrawn."
> *(She totals neither column — some books do not balance by candlelight — and instead she writes, in the margin, the day's true ledger, the one no accountant would accept: SPENT: one day of invisibility. GAINED: a country. COST: the comfort of being unseen without being unknown — Jenny saw to that, and Cecilia's runner saw to the rest. The grey is a tool, not a home, and she must remember to take it off.)*
> "And tomorrow?" — Rose
> *(Tomorrow: Élise's fitting. Honoria's campaign. Cecilia's purpose in buying her footsteps, still unpriced. Drummond's kindness, still unpriced — and the question beneath them both, the deepest purse: who pays Cecilia, and what are they buying? The river, running — in the direction she inclines it, for now. She closes the book, and the clasp clicks like Mrs. Pye's drawer — like a mouth closing on a secret, or opening on a decision.)*
> "Tomorrow we go on." — Rose

scenes.synopsis: Below stairs settles for the night — Rose unseen among them; the hall has accepted her.
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose goes down once more before bed — not to investigate, not to question, just to — be there, which is itself a new thing for her to want. The wanting is the change: yesterday she would have called it idleness. Today she calls it government. The hall is nearly empty: the lamps out, the table scrubbed for morning, the bell ropes hanging in their patient row, only Mrs. Pye left, locking the plate cupboard with the big key she wears at her waist like a sidearm.)*
> "Miss." — Mrs. Pye
> "Mrs. Pye." — Rose
> *(They stand for a moment in the lamplight, mistress and housekeeper, and the distance between those two words has narrowed today to something passable — not closed, never closed, but passable, like a road after rain. Rose thinks of the morning: the stool by the dresser, the visitor's place. She thinks of the passage: Cecilia's people pay him for news. She thinks of the hall at breakfast: the runner turned, the messenger redirected.)*
> "You did well with the boy." — Mrs. Pye
> "You ordered it. Plain, and face to face." — Rose
> "I ordered the manner, miss. The mercy was your own." — Mrs. Pye
> *(It is the closest thing to praise Rose has received below stairs, and she receives it the way she has learned to receive everything today: plainly, without performance, as a fact to be kept like a receipt. Mercy. She had not thought of it as mercy — she had thought of it as strategy, Letitia's diplomacy, the countermove. But Mrs. Pye is right, and Mrs. Pye is always right about the hall: it was mercy, and the hall knows the difference between mercy and manoeuvre even when the mistress does not.)*
> "Goodnight, Mrs. Pye." — Rose
> "Goodnight, miss." — Mrs. Pye
> *(Rose climbs the back stairs — the worn step in the middle, two hundred years of feet — and she is not followed, not watched, not reported; or if she is, it is by her own people now, on her own errand, carrying the news she chose. The house runs on people. She saw them today. That was the point of her. And somewhere above, in the drawing room, the ton is saying whatever it says about her quiet week — hiding, or hatching — and for the first time, Rose does not mind not knowing. Let them say it. She has a country now — and a messenger at the area steps, carrying her chosen truths to Cecilia by evening.)*

scenes.synopsis: Texture — final below-stairs image; the stripped thorn stem pressed in her prayer book.
scenes.prose:
> *(In her bedchamber, Rose takes the tussie-mussie apart — carefully, stem by stem, the way Dolly taught her without teaching, each flower laid on the dressing table like evidence — and she presses the stripped rose stem between the pages of her prayer book, where it will dry flat and pale and keep its secret. Safe to hold. Or disarmed before she arrived. She still does not know which, and she is learning to live inside the not-knowing — it is, she suspects, where everyone below stairs lives all the time, and where Cecilia lives too, purchasing certainty by the folded paper because she cannot bear the not-knowing.)*
> *(The rest of the nosegay she sets in water on the dressing table — rosemary for remembrance, heartsease, a sprig of something Dolly called "kiss-me" with a straight face — and the room smells suddenly of the stillroom, of green things and rosewater and honest work. Above stairs, flowers are decoration. Below stairs, they are correspondence. She has received a letter today, in petals, and she cannot quite read it, and that is all right. Some letters are meant to be kept unread until you are ready — like Drummond's, which she has read twice and still not answered.)*
> *(She touches the prayer book — the stem inside, the prickles gone — and thinks of Ned's boots, no longer armour now but only boots, paid for honestly by the house. She thinks of the bell ropes, hanging in their patient row, and of Mrs. Pye's key at her waist. She thinks of Tom asleep on the table, and nobody waking him. The day's last image, and the truest: a tired boy, allowed to sleep, in a house that runs on people. She blows out the candle. The flowers keep their counsel in the dark, and so, she decides, will she — until morning, when the river starts running again and Cecilia's runner comes to collect the news she has chosen for him.)*

scenes.synopsis: Beat 8 — the Gazette sting; the ton dislikes a vacuum.
scenes.prose:
> *(The Gazette arrives with the morning's papers, as it always does — Mrs. Nance Bell's paper, proprietor named on the masthead, judge of taste and narrator of the ton, never a mystery and never to be hunted. Rose opens it over chocolate, and finds herself, as she has found herself all Season, in its elegant, merciless eye — the eye that sees everything and accuses nothing, which is worse than accusation.)*
> *"Miss Hartwell keeps a quiet week. Hiding, or — the ton dislikes a vacuum — hatching?"*
> *(She reads it three times. Hiding, or hatching. The paper does not accuse; it never accuses — it judges, the way a looking-glass judges, by showing. A quiet week. The ash-grey gown. The stool by the dresser. The peas under her fingernails. None of it named, all of it — seen? No. Sensed. The Gazette senses the way hounds scent: a disturbance in the cover, a quiet where there should be noise. Somewhere between the hall and the town, between Cecilia's runner and the tradesmen's gossip, the paper's correspondents picked up the scent of her descent — and Bell, proprietor-only, printed exactly enough to let the ton do the rest.)*
> "Well." — Rose, to the empty morning room. "Hatching, then. Let us call it hatching — and let the ton wonder what, exactly, is under the shell."
> *(She folds the paper and lays it aside, and she does not — will not — wonder who tells Mrs. Bell's correspondents what. The paper is the weather: you dress for it, you do not interrogate it. That is the rule, and she keeps it. But she marks the sting for what it is: the ton has noticed her absence, and nature — ton-nature — abhors the vacuum she has left. Whatever hatches next had better be worth the quiet. She thinks of the ledgers, the river, Ned's redirected watching, Drummond's kindness, Cecilia's unanswered question. Oh, it will be worth it. One way or another, it will be worth it.)*
scenes.sting: Miss Hartwell keeps a quiet week. Hiding, or — the ton dislikes a vacuum — hatching?

scenes.synopsis: Beat 9 — Quill's note: "Come. Not to the office. To the chapel."
scenes.prose:
> *(The note comes at noon — not by post, not by Will, who is quick and honest, but by a boy Rose has never seen, who puts it into her hand in the hall and vanishes before she can tip him. No seal. No direction. Five words, in Quill's clerkly hand — the hand that taught her to rule a ledger, years ago, facts first, conclusions last, no adjectives.)*
> *"Come. Not to the office. To the chapel."*
> *(Rose stands in the hall with the note in her hand, and the house goes very quiet around her — or she goes very quiet inside the house; it amounts to the same. Quill does not summon. Quill requests, by letter, in office hours, with an appointment, and the appointment is kept to the minute. Quill does not write five words and send them by an unknown boy. And Quill — never, in all the years she has known him — names the chapel. The office is his country: ledgers, facts, conclusions. The chapel is — what? Sanctuary? Confession? Secrets too heavy for desks?)*
> *(The chapel. Where she knelt last night, alone, and laid the day on the altar like a stripped thorn stem. Where the servants pray with their eyes open or closed, and Mrs. Pye keeps count, and where she herself was prayed over or prayed about without knowing which. Not the office — not the place of Rackham's chain and Drummond's price and Cecilia's runner. The chapel. The place where the two countries meet and neither governs.)*
> *(She folds the note and puts it in her pocket, next to nothing — no, next to everything: the day, the hall, the river, the price, the question in the ledger's margin about who pays Cecilia. Her heart is beating like a drum at a review, and she tells it, firmly, to behave like a soldier's.)*
> "Jenny." — Rose, very calm. "The grey."
> *(Whatever waits in the chapel, she will meet it plain, and face to face. It is the only government she has got.)*

scenes.synopsis: Open from Chapter 3's cliffhanger — Quill's note: "Come. Not to the office. To the chapel." Rose goes at once. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:

> (T1 · look closer) *the hand — clerkly, hurried; the boy — unknown, gone; the absence — no seal, no direction.* — remembered: *The irregularity deepens.*
> "Jenny." — Rose, pocketing the note.
> (T2 · tone) *calm — the stillness that frightens Jenny; brisk — already moving; dry — "My solicitor summons me to church, Jenny. Church."* — remembered: *Jenny runs for the carriage.*
> "The grey. The ash-grey — yes, again. If anyone asks where I am, tell them the truth this time too. I am at the chapel. It appears to be the only room in London where my solicitor will speak to me."
> (T3 · stance) *tell the truth — trust is the policy; tell nothing — Jenny invents badly.* — remembered: *The summons is irregular.*
> *(The chapel at the end of the servants' passage, empty at noon — worn wood, dust, wax and old prayer books. Her steps too loud on the stone.)*
> (T4 · remembered micro-decision) *apologize to the empty air — the old reflex; check the impulse — plainness.* — remembered: *She walks the aisle.*
> *(He is already there — Mr. Quill, hat in hands, out of place among the pews: ledgers beached on sanctuary. He does not turn.)*
> (T5 · look closer) *the hat, turning; the funeral stance; the altar, awaiting ruling.* — remembered: *Too heavy for his office.*
> "Quill." — Rose
> "Miss Hartwell." — Quill, and does not move. "Thank you for coming. I apologize for the — irregularity. Of the venue. Of the summons. Of everything, in fact, except the necessity."
> (T6 · tone) *clipped — "Five words, by an unknown boy."; warm — a hand on his sleeve; iron — "You have my attention."* — remembered: *He steadies.*
> "Five words, by an unknown boy. You have my attention, which I believe was the object." — Rose
> (T7 · stance) *the family pew — a statement; the visitors' bench — a client, not a dynasty.* — remembered: *She sits.*
> (T8 · dialogue) *"Say it plainly, Quill."; "Tell me, and do not dress it."; "We are in a chapel. Plainly is the local custom."* — remembered: *He will speak plainly.*
> "Say it plainly, Quill. We are in a chapel. Plainly is the local custom."

scenes.synopsis: Beat B1 — the chapel meeting. Quill's warning: the leak is in his copying room. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> "The leak is in my copying room." — Quill, to the altar, not to her. "Not in your house, Miss Hartwell. Not below stairs, not in your passages, not in any room you govern. In mine. In the room I govern — or," he corrects himself with terrible precision, "in the room I believed I governed."
> (T1 · look closer) *her house, rearranged — the stool, the river, Ned's watching, aimed wrong; his face — arithmetic all night; the altar — the safer audience.* — remembered: *The hunt changes countries.*
> *(Mrs. Pye's maxim: the question is always who sent it. Not her house. His.)*
> (T2 · tone) *"How long have you known?"; "Tell me the rest."; silence — let the chapel ask.* — remembered: *He answers.*
> "How long have you known?" — Rose
> "Suspected — a fortnight. Known — since yesterday morning." — Quill turns at last. "The codicil schedule — the evidence from last Season, the paper that should have reached you before the Assembly and did not. I told myself it was lost in the copying. Paper is lost in copying the way men are lost at sea — often, and always plausibly. But it was not lost, Miss Hartwell. It was taken. In my office. By a hand I pay."
> (T3 · remembered micro-decision) *flinch at "a hand I pay"; stay stone-still; nod, once.* — remembered: *The confession continues.*
> "Which hand?" — Rose
> "Mr. Alder. My copying clerk." — The name falls between the pews like a stone into a well. "Seven years in my employ. Quiet. Diligent. The neatest desk in Lincoln's Inn — I used to praise it, Miss Hartwell. I used to hold it up as an example. A too-neat desk, it turns out, is not a virtue. It is a man with something to hide arranging the evidence of his innocence."
> (T4 · look closer) *the desk, imagined — squared, aligned; the seven years, praised; Quill's hands — the hat held still.* — remembered: *the examination, filed.*
> (T5 · dialogue) *"Why the chapel, Quill?"; "What do you need of me?"; "You should have told me a fortnight ago."* — remembered: *He answers the chapel question.*
> "Why the chapel, Quill?" — Rose
> "Because my office has ears." — Quill, simply. "And this is the one room in London where I am certain it does not."
> (T6 · stance) *accept the commission; name the price — "Then I am your investigator, Quill."; count his cost — a solicitor's capital is trust.* — remembered: *She will watch the office.*
> (T7 · remembered micro-decision) *touch the worn wood; fold her hands; borrow his safer audience, a moment.* — remembered: *The warning is delivered.*
> (T8 · tone) *"Then I will watch your office, Quill."; "Your office is my country now."; "No one will know but us."* — remembered: *He bows — the meeting is made.*

scenes.synopsis: Beat B2 — dialogue-heavy. The intercepted letter: S1's codicil evidence never arrived; it was taken in Quill's office. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> "Tell me about the letter." — Rose
> (T1 · tone) *"Tell me about the letter." — flat, exact; "Tell me everything — from February."; "Start with what was stolen."* — remembered: *The account is the same.*
> "The codicil schedule — the supplementary paper to the March codicil, the one that named the instruments Rackham used to enforce the debts." — Quill has stopped turning his hat; he holds it still now. "It was copied in my office in February. The copy was to go to you by my own hand. It never arrived. I assumed — I told myself — the copying room's ordinary attrition. A clerk misfiles. A bundle goes astray. These things happen, Miss Hartwell. They happen the way rain happens."
> (T2 · look closer) *the Assembly — a hand missing a card; the copying book — the entry without the copy; his voice — very quiet.* — remembered: *the examination, filed.*
> "And now?" — Rose
> "And now I have found the original — filed where no original should be, in a deed box of settled matters, as though it had been put away by someone who wanted it found only by accident." — Quill's voice is very quiet. "And the copy — the copy was never made. The copying book shows the entry, in Alder's hand, neat as everything Alder does. But the copy itself does not exist. An entry without a copy, Miss Hartwell, is not an error. It is a theft with the paperwork done properly."
> (T3 · dialogue) *"Who did he sell it to?"; "What did the schedule name?"; "What do you need me to do?"* — remembered: *He does not know the buyer.*
> "Who did he sell it to?" — Rose
> "I do not know." — Quill, and the admission costs him visibly. "That is why we are in a chapel, Miss Hartwell, and not in my office. In my office I am a solicitor with a clerk and a suspicion. Here — " he looks at the altar — "here I am a man asking his client what to do about a betrayal he cannot prove, in a room where he cannot be overheard arranging the proof."
> (T4 · stance) *"You want me to watch the office."; "Then we arrange the proof together."; "What are my instructions, Quill?"* — remembered: *The commission is the same.*
> "You want me to find it." — Rose
> "I want you," Quill says, "to watch my office. Not my clients — my office. The paper passes through there. The paper always tells the truth, because the paper does not know it is lying."
> (T5 · remembered micro-decision) *recognize the line — from Chapter 1; write it down; repeat it back — "The paper does not know it is lying."* — remembered: *the small thing, done.*
> (T6 · tone) *"I will watch, Quill."; "Your office is my country now."; "No one will know but us."* — remembered: *The chapel empties.*
> (T7 · look closer) *the dust on his shoulders; the side door; the empty pews — silent as paper.* — remembered: *the examination, filed.*
> (T8 · stance) *leave first; let him leave first; walk out together — two conspirators.* — remembered: *The new country is mapped.*

scenes.synopsis: Why the chapel — Quill's fear of his own office; the solicitor's professional ruin, priced. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> "You could dismiss him." — Rose
> (T1 · tone) *"You could dismiss him."; "Quill — why haven't you dismissed him?"; "Sack the clerk and be done."* — remembered: *The answer is the same.*
> "On what?" — Quill's laugh is short and joyless, and it dies between the pews. "On a too-neat desk and a missing copy I cannot prove was stolen? Miss Hartwell, I am a solicitor. My entire capital is the belief that paper in my office is safe. If I dismiss my copying clerk for theft I cannot prove, every client in London will ask what else has walked out of my copying room, and the asking will be the ruin — not the theft. The suspicion, aired, does what the theft only threatened."
> (T2 · look closer) *his capital — trust, once doubted, compounds like debt; the trap — no proof, no unseen inquiry; her debt — he taught her to rule a ledger.* — remembered: *the examination, filed.*
> (T3 · dialogue) *"You need a client to visit."; "You need me in the outer office."; "Thursday. The settlements. Say it."* — remembered: *He nods.*

scenes.synopsis: ★ DRESSING RITUAL — a business call at Quill's office. Dress to be underestimated by clerks. Twenty micro-decisions at 5 coins each; jewels from owned pieces only, never a ritual step; no Crown SKUs. (Turns: 21)
scenes.prose:
> **Occasion brief — A Business Call at Lincoln's Inn**
> *Quill's outer office, Thursday afternoon. Dress to be underestimated: business dress for a young lady who understands nothing and expects to be bored. Every choice is judged on whether it says* nothing to see here *without saying it so loudly it becomes something to see. Fine is fatal; fashionable is suspect; forgettable, cut well, is the art.*
>
> **A. The Grey Mouse** — dove-grey jaconet, plain pelisse, the demure straw; invisibility as policy. Motif: none applied — self-fabric pin-tucks, shadow stitching, the embroidery of absence. Thread: **matching dove silk** (invisible) / **ivory whitework** (the hem's hidden vanity) / **silver** (a whisper).
> **B. The Pretty Client** — jonquil muslin, fashionable spencer, the chip bonnet; pretty enough to be dismissed as decorative. Motif: trailing honeysuckle up the flounce, small and openly pretty. Thread: **rose silk** / **copper** / **polychrome** (blush, lavender, butter).
> **C. The Quiet Businesswoman** — slate merino, severe felt, no ornament; uninteresting, not silly. Motif: restrained oak-leaf at cuff and hem. Thread: **black silk** / **steel** / **silver**.
>
> *(System: commit to a direction — remembered for the office visit. Then the pins begin. Each pin costs 5 coins; no Crown SKUs; jewels from owned pieces only, never a ritual step.)*
>
> (T1 · choice — the direction) *She commits: A, B, or C — the afternoon's thesis, remembered.*
>
> **Pin 1 (T2 · micro-decision) — The gown's ground:** jaconet, muslin, or merino — the fabric that carries the whole dismissal. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 2 (T3 · micro-decision) — The color's depth:** dove, jonquil, or slate — each a different degree of uninteresting. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 3 (T4 · micro-decision) — The neckline:** high and plain; nothing for a clerk to remember. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 4 (T5 · micro-decision) — The sleeve:** long, fitted, no flounce; nothing that moves when you do not. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 5 (T6 · micro-decision) — The bodice's motif and thread:** the direction's embroidery — honeysuckle, oak-leaf, or the honest absence — worked in the chosen thread (gold, silver, copper, ivory whitework, steel, black silk, or polychrome). The motif is the sentence's secret grammar. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 6 (T7 · micro-decision) — The skirt's sweep:** walking length; a lady who will sit, not sweep. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 7 (T8 · micro-decision) — The pelisse or spencer:** plain wool or fashionable cut — the outer layer clerks see first. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 8 (T9 · micro-decision) — The bonnet:** the remembered [F] choice, pinned ready — the advance guard. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 9 (T10 · micro-decision) — The bonnet's ribbon:** grey, rose-pink, or black band — the sentence's punctuation. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 10 (T11 · micro-decision) — The glove's fit:** kid, plain, immaculate; hands that hold embroidery, not evidence. *5 coins.*
>
> *(Story morsel: Jenny pins the sleeve, very low: "Miss looks like a young lady with nothing in her head but the ball, miss." "Then the gown is working," Rose says. "Pray it keeps working till Friday.")*
>
> **Pin 11 (T12 · micro-decision) — The shoe:** low, quiet; the outer office has a stone floor, and heels announce. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 12 (T13 · micro-decision) — The stocking:** plain silk; no clocking to catch a clerk's eye. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 13 (T14 · micro-decision) — The reticule:** small, dark, closed; nothing that glints or suggests papers. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 14 (T15 · micro-decision) — The embroidery:** Letitia's dull piece, hoop and thread — the prop, the cover, the reason to sit still. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 15 (T16 · micro-decision) — The hair:** low chignon, severe; severity reads as dullness to men. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 16 (T17 · micro-decision) — The full accessory set:** tortoiseshell hairpins, invisible; earrings — none, the ears bare; necklace — none, the throat plain; the deliberate absence, pinned as carefully as any jewel. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 17 (T18 · micro-decision) — The scent:** none. A lady on business wears no perfume; perfume is remembered. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 18 (T19 · micro-decision) — The handkerchief:** plain linen; a clerk notices lace. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 19 (T20 · micro-decision) — The posture rehearsal:** Jenny walks Rose the length of the room — the slump of the bored, the embroidery held just so, the eyes lowered at exactly the angle of inattention. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 20 (T21 · micro-decision) — The final mirror:** the whole dismissal, head to heel, judged against the brief's single question — *does it say nothing to see here?* *5 coins.*
>
> *(Story morsel: at Pin 20, Jenny steps back and frowns. "Miss, you look — " "I know, Jenny. That is the point. Tomorrow I am the least interesting woman in Lincoln's Inn.")*
>
> *(System: 20 pins × 5 coins = 100 coins. The completed direction is remembered. Owned jewels may be added freely from the open shelf, never as a step.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — ALDER: confront him now, follow the letter, or lay a trap with a false document. Convergent: the trap is laid — Quill forbids an unproved accusation; the means are hers. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The carriage home. Rose sits with the embroidery in her lap — the dull piece, honestly advanced — and does the arithmetic of the afternoon. Alder: quiet, smooth, too-neat. The blotter's pale corner. The empty pigeonhole. The fresh sand. The deference like varnish. She is certain — the way she was certain about Rackham, the way she is certain about a hem — that the clerk is the leak. Certainty, Quill taught her, is not proof. And proof is the only currency a solicitor's office accepts.)*
> *(Three roads. The destination is fixed — the proof must be taken, in Quill's office, by Quill's rules — but the means are hers to choose. She prices them: confrontation — boldness, the rattling, the risk of accusation curdling to slander; following — patience, the dusk, the letter she cannot intercept; the trap — cunning, the lie, the waiting. Each road ends at the proof, but each walks her through different country.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — ALDER:*
- **Confront him now** — *Boldness+, Alder rattled.* Walk back into the copying room and accuse him to his face — the direct assault. *(Quill will forbid the accusation — an unproved charge is slander, and slander is the office's ruin — but the confrontation itself, the nerve of it, will rattle Alder, and a rattled clerk makes mistakes. The trap becomes necessary anyway; boldness is the price of the proof.)*
- **Follow the letter** — *Patience+, the posting habit learned.* Watch Alder, not the desk — learn when the stolen copies leave, and where they go. *(She cannot intercept the post — but she can learn the habit: the dusk posting, the letter that is not office business. Knowledge is the price of the proof; the trap becomes necessary anyway.)*
- **Lay a trap with a false document** — *Cunning+, Quill's full cooperation.* A decoy — a paper Alder must copy, containing a lie only the leak would carry out of the office. *(The patient hunter's road: the false codicil reference, left where the copying book demands it be copied. When the lie surfaces in the wrong hands, the proof is complete. Cunning is the price of the proof.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: bold, patient, or cunning. The destination was never in doubt. The signature is hers.)*
